#162770. Playing GTA 6 this weekend? Here's 16 spoiler-free tips for your first playthrough

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1797 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

Playing GTA 6 this weekend? Here's 16 spoiler-free tips for your first playthrough

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1797 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's launch weekend for GTA 6 - in case you hadn't noticed - and since I've played the best part of a hundred hours of this thing, I thought it might be useful to share a few pieces of advice from my time with it.
  • It has been revealed that many of these are most applicable for the early game, but there are a few that'll be worth bearing in mind throughout.
  • The below list is spoiler-free, so you can relax if you're anxious about going through the story entirely fresh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's launch weekend for GTA 6 - in case you hadn't noticed - and since I've played the best part of a hundred hours of this thing, I thought it might be useful to share a few pieces of advice from my time with it.

It has been revealed that many of these are most applicable for the early game, but there are a few that'll be worth bearing in mind throughout. After last night's driving around I would also maybe add in a quick bonus one, come to think of it: watch out for cyclists making last-minute left turns. Or don't, actually. Half of this lot deserve it….

The below list is spoiler-free, so you can relax if you're anxious about going through the story entirely fresh. Though naturally I do explain the way some parts of this game work, taking away some of the sense of discovery. You can take my word for it that there's plenty more to discover beyond this though, so worry not.

If you'd like even more help navigating Leonida, then check out our wonderful guide team's GTA 6 walkthrough.

Industry observers note that the number one thing I'd tell people to do in GTA 6 is to create lots of save files and, as you progress and start needing to overwrite them, to try to keep a roughly even spread of files through each chapter. There are various reasons for this - for one, while the game autosaves, it doesn't seem to do that successfully if you suddenly lose power to the console or witness a rare game crash, so it'll preserve your progress. More than that: GTA's story and missions are surprisingly, perhaps mysteriously reactive. Quite a lot can differ, and so being able to go back and make different choices, or play the game differently, will be something 'future you' likely appreciates.

Industry observers note that in the very early game you won't have access to a bank account, but once you do: you should put every bit of cash you have in there as soon as you can. Cash is lost on death or arrest - which can happen quite often in GTA 6, funnily enough - and there's no real benefit to carrying it around. Just about everything, besides in-game strippers, can be paid for via your BuckMe account directly. And there's a relatively low $20,000 limit you really don't want to hit in the middle of raiding a gang hideout, either.

GTA 6 has a luxurious range of customisation settings, from hiding notifications about your relationship to reinstating the old 'tap to sprint' control scheme. The accessibility settings - while crucially I'm not an expert - seem considerable. And there are somewhat disguised difficult settings here around enemy damage taken and encounters with the police.

Fairly early in the game you'll gain access to the Scooter Bros. App, which lets you repair or summon your owned vehicles at will. Crucially, there's also an option to pay a one-off fee to unlock three free uses of the app per day. At $12,000, in the early game this is a lot of dosh, but once you rack up that kind of money after advancing through the game a little, it's well worth the initial cost. The sooner you unlock it, the more value it provides over time on a cost-per-use basis. And trust me when I say: as the game's intensity ramps up, you will probably find yourself needing to repair and recover your vehicles quite often. (Also, in Chapter 1, before you get access to the app, you can access the same service by going to your phone's contacts and calling Joey - handy!).

Rockstar has somewhat disincentivised it by adding a cost and putting it in your phone's apps rather than the main map screen, but you can fast travel around Leonida if you ever want or need to. This is done via the RideMe Uber-like app. It's not cheap - you'll need to pay both the fee for the journey and an additional $100 to skip that journey and instantly arrive at your destination, but in certain scenarios it might prove useful. To skip the journey, hold L2/LT once in the cab, and then hold down Triangle/Y when the option is shown. However….

According to recent reports, while it's possible to journey-skip your way around this world, having tested that first hand I'd advise against it. It might be obvious, but GTA 6 is genuinely designed around you manually travelling around, typically in the car. If you skip all your commutes between missions or locations, you'll miss out on the game's dozens and dozens of emergent events, which lead to anything from one-off jokes to entire mission chains. The car is also, in a way, kind of the heart of the entire game. Relish the intentional slowness!

Industry observers note that again, avoiding spoilers here, but in the mid game the 'true' loop of GTA 6 gameplay will properly reveal itself, in all the many methods of earning money and the increased emphasis on doing so. You can of course play the game however you like, but having reached the end and looked back from that point, I found that if there was a particular moment to set aside as the time for aimlessly exploring the world, it was from around Chapter 3 onwards. You'll have enough tools to be able to see it at more or less its fullest then, but also won't have missed anything essential by waiting until that point to take your foot off the pedal either.

A handy early-game tip here that even I missed when I was playing, but have since discovered: two islands in the small cluster of them to the south-west of Jason's early game home each house a really useful weapon, in a silenced pistol and a handy shotgun. You'll own these permanently once found, and so they can be incredibly helpful for navigating missions with maximum or minimal violence. Look for shipwrecks on those islands to find them. The pistol is hidden under a little hatch on the deck of a shipwreck on the southernmost point of the south-easternmost island. The shotgun is next to a small wooden wrecked boat around the middle of the northernmost island.

Recent findings suggest that A mechanic I slightly underused at first was the ability to 'save' a given outfit to your car. You can do this either from your car's trunk or from the wardrobe, and it's hugely useful as you start to get into more elaborate scrapes with the police (and also if you just like to role-play a bit and don the right outfit for the right occasion).

There are lots of reasons for this, from the moments of intimacy it affords you with your partner, to the extra buffs you can get from resting. Sleep at home, for instance, and you can then immediately pet your snake (ahem), down a coffee or drink from the fridge, grab an apple and take a shower for a range of buffs across health, stamina, and focus. Each of these will last quite some time, so it's worth the few minutes of time to do them. Eating and drinking regularly also helps you maximise gains in the gym.

According to recent reports, rockstar seems to enjoy the concept of a game within a game, and that's exemplified well by the in-game phone. You can find missions via scrolling Snapmatic, it's in-game social media, or from texting various contacts you pick up as the game progresses. It's worth checking it every now and then just to see if anything interesting - or just funny or absurd - might pop up.

Industry observers note that car trunks, both those belonging to the public and the police, are often well worth a look. Even if you're swiftly nabbing a car for a short-term dash, take a moment to check the boot for anything worthwhile. We've found everything from sellable narcotics to very useful weapons in there. In cop cars, that goes up several notches, too.

In a recent development, A small thing, but in-mission checkpoints are relatively generous in GTA 6. If you really wanted to complete a mission a certain way - undetected or non-violent, say - then don't be afraid to quickly re-load rather than feeling you need to manually load up an earlier save, or give up on your goal entirely. It's also helped me out with a few minor progress-jamming bugs along the way too.

This might seem obvious, but it's worth emphasising for early-game players: it's very, very rare that you actually need to kill anybody in GTA 6. Enemies are fully incapacitated when you see a yellow hit marker over your crosshairs, even if that just comes from blasting away at their toes. If you make a habit of navigating combat this way then that also makes it much easier to recover your 'Professional' criminal status if you ever do decide to go full rampage. Though you can, of course, ultimately play this game however you like. Just be aware there may be consequences, known and unknown, as you go. Also: don't forget to click the right analog stick to aim down sights - it's an easy thing to forget when playing a third-person shooter like this, and not always the best way to operate, but incredibly helpful in select circumstances.

Throughout the game you'll have a 'family savings' goal to hit. As you progress you'll find more ways to earn money much faster, and so it's easy to make up for lost time here if, later on, you decide that actually you do want to think about the future after all. But that grind will be a fair bit less painful if you chip away at the target as you go. As long as you save yourself some fun money - a few hundred in the early game, few thousand in the mid game, and a few tens of thousands late on - then you'll have enough to do key things like buying new garages to register vehicles, or paying to register them themselves.

Throughout your time with GTA 6 you'll encounter moments when you need to make a choice. Interestingly, I noticed at least a few occasions where a scenario changed when I just waited, doing nothing at all. Sometimes that might mean a choice is made for you - so waiting is a risk - but on other occasions fresh options become available. Sometimes they might mean a genuinely different consequence, others they might just lead to characters reacting in a certain kind of way. But it's worth experimenting - your first options aren't always your only ones.

Sources indicate that back before Grand Theft Auto 6 was released, fans eagerly anticipated what Rockstar Games had up their sleeves for different features. One of the most-talked-about features pre-launch was the weather.

With Florida – sorry, Leonida – having some pretty extreme weather shifts, replicating that in-game seemed like a significant task. Rockstar ultimately confirmed that the game would have the “most advanced” weather system to date. That means having torrential rainstorms, hurricanes, and massive waves hitting players.

Industry observers note that the hurricanes, though, don’t appear to unlock until you’ve completed a Strangers and Freaks mission in Lake Leonida with Freddie Gibbs, as he asks you to stay inside his doomsday bunker with him. It doesn’t have any bearing on the story, bar the new weather, which you can choose to deal with.

Veteran storm chaser Reed Timmer – who starred in the TV show Storm Chasers – weighed in on that exact part of the game.

In posting a video of the hurricane effects, Timmer noted that it was “pretty realistic for a hurricane chase,” and added that he had gone “chasing a hurricane.”.

Timmer’s video put a focus on how trees reacted to the intense wind gusts, as well as how much vehicles struggled to deal with it too. “You can really see the wind here,” he said at one point while driving an excavator. “Look at that!”.

Chasing a hurricane in GTA6 #stormchasinThis looks pretty realistic for a hurricane chase pic.twitter.com/SF91VXy2hm.

As noted, you can opt to leave Freddie’s bunker and go out in the upcoming weather, just like Timmer did, or you can ride it out from inside.

Choosing the latter option will frustrate either Jason or Lucia, depending on who you complete the mission with, seeing as you won’t contact them for a few in-game days.

When you complete GTA 6’s story, you will unlock a cheat code that allows you to cycle through weather systems. Activating a cheat will remove your ability to unlock trophies and achievements, but it provides some fun.

Elsewhere, a birdwatching expert has weighed in on GTA 6’s wildlife, seeing as they finally found all the birds in the game.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that thermal Grizzly has just added another product to its list of CPU delidding tools: The Delid-Heat-Mate. After loosening the integrated heat spreader (IHS) with the Delid-Die-Mate, you can use the latest "Heat-Mate" to hold your CPU, baking it in the oven to allow the solder to melt, before the CPU falls away under its own weight. The tool is compatible with AMD AM5 and Intel LGA 1700/1851/1954 sockets and only costs $23.28, unlike the Delid-Die-Mate Heater that costs $127.41 and is only compatible with Intel LGA 1851 socket CPUs.

If you’re serious about chasing lower temperatures and higher performance, delidding your CPU and cooling the die directly is one such way to get there. However, delidding is a scary process, with a real risk of chipping your CPU die or prying off small components under the IHS and turning your CPU into a paperweight. Thermal Grizzly has been at the forefront of making that process easier and less risky with its various delidding tools. The Delid-Die-Mate is the first step in this process, exerting a shear force against the IHS and PCB; you could use the delidding tool alone, but using heat is a less mechanically stressful process.

That’s where the Delid-Heat-Mate comes in; it’s a CNC-machined aluminum tool meant to be used after loosening the IHS with a delidding tool. “The CPU is placed in the fixture with the heat spreader facing down and heated in an oven,” Thermal Grizzly states on the Delid-Heat-Mate’s product page. The heat liquefies the indium solder between the IHS and CPU die, and the IHS simply drops under its own weight.

In a recent development, while you still need to buy a Delid-Die-Mate compatible with the type of CPU you have, the Delid-Heat-Mate is compatible with AMD AM5 and Intel LGA 1700/1851/1954 CPUs. In case you don’t have an oven, Thermal Grizzly does have its Delid-Die-Mate Heater V1, requiring only a 65w USB-C power source — but it’s an add-on for the Delid-Die-Mate V1 for Intel LGA 1851 and costs almost $130.

It has been revealed that the Delid-Heat-Mate is a much simpler, more universal, and more affordable option priced under $24 and doing away with any electronics and active heating elements. Your grandmother might have some questions about why you’re baking a block of metal in her oven, though.

DeepSeek-V4: a million-token context that agents can actually use

📅 24 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1380 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that deepSeek released V4 today.
  • Focusing on long running agentic workloads.
  • This post covers three things: what the architecture does differently to make long-context inference cheap, the agent-specific post-training decisions that compound on top of it, and some takeaways from the paper that help reason about these changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that deepSeek released V4 today. Two MoE checkpoints are on the Hub: DeepSeek-V4-Pro at 1.6T total parameters with 49B active, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 284B total with 13B active. Both have a 1M-token context window. The benchmark numbers are competitive, but not SOTA. It doesn't matter. The real innovation is how DeepSeek v4 is designed for efficient large context length support, and hence as one of the best candidates for agentic tasks.

Focusing on long running agentic workloads. Running a frontier open model as an agent today breaks in predictable ways. The model stops. You reprompt. The trace blows past the context budget, or the KV cache fills the GPU, or tool-call round trips degrade halfway through a long task. V4 is built to fix these known failures, and point the way for the community to follow.

This post covers three things: what the architecture does differently to make long-context inference cheap, the agent-specific post-training decisions that compound on top of it, and some takeaways from the paper that help reason about these changes.

A 1M context window is just capacity, not performance. Whether you can use it depends on the cost of every forward pass at that depth. For an agent running a long tool-use trajectory (a SWE-bench task, a multi-step browse session, a terminal session with hundreds of commands), every tool result is appended to the context, and every subsequent token pays the full attention cost against everything that came before.

Two numbers matter: single-token inference FLOPs and KV cache size. Both grow with sequence length. At 1M tokens, DeepSeek-V4-Pro requires 27% of single-token inference FLOPs compared with DeepSeek-V3.2, so it runs faster on the same hardware. It also uses 10% of the KV cache memory. V4-Flash drops these numbers even further: 10% of the FLOPs and 7% of the KV cache.

If we compare the KV cache memory against a established architecture like grouped query attention with 8 heads, stored in the usual bfloat16 format, DeepSeek v4 requires roughly 2% the cache size. This makes it much easier to deploy for very large context handling.

Figure 1: benchmark comparison (left), per-token FLOPs and accumulated KV cache against sequence length (right).

The efficiency gain comes from splitting attention into two mechanisms and interleaving them across layers.

Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) compresses KV entries by 4x along the sequence dimension using softmax-gated pooling with a learned positional bias. A lightning indexer (FP4, ReLU-scored multi-head dot product) picks the top-k compressed blocks per query. It inherits the sparse-selection idea from DeepSeek Sparse Attention in V3.2, but runs it over blocks that are already 4x shorter than the original sequence. The indexer's search space shrinks with it.

Industry observers note that figure 3: CSA. The compressor collapses every 4 tokens into one compressed KV entry. The lightning indexer picks the top-k compressed blocks per query. A sliding-window branch handles the most recent uncompressed tokens.

Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) compresses KV entries by 128x and drops the sparse selection. Every query attends densely to every compressed block. The compressed sequence is short enough that dense attention is cheap.

In a recent development, figure 4: HCA. A heavier compressor (128x vs. 4x) followed by dense attention over the compressed stream, with the same sliding-window branch for recency.

Industry observers note that the layers alternate between CSA and HCA. Different layers carry different attention patterns, and forcing one mechanism across all of them wastes capacity. In V4-Pro's 61-layer stack, layers 0–1 are HCA, layers 2–60 alternate CSA and HCA, and the MTP block at the end runs sliding-window only.

Recent findings suggest that both paths use FP8 storage for most KV entries and BF16 only for the RoPE dimensions. The lightning indexer inside CSA runs in FP4. These storage choices compound with the compression ratios to produce the 2% KV cache figure.

Industry observers note that figure 2: overall architecture. Attention layers alternate between CSA and HCA. Feed-forward layers use DeepSeekMoE. Residual connections are replaced with manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC).

In a recent development, efficient long-context attention is necessary for agent workflows but not sufficient. The paper describes three post-training and infrastructure choices that target agent use cases directly.

V3.2 kept reasoning traces across tool-result rounds but discarded them whenever a upcoming user message arrived. For an agent handling a single user turn, this was fine. For multi-turn agentic workflows, where the user sends a follow-up after the agent has already chained several tool calls, the model lost its accumulated reasoning and had to reconstruct state.

V4 preserves reasoning content across user message boundaries when the conversation contains tool calls. The model retains the complete reasoning history across all rounds, including across user turns. This allows a coherent, cumulative chain of thought over long-horizon agent tasks. For conversational use without tools, the old behavior is preserved: reasoning is flushed on each turn to keep context concise.

Recent findings suggest that figure 7: thinking with tools (top) preserves reasoning across all turns. Thinking without tools (bottom) discards reasoning at each fresh user message.

Industry observers note that V4 introduces a |DSML| special token and an XML-based tool-call format. The XML format reduces escaping failures compared to JSON-in-string tool calls, a common failure mode when models emit nested quoted content.

Sources indicate that the schema separates string parameters (passed as-is with string="true") from structured parameters (passed as JSON with string="false"). This removes a class of parsing errors around numbers and booleans that JSON tool-call formats routinely hit.

The agent behavior was trained with RL against real tool environments. The paper describes the sandbox infrastructure built for that purpose. DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec) is a Rust platform that exposes four execution substrates behind one Python SDK: function calls, containers, microVMs (Firecracker), and full VMs (QEMU). A single cluster runs hundreds of thousands of concurrent sandboxes.

Three DSec features matter for agent training: fast image loading via layered 3FS storage (so RL rollouts do not wait on container startup), preemption-safe trajectory replay (so interrupted training steps resume without re-running tool calls), and a uniform API across substrates (so training harnesses target function calls or full VMs without rewriting). These infrastructure decisions underpin the agent benchmark scores.

Sources indicate that the knowledge and reasoning numbers are competitive but not leading. The agent numbers are where V4-Pro-Max separates from the field.

Specific numbers from the agent section of Table 6:.

Industry observers note that in the paper's internal R&D coding benchmark, 30 curated tasks across PyTorch, CUDA, Rust, and C++, V4-Pro-Max hits 67% pass rate, versus 47% for Sonnet 4.5 and 70% for Opus 4.5. In a survey of 85 DeepSeek developers using V4-Pro as their daily driver, 52% noted it was ready to replace their current primary coding model and 39% leaned toward yes.

The long-context retrieval numbers are in Figure 9. MRCR 8-needle accuracy stays above 0.82 through 256K tokens and holds at 0.59 at 1M.

Figure 9: MRCR 8-needle retrieval. V4-Pro-Max stays above 0.82 through 256K and holds at 0.59 at 1M.

Four checkpoints are on the Hub. The instruct models use FP4 for MoE expert weights and FP8 for everything else. The base models are FP8 throughout.

In a recent development, both instruct models support three reasoning modes: Non-think (fast, no chain of thought), Think High (explicit reasoning in blocks), and Think Max (maximum reasoning effort with a dedicated system prompt). Think Max requires a context window of at least 384K tokens. The recommended sampling parameters across all modes are temperature=1.0, top_p=1.0.

The V4-Pro numbers on SWE Verified, MCPAtlas, and the internal R&D benchmark put it at parity with frontier closed models on agent tasks. The open question is how the community's tool harnesses adapt to the |DSML| schema and whether the interleaved thinking gains transfer to out-of-domain agent frameworks.

Figures in this blog post are from the technical report at DeepSeek_V4.pdf.

It has been revealed that according to my personal tests DeepSeek V4 Flash (Non-thinking mode) passed the Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval test on both 32k and 435k actual prompt tokens with a 100% result across depths of 0-100%. In no-needle negative control with the NOT_FOUND instruction, the model also returned 100% correct failures, reducing the risk of contamination and false positives.

So thinking mode may degrade behaviour in some tests.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The ideal UI testing tool is the one that discovers what your owners discover first: broken layouts, usability issues that no longer work, and fresh accessibility issues in all the browsers your users use before a change goes into the repository.
  • In a recent development, even with the right stack, it still relies on what your team needs to catch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

The ideal UI testing tool is the one that discovers what your owners discover first: broken layouts, usability issues that no longer work, and fresh accessibility issues in all the browsers your users use before a change goes into the repository. In 2026, most frontend teams don't rely on a single tool to do all of that. The best setups involve two layers: a test runner layer that launches the browser and monitors behavior, and a UI testing and review platform that visually checks the outcome and routes changes to the right stakeholders for sign-off.

In a recent development, even with the right stack, it still relies on what your team needs to catch. Different teams will focus on different points: a QA team trying to automate checkout flows, a design system team defending shared components, and a single developer working on a tight budget will all be somewhere different. This guide is categorized by the job these UI testing tools do, then connects them.

Most "best UI testing tool" lists rank test runners and visual testing platforms against each other as if they were interchangeable. They aren't. UI testing covers four distinct jobs:.

Functional testing: Does the UI respond correctly when a user clicks, types, or hovers?

Visual testing: Does the UI still look right across layout, color, typography, and spacing?

Accessibility testing: Can people using keyboards and screen readers use it, and did this change introduce new violations?

Cross-browser and device coverage: Does it work in Safari on mobile, not just Chrome on a developer's laptop?

In a recent development, there are also other levels of UI tests. Unit tests test the logic but don't interact with the UI. End-to-end (E2E) tests represent the full user journey in a browser but are difficult to set up, hard to troubleshoot when the bug is a visual detail, and can't practically test every state. Between the extremes of unit tests and E2E tests, component tests simulate each component's behavior in a real browser using fixed inputs, offering speed closer to unit tests and user-level coverage closer to E2E. Many teams maintain a thin layer of E2E tests for critical journeys, and they have component tests for the dozens of states a component may be in.

These tools are organized by job so you can stack them rather than choose one winner.

According to recent reports, these platforms sit on top of your test runner. They capture rendered UI, compare it to approved baselines, and give your team a place to review what changed.

Industry observers note that chromatic is a UI testing and review platform made by the Storybook team. It catches visual, interaction, and accessibility bugs in components and pages before they merge, and it gives developers, designers, and product managers one place to review UI changes and sign off. Chromatic's team is the core maintainer of Storybook, which has about 90,000 GitHub stars and 17 million weekly npm downloads, and a Vitest core maintainer on the team built Chromatic's Vitest integration. Chromatic is used by 45 Fortune 100 companies, including GitHub, Shopify, Microsoft, Adobe, the BBC, and monday.com.

Recent findings suggest that pricing: Free plan with 5,000 snapshots per month (Chrome only), unlimited projects and owners. Starter is $179/month for 35,000 snapshots and adds Safari, Firefox, and Edge. Pro is $399/month for 85,000 snapshots. Enterprise is custom, with SSO, SCIM, SLA support, and data retention. TurboSnap snapshots count as 0.2 of a regular snapshot.

Trade-offs: Chromatic is strongest when your UI is built from components. Teams with no component tests can start from Playwright or Cypress E2E tests, but they'll get the most value once components are covered too. Snapshot usage also grows with each browser and viewport you add, so plan coverage before you scale it.

Best for: Design system teams, product teams that want designers and PMs to approve UI changes, React Native teams, and Vitest-first teams that want visual testing without baselines stored in the repo.

Percy is BrowserStack's visual testing platform. It captures screenshots from your existing tests, renders them across browsers and responsive widths, and highlights pixel differences for review.

Strengths: Framework-agnostic SDKs for Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, and Storybook. App Percy covers native mobile apps. The free initiative includes 5,000 screenshots per month with unlimited customers and projects.

Industry observers note that trade-offs: Percy is page-oriented, and each page rendered in each browser at each width counts as a separate screenshot, so usage climbs rapidly with cross-browser coverage. Percy compares feature branches against a base branch, which teams with complex branching should test early. Reviewers see rendered screenshots rather than an inspectable copy of the code under test, so debugging a diff usually means reproducing it locally.

Pricing: Free tier, then paid plans with fixed screenshot allowances and overage.

Best for: Teams already paying for BrowserStack that want visual checks on page-level E2E tests.

Industry observers note that applitools Eyes uses Visual AI to compare screenshots the way a person would, with match levels that can ignore content changes and focus on layout. Its Ultrafast Grid re-renders captured page states across many browser, viewport, and device combinations.

Strengths: Mature AI matching, broad browser and device coverage, Figma and Storybook testing, accessibility testing, and an MCP server. Higher tiers add AI-driven functional testing and plain-English test authoring.

In a recent development, trade-offs: Applitools is priced and packaged for enterprises. There's a free trial but no free plan, and the Starter plan is $667/month billed annually for 100,000 component checkpoints or 1,000 page checkpoints. Professional and Enterprise are custom-priced.

Best for: Large QA organizations with substantial cross-browser matrices and budget for a dedicated visual AI platform.

It has been revealed that backstopJS is a free, open-source visual regression testing tool released under the MIT license. You list the URLs, viewports, and CSS selectors to capture in a config file, and BackstopJS renders them in a headless browser through Playwright or Puppeteer, then compares the results against approved reference screenshots. The core workflow runs on three commands: backstop init, backstop test, and backstop approve.

Strengths: Completely free, with no screenshot limits. A built-in browser report shows reference and test images side by side with a visual diff inspector, and changes can be approved from there. Optional Docker rendering keeps screenshots consistent between laptops and CI; Playwright adds Firefox and WebKit, and click, hover, and keypress selectors capture interactive states. JUnit reports plug into existing CI pipelines.

Recent findings suggest that trade-offs: BackstopJS is self-hosted, so there's no cloud dashboard, shared team review, or pull request status checks out of the box. Reference screenshots are usually committed to your repository, and every page or component state you want to test needs its own URL and scenario in the config. Someone on the team also has to own the setup, CI integration, and maintenance.

Best for: Developers and small teams with no budget who are comfortable running and maintaining their own visual regression setup.

According to recent reports, test runners click, type, and assert. They're free and open source, and every platform above builds on them. On their own, they offer limited visual testing: built-in screenshot assertions store baselines in your repository, rendering can drift between laptops and CI, and designers have no review interface.

It has been revealed that playwright is Microsoft's open-source browser automation framework. It runs tests across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, with auto-waiting, trace viewer debugging and code generation, and supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET.

Visual testing: Playwright's toHaveScreenshot assertion compares screenshots against baselines stored in Git. It works, but baselines must be regenerated per operating system, and accepting a change means rerunning with an revision flag.

Best for: Teams automating critical user journeys such as sign-up, checkout and login. Pair it with a platform like Chromatic for visual review across real browsers.

Cypress is an open-source testing tool that runs inside the browser, with time-travel debugging that shows the app at each step of a test. It supports both E2E and component testing.

Visual testing: Cypress has no built-in visual comparison and relies on plugins or a platform such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools. Cypress Cloud, its paid service, adds recording, parallelization, flake detection and add-ons for accessibility and UI coverage.

Best for: Frontend developers who want fast feedback and an interactive test runner while they build.

Sources indicate that storybook is the open source workshop for building UI components in isolation. Each story captures one component state, and those stories double as test cases.

Testing features: Interaction tests with play functions and Testing Library, accessibility checks with the a11y addon, and a Vitest integration that runs stories as component tests.

Visual testing: Storybook doesn't diff screenshots on its own. Chromatic, built by the same team, is its visual testing and review layer.

Best for: Design system and component library teams, and any team practicing component-driven development.

Vitest Browser Mode runs component tests in a real browser instead of a simulated DOM, using Playwright or WebdriverIO under the hood.

Visual testing: Vitest's toMatchScreenshot assertion stores screenshots in the repository. For large projects, this can bloat the repo and baselines drift between machines. Chromatic can take Vitest Browser Mode tests with no code changes and run them in a stable cloud environment instead.

Best for: Teams already writing Vitest tests who want them to check how the UI looks without adopting a latest framework.

Start from the problem your team is trying to fix:.

"Shared component changes keep breaking other teams' screens." Test at the component level with Storybook or Vitest Browser Mode and Chromatic, so the change demonstrates up on the pull request that caused it.

It has been revealed that "Our Playwright tests pass, but the layout still breaks in Safari." Functional assertions don't check appearance. Add a visual testing platform that renders in Safari, such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools.

"We turned off screenshot tests because of false alarms." Look for deterministic component states and flake controls such as Chromatic's SteadySnap, or AI matching such as Applitools.

"Designers find UI bugs after release." Choose a platform with a review and approval workflow, and make sign-off a required pull request check.

"AI coding agents keep inventing components." Give agents access to your real component library, for example through Chromatic's hosted MCP, and run every agent-built change through the same UI tests as human code.

"We have no budget." Use Playwright or Vitest screenshot assertions, self-host BackstopJS, or start on the free tiers of Chromatic or Percy.

A practical, well-covered setup for a React web app looks like this:.

Unit tests in Vitest for logic and utilities.

Storybook stories or Vitest Browser Mode tests for every meaningful component state, with interaction tests on key components.

Chromatic running visual, interaction and accessibility tests on those components in Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge on every pull request, with designers assigned as reviewers.

A thin layer of Playwright E2E tests for sign-up, checkout and other critical journeys, also captured in Chromatic so page-level visual changes go through the same review.

This keeps most UI coverage in fast, deterministic component tests, while E2E tests confirm the journeys that matter most still work end to end.

Playwright is the best free tool for E2E UI testing, and Storybook is the best free tool for testing component states. For visual testing, For visual testing, Chromatic and Percy both offer free tiers of around 5,000 snapshots or screenshots per month, and BackstopJS is free to self-host.

UI testing is the broad practice of checking that an interface works for users, including functional, visual and accessibility checks. Visual testing is one part of it: comparing rendered UI against approved baselines to catch unintended changes in layout, color, typography and spacing.

Sources indicate that no. Chromatic was built by the Storybook team, but it also runs visual tests from Vitest Browser Mode, Playwright and Cypress tests, and from React Native Storybook on iOS and Android simulators.

It has been revealed that playwright's toHaveScreenshot covers basic visual checks, but baselines live in your repo, rendering can differ between machines, and there's no review interface for designers. Teams with several reviewers or many browsers usually add a platform on top.

It has been revealed that most teams use both. Component tests cover individual UI states rapidly and reliably, while a smaller set of E2E tests confirms that critical user journeys work across the whole app.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clicks is still on track to release the phone with a physical keyboard within the next few months, but a Communicator launch before the end of this year isn’t looking very likely as shipping gets pushed back.

The Communicator is a fresh take on what an Android phone can be. It was first introduced at CES earlier this year, with the main selling angle being the physically integrated keyboard. Clicks wants to target those who are looking for a second device, and the Communicator fits the bill.

Industry observers note that last we heard, the Clicks Communicator was on track to launch and ship in December, following a cheery patch detailing an upgrade to 12GB of RAM and other changes. However, Clicks posted a new update today stating that the timeline has shifted out a month because of supply chain concerns caused by something other than RAM.

Unfortunately, we’ve encountered a delay with securing a critical supply chain component needed to fabricate our printed circuit board ahead of manufacturing and final assembly. Assembly will now begin in early January, with deliveries expected to start in late January.

It notes that the “critical supply chain component” is the essential fabric used for the company’s printed circuit boards. The blog post dives into some neat details about the component holding things up. The PCBs Clicks is using are made up of more material layers than some competitor boards. But the fabric used to layer those boards is in short supply at this sort of demand, with four manufacturers reportedly unable to meet the company’s required volume.

In a recent development, the post also spells out difficulties caused by troubles in the Middle East, and rising memory costs straining the chain of supply further, even if memory – surprisingly – isn’t the cause of this small delay. Those compounded issues have pushed production back, and consumers are now told to expect their Clicks Communicator pre-orders to be shipped in late January, at the earliest. Many pre-orders will likely be shipped after that because of further time constraints before Chinese New Year.

In an act of good faith, Clicks notes it’s including a set of 3.5mm wired headphones in each box for orders placed prior to today.

Industry observers note that A push from December to January isn’t massive, and Clicks still seems to be making solid time on developing a form factor we don’t often see. You can still pre-order the Clicks Communicator starting at $649.

#162764. I completed GTA 6's indie game darling pastiche, Tenebrae Lux, and all I got was this lousy sense of accomplishment

I completed GTA 6's indie game darling pastiche, Tenebrae Lux, and all I got was this lousy sense of accomplishment

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "We are but Promethean wanderers on the fringes of oblivion, clinging to a semblance of light amidst the vast abyss of our own ignorance.
  • Developed, seemingly single-handedly, by an eccentric developer called Johannes Zuch - auteur, pseud, charlatan - you first get introduced to this curious little experiment in one of GTA 6's earliest missions, where protagonist Jason is forced to play it during a 'lad's night in' with buddy Cal.
  • The first thing I notice about Tenebrae Lux is the name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"We are but Promethean wanderers on the fringes of oblivion, clinging to a semblance of light amidst the vast abyss of our own ignorance. Voyaging uncharted waters may appear foolish to some, yet folly and heroism can often appear the same to the undiscerning eye," so notes the voice of Johannes Zuch - creator, writer, director, composer, and 'perceptual architect' behind Leonida's latest favourite indie darling art game, Tenebrae Lux. It's pretentious, it's deeply up its own arse, and it's awkward and off-putting to play. A must-review for Eurogamer.

Developed, seemingly single-handedly, by an eccentric developer called Johannes Zuch - auteur, pseud, charlatan - you first get introduced to this curious little experiment in one of GTA 6's earliest missions, where protagonist Jason is forced to play it during a 'lad's night in' with buddy Cal. Jason is quick to dismiss Tenebrae Lux in firm, but once Cal slinks off home - hungover and dreary - I slide the disc back into my JoyStation console and sink my teeth back into it. Jason loves this stuff, really. He only keeps Time Jackers: Rewind installed so his mates don't judge him.

The first thing I notice about Tenebrae Lux is the name. It's Latin for 'darkness and light', or something similar. Is this riffing on Clair Obscur, which is French for 'light dark'? No, it's too cerebral for that - too plodding and navel-gazey. Sandfall Interactive wouldn't be this pretentious. Maybe it's a pastiche of Dear Esther, then, drawing on the tenets and schema of the 'walking simulator' genre and using that washed-out film noir aesthetic. But then, it's too wordy for that, with too many interactive and puzzle-adjacent elements. Ah, it must be mocking The Witness, instead - there's the telltale lighthouse, the 'I'm definitely not telling you where to go and what to do' internal narration, and of course the fingerprints of Johannes Zuch are all over it. Johannes Zuch, Jonathan Blow - see how they braided them together? (Sorry).

According to recent reports, whilst this has been created by Rockstar as a pastiche - as much loving send-up as it is withering take down - and designed to make a quick joke in the early 'Feng Shui' mission, the game is playable from start to finish if you so desire. You boot it up by inserting a physical disc, too, which is funny given the context. And it's good! Well, not good good, but it's a proper brainteaser, and ribs 2016's The Witness with such knowledge and (I think?) respect that it's hard not to be charmed by Rockstar's game-within-a-game. There are collectibles to be found that riff on Mark Z. Danielewski's House of Leaves, too, a knowing nod to the most try-hard of all try-hard literature.

Within seconds of the title screen, too, you're presented with a game-within-a-game-within-a-game. You must clear four boards filled with puzzle pieces as the protagonist mutters something mysterious and weird in his posh voice. Do so, and you unlock the door to the next location. Head up to a bunker, and you'll see a room filled with various clues - maybe it's a flashing lamp flickering in morse code, maybe it's a malfunctioning clock presenting a maths puzzle, maybe it's a pricetag on a record that changes on every visit, maybe it's a photograph with anomalous elements, maybe it's a "Developed Using Zuchworks Engine" easter egg hidden in the environment. You need to keep your wits about you, because one of these clues changes every time you enter - and the clue corresponds to a date that changes on a calendar on the wall.

Recent findings suggest that you can look up a guide if you need to, or you can spend far too long figuring out how all this relates to the telephone you can find in the room on your own, like muggins here, before opening up the path to the next puzzle. Look at the image below to see the level of record-keeping and brainteasing this bizarre little game prompted from me. I will say, the sense of achievement you get from playing around with this stuff is pretty remarkable, given - let's not forget I'm actually playing Grand Theft Auto 6 whilst I'm wandering around in the black and white murk trying to complete a puzzle game for no actual reward.

In a recent development, the bunker room is, by far, the hardest part of Tenebrae Lux. From here, things ease up: you need to figure out the right sequence of glyphs on a bridge, and then put some distance between yourself and a curious and rather creepy suited man that's seemingly figuring things out ahead of you in a location inspired by, I think, The Backrooms (or Portal, or Superliminal, or maybe something else entirely. Who knows what Zuch was thinking?).

"With the last enigma finally mastered," the narrator drones in his bumbling monotone, "I step forward into the void, the shadows swallow, consuming all, and then finally the sweet embrace of darkness of which there is no end." 'You have just experienced a Johannes Zuch experience', Tenebrae Lux tells me, before cutting to the best joke of the whole thing: the credits roll much akin to something Hideo Kojima would produce.

Sources indicate that so, what do you get out of all of this? Well - just like real puzzle games in the real world - nothing, really. If you've not completed one of the other three fully playable games in GTA 6, you will get a trophy/achievement. But given the main game is all about Jason and Lucia's desperate scramble to escape the poverty trap, to try and break free of the cycle of debt, violence, and consequence that keeps them clinging to Leonida's seedy underbelly, there's no monetary reward. There's no 'progress' in the sense of the protagonist's shared story.

In a recent development, even in terms of your own cold, hard, mathematical 'completion' you only need to boot each of the four games up once in order to work towards GTA 6's 100% completion. So what's the point of all this? Why did I spend the better part of 90 minutes trying to figure out how to find a sliver of light in the dark in Tenebrae Lux? The game is a wonderful pastiche in that, essentially, it's not really saying anything. You can probably project some vague meaning onto it if you wish - I'm pretty certain the protagonist literally 'finds himself' at the end - but glib little readings like that are ten-a-penny in this genre.

In a recent development, I think the most impressive thing about Tenebrae Lux is that it exists. You're teased with it in an early mission - Rockstar may as well say 'look, we put a game in a game, lol' - but it's more than that. This is what happens when Rockstar's 4700-plus developers are given the room to… develop. Tenebrae Lux could very easily have been a non-interactive experience, a quick, cheap joke shown over-the-shoulder taking a drive-by pop shot at Johnathan Blow, Hideo Kojima, Dan Pinchbeck, or any and all of the above. Or maybe it could be a 'vertical slice', an incomplete demo, a teaser. But it's not, because nothing about GTA 6 is quick or cheap.

Sources indicate that GTA 6, in every single conceivable way, is a premium experience - part-sandbox, part-simulation, part-otherworld. To create not just one, but four fully playable and completable games within that framework is showboating, sure, but to make that game actually good and - perhaps controversially - even better than some of the games it's pastiching… Well, it's just rubbing salt in the wound, really.

A code for the game was provided by Cal Hampton.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A GTA 6 developer has thanked Rockstar Games for immortalizing his baby daughter in an in-game memorial after he and his wife lost her five months into the pregnancy.

Since GTA 6 released on November 19, millions of players have been exploring Leonida, uncovering hidden secrets and Easter eggs scattered throughout Rockstar’s sprawling open world.

However, some of the game’s most meaningful discoveries have been deeply personal tributes to the loved ones of those who spent years developing it.

Rockstar lead game tools programmer Bradley Stone took to X to share footage of himself visiting a memorial bearing his daughter’s name, Evelyn Stone, alongside the date April 8, 2023.

“To our baby we lost at 5 months pregnancy, you have been forever memorialised and honoured,” he wrote.

“Thank you, Rockstar for giving us this place to remember our loved ones, to show this game was made by real people and thank you for all the support/care you gave me through my grief.”.

Stone explained that he and his wife had already experienced multiple miscarriages when a scan in 2023 revealed their baby had a severe case of spina bifida.

Recent findings suggest that after further examinations and consultations with doctors, the couple learned that their daughter would not survive. They were left facing a medical termination, with Stone’s wife having to endure nearly 24 hours of labor.

This was the darkest moment of our lives and I cannot put into words the strength and courage my wife showed and I can only love her more for that.A few years of ups and downs and more sadness we were finally blessed with a beautiful baby girl.

Sources indicate that “We cried and held each other close as she delivered the baby,” he recalled. “The next hardest part was leaving the hospital without our baby. This still breaks me to this day.”.

Stone described the experience as the “darkest moment” of their lives, praising his wife’s strength and courage. He also revealed that, following several more years of ups and downs, the couple had welcomed a baby girl.

“To the baby we lost, we named you Evelyn,” he wrote. “You will forever be in our hearts.”.

Stone isn’t the only Rockstar employee whose loved ones have been immortalized in GTA 6. Fellow developer Matt Green previously revealed that his late mother, Bev, had been honored at the memorial just north of Hamlet.

While GTA 6 continues to shatter records around the world, the memorial serves as a touching reminder of the people behind the game and the loved ones they lost along the way.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that are you wondering how connected the worlds of GTA 5 and GTA 6 are?
  • Right, if you're reading from this point onwards, you're clearly here for the tea.
  • It has been revealed that called 'Body Copy' - a joke I appreciate as a former magazine editor, naturally - this publication features a few different articles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that are you wondering how connected the worlds of GTA 5 and GTA 6 are? Well, I've got some news for you. Keep on reading below if you'd like some very minor spoilers for the early game of GTA 6, spoilers for GTA 5, as well as some information about how the new game links to GTA 5 and other Rockstar games.

Right, if you're reading from this point onwards, you're clearly here for the tea. In the first hour or so of GTA 6, when you finally get control of Jason and head to your first property (the green stilted house) in the Leonida Keys, you will be able to explore a little. On my way to do a workout - you need to keep Jason a peak physical instrument for his work's sake, right? Right? - I happened upon a fitness magazine resting on a table on the decking out front.

It has been revealed that called 'Body Copy' - a joke I appreciate as a former magazine editor, naturally - this publication features a few different articles. There's Morning Glory, where Nolan Crockett jacks you with his early workout; Skindecent Exposure, a photo spread about why beaches are 'crazy' places to work out; Shrediquette, a piece dedicated to proper in-gym decorum; and Twilight Tantra, an interview feature and yoga masterclass with 'gerontophile' Fabien LaRouche.

Hang on, Fabien LaRouche… isn't that the French wellness guru and shyster that was a "close friend" to Amanda De Santa in Grand Theft Auto 5? Yes, yes it is. In fact, Fabien played quite a large role in that game, acting as the antagonistic force that eventually fractured Michael and Amanda's relationship. After conducting an affair under the guise of 'yoga lessons', Amanda left our protagonist, and moved in with Fabien, taking Michael's kids - Jimmy and Tracy - with her. In a totally healthy and normal way, you could follow their new life via updates posted to GTA's Facebook surrogate, LifeInvader. It's clear the kids never liked the pretentious, annoying man - but for Amanda, the penny is a little slower to drop. Eventually, Amanda and Michael reconcile their differences - with the latter whalloping Fabien in the process. The married couple pledge to resolve their differences, and Fabien is never seen again.

It has been revealed that until GTA 6, at least. Here, in what we assume is supposed to be 2025 or 2026, it's been about 13 years since we last saw the character (it is widely agreed that GTA 5 is set in 2013 - the game's original launch year). And it seems that the events surrounding Michael and his family really did a number on Fabien. Which - of course - he blamed on the universe, rather than taking any personal responsibility. Naturally.

Industry observers note that "Ever since the karmic decay of Los Santos was made perfectly clear to him in the early 2010s, yoga instructor Fabien LaRouche has been on an epic pilgrimage of enlightenment through the remotest ashrams and finest 5-star resorts and plastic surgery retreats of The East," reads the Body Copy article. "Having completed his chakric education and returned to the United States, we meet with him on the final week of his six-month residency at Dwindle Wood Retirement Community.".

Here, the article goes on to explore Fabien's penchant for older women - he seems to like their nature, their desire to learn about self-improvement and wellness, and (perhaps most importantly) their bank accounts. "Being over the hill doesn't necessarily mean you have nothing left to live for," he opines in the article. Thanks for that, Fabien.

Sources indicate that it's interesting to see - very early in the game and quite plainly telegraphed - that Rockstar is willing to reintroduce us to people from previous games. This isn't a megaton addition by any means - Fabien was never a 'main character' - but I love that a nod to him, in a feature tucked away at the back of a magazine, sets the scene for more cameos, perhaps, later in the game. It shows us, nice and early, that GTA 5 and GTA 6 are indeed connected. By inference, then, we know that GTA 4 is included in that same picture; there were recurring characters in GTA 5 that appeared in GTA 4, after all - Patrick McReary, Johnny Klebitz, Rocco Pelosi and more come to mind.

It may seem like a small thing, but it's just another example of Rockstar using its expansive toolset, ridiculous budget, and well-established legacy to inject a sense of scale into the world of Grand Theft Auto 6. There are other nods to the universe out there, too. I won't spoil them here, but I've been a little bit dewy-eyed to hear rumours of some of the other nods to Rockstar titles hidden in the world of Leonida: it makes all the experiences I've had in past games, the emotional response I've had to previous Rockstar worlds, feel in some way valid and meaningful here, too. I'm looking forward to seeing what other little secrets await me across the keys and into the glowing neon promise of Vice City proper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As much as I love high-priced tech like my RTX 4090-equipped custom gaming rig or the 65-inch LG OLED TV I use as my monitor, most of us can't afford to spend several hundred dollars or more on a tech gift, no matter how important the recipient might be in our lives. But you can still improve the tech lives of your friends and family (or yourself) while spending a comparatively small amount of money during the Black Friday deals season.

I own all of the affordable devices listed below, and they all typically sell for less than $50. Some are even under $20! All of these products have made my tech-saturated world a little lighter, brighter, or just plain nicer in their own way. If you're looking for a small tech splurge for yourself, or an affordable gift for that tech-savvy friend or family member, one of these $50-or-under options might be a good fit and a great deal while Black Friday deals keep their prices lower than normal.

According to recent reports, last year, a family member asked for help with an older desktop PC that was struggling to run Windows 10 and several programs on a cramped 110 GB SSD. I figured I could clone the boot drive onto a more spacious drive, so the OS and programs had more space to stretch out.

But the thought of juggling multiple USB enclosures or having to take the drive home and shuffle it in and out of my desktop filled me with dread, as I pictured hours spent getting everything done and the system back up and running. So I looked into getting an M.2 SSD cloner and was surprised to see they can be found for less than $50.

It has been revealed that with support for NVMe M.2 SSDs and offline cloning, this handy device makes it simple to move your files or OS from one drive to another. And with a 20 Gbps USB-C interface, it's also speedy in your OS of choice if you want to use software to clone or move your data between drives.

It has been revealed that while I don't love the glossy plastic shell of Rosewill's cloner, it's one of the more affordable options. And it supports both NVMe M.2 drives and older AHCI models (Sorry, SATA). Using the cloner is pretty straightforward. You plug in the included USB-C power adapter, put your source drive in the left slot, the destination drive in the right slot, press the power button on the back, and a few logos light up, letting you know you're ready to go. Press the clone button on the top, and the drive cloning will commence (provided your destination is the same size or larger than your source).That's assuming you want to do an offline clone. But because I needed to also resize the partition between the old 110 GB and a newer Team Group 512 GB SSD, I used the second included USB-C cable to connect the Rosewill cloner to my laptop and powered up the device. Within seconds, both drives were recognized in Windows, so I fired up the excellent free DiskGenius software, cloned the old partition to the newly introduced drive with a few clicks, and then used the software to drag the boot partition to the full size of the new drive. The whole process took just a few minutes, since the Rosewill cloner supports 20 Gbps USB, and I wasn't exactly copying a huge partition. When the cloning process was finished and the partition expanded, it was hard to believe it was all that easy. I had expected to be at the task for hours, but I was done in less than 30 minutes. Sure, unless you're in IT, a drive cloner might not be something you use regularly, but it's sure handy to have around when you need it. You could also use it to save some money by buying a laptop with a cramped SSD and swapping in something much roomier – provided, of course, the laptop's storage isn't soldered to the motherboard. The Rosewill cloner is also handy for just checking the contents of old M.2 drives you may have lying around. But if that's all you need, you can buy an NVMe enclosure or a single-drive dock. I also own a version of this model from Suitok, which costs $15.99.

Industry observers note that I picked up the OLIGHT IMINI 2 mini flashlight last year on impulse because it looked well-designed and cost around $20, but it's often on sale for much less. Its simple design and built-in USB-A plug for charging make it fun to use – just pull the back off, and it turns on. The magnet at the back lets you easily mount it anywhere you need a little extra light. I've used it inside a steel PC case while fiddling with RGB wires, and under my sink while attaching a glass rinser.

At just 2.17 inches long, this flashlight is rated to 50 lumens, and it sports a magnetic back with a USB-A plug for charging. Pulling the back off turns on the flashlight, and the magnetic back makes it easy to mount the light on anything made of ferrous metal.

It has been revealed that the OLIGHT IMINI 2 is also small enough for your keychain, is designed to live with your keys, and includes two silicone covers for the USB port and a little carabiner clip. But the flashlight portion is only held to the charging port via a magnet, and I feel like (for me, at least) it would likely fall off and get lost before too long if left on my keys.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

I build a lot of PCs, though not as many lately thanks to the RAM apocalypse, and I also do regular home improvement work around my apartment. So a cordless screwdriver is a nice thing to have. I also own a much slimmer Wowstick, but have found HOTO's NEX O1 Pro to be much more useful thanks to its extra (and variable) torque. It's great for loosening those factory-installed screws on PC cases that just don't want to let go, and also good for assembling furniture.The HOTO won't replace my DeWalt drill for bigger, tougher jobs. But for everyday tasks, it's powerful enough, easy to charge over USB-C, and even looks good on my workbench.

According to recent reports, hoto's wireless screwdriver has three torque settings, charges over USB-C, and looks surprisingly good. It's even proven quite durable, as I've dropped it off of ladders and my workbench at least a dozen times over the past few years, and it's still working flawlessly.

Sources indicate that for those of us who grew up in the 1900s, few things beat a chunky tactile volume knob and physical buttons for controlling media. And Vaydeer's USB device provides that, and then some. I own the previous version of this device, and love it for controlling and muting music at my treadmill desk while I work.

It has been revealed that I use the buttons on it to play / pause audio and video and move forward to the next track or backward to the previous one. It's totally plug-and-play, as no drivers are needed.

Just plug this simple USB device into a USB port and you can control the volume and select tracks without fiddling with your keyboard or mouse.

In a recent development, what's not to love about a SNES-inspired wireless gaming controller that's compatible with Windows, Mac, Android, and the Nintendo Switch? Not much, as far as I'm concerned. Especially considering it's not super expensive.As you might expect, given the SN30 Pro's small size and many more buttons than the SNES controller it was based on, its Rumble motors aren't the strongest. And the layout can feel a little cramped for some modern games. But for any retro game, and especially platformers, this is my go-to controller. It feels familiar and nostalgic, which, for me at least, goes well with those occasional long game sessions.

Recent findings suggest that with its SNES-inspired design, this controller will entice gamers of a certain age. But its appeal goes beyond its looks, with Hall Effect joysticks and support for the Switch 1 and 2, PC, macOS, and basically any OS that supports games and Bluetooth.

Sources indicate that there are so many gaming mouse options, most with specs that go well above and beyond my wrist-twitching capabilities. So I instead chose something with style that caught my eye, 8BitDo's Retro R8 Mouse with Charging Dock. This NES-inspired mouse is designed for nostalgia, with its black, gray, and red color scheme and round red side buttons. And 8BitDo went the extra mile (or two) by designing a weighted charging dock (with its own NES-like touches) and a spot for the 2.4 GHz dongle. This is the kind of extra feature that's more common in mice that cost twice as much.

Industry observers note that the nostalgia of this mouse's design is nice. But it also sports a 26,000 DPI sensor, 4K polling, and a really nice charging dock that also houses the 2.4 GHz dongle. If you're in a pinch or not gaming, Bluetooth is also supported.

Recent findings suggest that under the hood, you get a decent 26,000 DPI sensor and 4K polling (plenty for us non-esports gamers), an ambidextrous design with two side buttons on either side, and a clicky, rubberized scroll wheel. The side buttons, which are concave, took a little getting used to for me. But they are also so distinctive that now I miss them while I game using other mice. If the NES theme isn't your thing, the company also sells a translucent-green XBox version, as well as a champagne-hued C64 Edition.

If you're like me, you never have access to enough USB ports. I solved this problem by picking up this Ikai hub, with 60W of power for your external drives and peripherals, and a premium metal shell. It sports three speedy 10 Gbps ports (two USB-C), along with seven 5 GBps USB-A ports. The final USB-C on the end of the hub is for charging your phone or other devices, and delivers 20W.The other nice feature is that all the data ports have a side button, so you can toggle them on and off to save some power. I also find this handy for swapping between wireless mice and keyboards, while keeping the tiny dongles plugged in so I don't lose them.

Recent findings suggest that with 11 ports and up to 10 Gbps of bandwidth, a solid aluminum shell, and buttons so you can cut power to individual ports you aren't using, this USB hub is a great addition to your desk. It has external power for better stability and even a 20W USB-C PD port on the end for charging phones or peripherals.

The sole thing to keep in mind about this (and basically any) hub, is that it has a single 10 Gbps connection to your PC. So don't expect to plug in multiple high-speed devices (like SSDs) and have them run simultaneously at full speed. If that's what you need, you should look at one of the best Thunderbolt or USB4 hubs (which cost significantly more).

According to recent reports, OK, this one's only for the DIY-inclined, because it involves cutting a rectangle in your desk (or anywhere else you might want some flush-mount power ports, like a nightstand). Jgstkcity's recessed power strip lets you drop a couple of AC outlets and two USB charging ports (one 30W USB-C) anywhere you need them – again, once you've cut a hole for it.It is, of course, smart to be cautious of no-name power accessories and strips. But I've used two variations of these strips for roughly three years now, and nothing has ever felt hot or failed. I have this model installed in the narrow stand I built that lives right behind my couch, up against the wall. It's a super-convenient place for power outlets, especially when friends or family stop by. I just warn people not to put drinks near there. Thankfully, the coffee table, in front of the couch, is an even more convenient place for those.

Sources indicate that you'll probably need a drill and a saw to install it, but having a couple of power plugs and USB-C PD power right on the surface of your desk or nightstand is super convenient. And once you have the hole cut, this strip is dead-simple to install.

When you're traveling to another country for more than a few days, every small bit of space you can save helps. But you also usually need a travel adapter to plug your devices into the outlets of other countries. Anker's Nano Travel Adapter serves both needs well, as it's roughly half the thickness of other adapters and is designed to work in over 200 countries. The Nano Travel Adapter also has four USB ports for charging, which is super convenient for keeping my phone, e-reader, and earbuds juiced up without needing a separate charger. There are two USB-A ports on the bottom and two USB-C ports on the side, with the latter delivering up to 20W. The adapter also comes in black or white/silver. I opted for the white one, which makes it easier to find after months in a drawer when I'm not traveling.

According to recent reports, anker's slim travel adapter is 43% smaller than many other adapters, while supporting over 200 countries with its fold-down plugs. It also has two USB-C and two USB-A ports for charging, at up to 20W.

In a recent development, the major downside over other travel chargers is that the Nano Travel Adapter doesn't support plugging in devices with three-prong (grounded) plugs. But I haven't found this an concern since I typically plug things like my Baseus flat laptop charger in while traveling, rather than high-power devices like a desktop PC or hair dryer.

For anyone who spends their days (and/or nights) in front of a keyboard, a good wrist rest is key for both short-term comfort and long-term limb health. And having stumbled onto these combo wrist and elbow rests earlier this year, I never want to use anything else.Even if you have a wrist rest you've been using for years, there's a good chance it's a little funky or the fabric is worn out. Gel and fabric rests only tend to last a few years before they get funky, so even if you don't quite need a fresh one now, it's nice to have a replacement waiting in the wings.

These unique wrist and elbow rests are designed to hang over the edge of your desk, which makes them a great option for people who lean on their elbows or if you just have a cramped desk setup. Available in multiple colors and sizes, the 11.8-inch version is wide enough that I use one for my compact keyboard at work, and the other at home for my gaming setup.

Recent findings suggest that after the good experience I've had with the tech giant's NiMH batteries, I bought Powerowl's Lithium rechargeable batteries earlier this year. And boy am I glad I did. These last months longer in my smart door locks than those older batteries, which means I only have to swap the cells on two doors a few times a year now.Full disclosure: I have had one of these batteries refuse to recharge after its first power cycle. But out of the three sets I now own, that's not a terrible track record. I just wish the company also made AAA lithium cells for my other devices.

In a recent development, these 1.5V lithium batteries are designed for high-drain devices and rated at 3600 mWh. The charger plugs in over USB-C and can also charge older NiMH batteries.

According to recent reports, have you upgraded your router to Wi-Fi 6 or later, but your desktop or laptop doesn't have the requisite hardware to take advantage of your recent network tech? TP-Link's AX1800 WiFi 6 USB Adapter is here to solve that problem for you. It's quite large by USB Wi-Fi dongle standards, but I've found it works quite well with my Wi-Fi 6 router.

I have the router running downstairs from my office, and it instantly fixed an concern I was having with very poor reception from the SFF PC I built in the Fractal Terra case.

Sure, it's substantial and bulky with two antennas, but this Wi-Fi 6 USB adapter can deliver some serious speed to your desktop or laptop when paired with a Wi-Fi 6 or later router.

This is a four-port, 5Gbps USB-A hub that's designed to clamp onto your monitor or desk and give you extra convenient connectivity.

Industry observers note that it comes in black or silver and has a nice, sturdy metal frame. Just note that its clamp section is pretty shallow, and its adjustable screw can only open between 10 and 32 mm, so it won't fit on all monitors or desks.

An otherwise standard four-port USB 3.0 hub, this Orico model stands out for its metal frame and clamp design.

It has been revealed that if you to get a handle on the PC cables in your home or office, some cheap cable management trays will do the job. This two-pack comes with tape, though heavier loads will ultimately require some screws.Besides the trays, this kit also comes with cable ties and a few cable clips you can place along the bottom or sides of your desk. One of these has been holding up the PC cable clutter in my living room for the past year. But I had to screw it into my desk because it's holding an Anker power strip, plus the large external power brick from my TV / Monitor.

Industry observers note that if there's a rat's nest of cables under your desk, attaching some trays down there can help you clean it up. This set has tape for light loads, but for longer-term cleanliness, you probably want to consider screws.

You may, like me, be swimming in a world of USB cables. But that doesn't mean you always have one when you need it away from home. This short 240W USB4 charging cable from EndlesShine solves that by being small enough to attach to your keys. It's not always the most convenient option, at just over 5 inches long, but it will do in a pinch and has come in handy more than once, particularly on trips when I'm traveling light.

Industry observers note that it's short in length, at 5.11 inches, but this keychain cable supports 240W charging and USB4 (40Gbps speeds). Clip it onto your keys, and you'll always have a fast cable when you need one.

Industry observers note that if you're the type who is rough with your keys, the plastic cap may wear out over time, so you might want to just keep the cable in a pocket or your bag. It even comes in white and yellow if you don't like basic black.

Breaking: How to build scalable web apps with OpenAI's Privacy Filter
