#162745. At last, I've finally played Faraway, an enigma I've been waiting 16 years to see

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2295 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

At last, I've finally played Faraway, an enigma I've been waiting 16 years to see

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For 16 years I've been watching the skies.
  • According to recent reports, faraway is one of those wonderfully cludged together childhood words, like "nonesuch".
  • Recent findings suggest that okay, Faraway came with one other bit of info I could cling to at the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For 16 years I've been watching the skies. It was 16 years ago, back in the first giddy rush of smartphone gaming, that I saw a 30-second trailer for a game set in space. It was a game about a comet, hurtling through the unknown. It wasn't clear what you'd do in this game, whether you'd control the comet itself or the space it moved through. It wasn't clear if this was some kind of arcade game, or a new spin on the endless runner, or even just a kind of cosmic sandbox. All I had was the comet and a name: Faraway. Faraway! I was captivated.

According to recent reports, faraway is one of those wonderfully cludged together childhood words, like "nonesuch". Where is the edge of the galaxy? Oh, it's faraway. Where is the edge of the universe? Oh, there's nonesuch thing.

Recent findings suggest that okay, Faraway came with one other bit of info I could cling to at the time. It was being made by Steph Thirion, a musician and designer and, I sensed, many other things too. At the time Faraway was announced I'd just played his game Eliss, which was an early smartphone hit. In the absence of any more information on Faraway itself, I had to make do with that. Maybe Faraway would be a bit like Eliss?

It has been revealed that eliss itself, though? Oh, boy. This thing is beautiful, frantic, strange, compelling and indescribable. And think what that means, just for a second, for something to be both compelling and indescribable. I am driven to do these things, but I don't really know what these things are. I'm prodding little bits of colour around, maybe planets, maybe molecules? I am combining them, gathering them, turning them into something greater together than they are by themselves?

Last week I spoke to Thirion - as for why, well, we will get to that - and at the start I asked him about Eliss, about how it felt to make a game that was so hard to put into words, and if he actually had any words for it himself.

According to recent reports, "I love that question," he laughs. "I guess I would say that for Eliss, it was all about that interaction of moving things, moving those little circles with each of your fingers individually." He pauses, thinking back. "It's not something I had envisioned. I was programming, and I was basically testing touch controls because I was trying to build a different game. But then I was playing with that [stuff]. I was like: that feels really nice. Can I build a game around that? So I guess there is something beyond language about that interaction. I was attracted to it in that way. It wasn't rational. It was a feeling. It feels good.".

According to recent reports, it's both thrilling and slightly melancholic to think back to the days of Eliss. Apps were in ascendence, but nobody fully understood them yet. There weren't yet consultants or established monetisation pathways. There wasn't even much agreement on the best ways to approach the touchscreen. Eliss and other weird, memorable, hard-to-talk-about games were all part of this Cambrian explosion. You'd get up in the morning and check socials and there was a latest game everyone was enthusing about. There was a new world to get lost in.

"I would say that's true even outside of mobile," Thirion tells me. "Just indies in general. There was a lot of excitement going around and a lot of eyeballs. What are people gonna think about next?" He takes a long breath. "It felt like there's a lot of opportunity for upcoming things and new ideas, and people were excited about that. Everything was set up for innovation. It felt like I was part of something.".

This is the world that Faraway and its comet first emerged from, streaking across a night sky in which any kind of discovery felt possible. "The real genesis was actually just before Eliss," Thirion claims. "I was really spending a lot of time thinking about a possible career in video games. I was an interaction designer and programmer doing interactive experiences, mostly for advertising.

In a recent development, "And for some reason, the iPhone was the thing that made me think I could do something on my own, and what I'd like to do is probably video games. So I was I was thinking a lot about that, maybe obsessively, to the point where there was a night that I was in the countryside in France and just looking at the stars and thinking: it would be great to have a video game where you can fly in the sky that I'm looking at, in this 2D firmament, right? That was it.".

Industry observers note that the next step towards Faraway came at GDC in 2010, with a call for games that could be controlled with a single button. "I started prototyping," Thirion says. "I tried a few things, and I had this idea of using this kind of physics-y thing about swinging around stars. It actually worked pretty rapidly.".

Industry observers note that then? Sixteen years pass. What was happening during this time?

It's a long answer with, perhaps, a short answer buried inside it. Let's deal with the long answer first.

Recent findings suggest that "It's not like I worked 16 years on this game," Thirion laughs. He explains that the first prototype was begun in 2010 for the GDC one-button competition. It was playable by March. "That was basically at the beginning," he indicates. "I was like: This is a very simple game, and I'm just going to put it out in a couple months.".

Sources indicate that and after that? "I started to have greater ambitions, and then life happened," he notes. He didn't work on the game for seven years, and then Annapurna Interactive found him and asked him to return to Faraway, offering support. "And so, after that, the journey was to turn [the game] into an audiovisual experience.

"And so I started doing an audiovisual experience, but it was still aesthetically like Ellis: low-resolution pixel art. I had the ambition of taking it to a different language. I basically wanted to make the jump from procedural low-resolution to procedural infinite resolution!" He ended up with a very smooth, almost vector-like aesthetic. It looks beautiful, but it came at a price. "That took a lot of effort," he notes. "Also to make it performant? That required a rewrite of the game into a completely fresh engine. It was a new language for me as well, so I had to learn this new language.".

All of this is extremely convincing, as are a hundred other bumps in the road. It makes sense. I've written about games for twenty years, and my sense is that game development is hard, and that it takes time.

According to recent reports, but there's something else Thirion says. And this makes me wonder if part of the truth as to why Faraway took so long to make is actually a lot simpler, and a lot more human.

"I was thinking a lot about Tetris," Thirion states. "I had just started making video games, and I thought a lot about Tetris because it's a very simple rule set that seems to be compelling whether you're two hours in or 1000 hours in, right? And that's like kind of a rare thing.

Recent findings suggest that "And at the time we were talking about: are game's art and so on. And I was like, man, to me, Tetris is art. It does something almost impossible. At least now I look at it and I think it does something almost impossible. But at the time, I was like, well, why are games growing in complexity and quantity instead of staying simple and going deep? And so, I was really asking myself the question: where can I find that balance of just being compelling at any skill level with a very minimal rule set, and that kind of took me into this rabbit hole of experimentation.".

Sources indicate that it's hard for me not to sympathise with this. Thirion had worked on something for a very short period of time, and he'd found something that felt - well, that felt kind of eternal, boundless in there. A comet swinging through space with one touch controls! What could be more pleasing, more engaging than that? But with that came a lot of challenges. It wasn't just a question of what to add. Adding things would be easy. It was how to create a deep experience that didn't overburden the whole idea and make you lose sight of its simplicity. Put like that, 16 years doesn't seem like a very long time at all.

According to recent reports, that's his journey, anyway. As for mine? Well, 16 years is a lot of time if you aren't a comet. I continued writing about games. I got married. I had a daughter. My daughter grew up and went to primary school and is now at secondary school. The whole games industry transformed and then transformed again and is transforming again now. I started learning to swim!

And throughout all this, every few years I would email Thirion and ask if he was ready to talk yet, whether he was ready to talk about Faraway and whether his comet was still blazing somewhere in some private night sky.

Earlier this year I looked him up once more and saw a latest trailer. It was short again, and there was the comet I had seen all those years ago. And then, at the end, there was a date. A release date. That comet was finally swinging by the earth.

Recent findings suggest that and so a few weeks ago I loaded up a game I had been waiting to play for 16 years and which I realised, as I paged through the early screens, that I still knew absolutely nothing about. Well. Do you want to hear about it? Or would you rather discover it for yourself?

Industry observers note that I would rather you discover it for yourself. But if you don't want to, listen:.

Faraway is a game about a comet. The comet is racing through space, and you are the comet, even if you only control it indirectly. Touch a button - there is only one button - and you can bind the comet to the gravity of a nearby star. Keep your finger pressed down on the button and you will remain gravitationally bound, which means you can use stars to adjust your course, your trajectory, your speed. Let go of the button and you're off again. Off into the depths of space. And out there, new stars await.

Industry observers note that from this simple interaction, Faraway builds a constellation of challenges that I find both simple to understand and - yes - incredibly difficult to adequately put into words. I'm not going to tell you too much, because I really want you to play this thing, but Faraway at its core is a bit like sewing, a bit like driving, a bit like counting and making shapes and a bit like desperately trying to stay alive. That's it. It's beautiful and serene, but it's also desperate. It's abstract and reliable and I find it extremely moving to play.

Sources indicate that more than anything, I think I love the feel of it. The steady arc of the comet bends and flexes beneath you as you push and hold the button. There's a thrilling sense of just about bending something elemental to your will. There's beauty to be found in timing your escape from an orbit, and the orbit paths themselves, when you press and hold the button and upcoming trajectories announce themselves, have a Spirograph delight to them. Does it really matter what you do in a game when it has stuff like this in it?

It has been revealed that now, I am weird, and I spend a lot of my time on Earth thinking about the wilds of space and the vast distances and the places we will never get to see and all the things that are so hostile to life that we wouldn't survive a second in their presence. I think about the Wow Signal and the Great Attractor and Tabby's Star and all of that beautiful, terrifying stuff. It calms me down. It puts my own problems in perspective. It's probably the closest thing I get to any kind of religious observance.

And Thirion thinks about this stuff too. I know because, after 16 years, I asked him. "It really resonates with me," he states. "I do spend a lot of time thinking about [the universe]. I don't know why there is anything at all, right? And the fact that we can never answer that question, and the fact that there are many questions that we'll probably never be able to answer.

It has been revealed that "But I also spend a lot of time looking at the clouds and looking at the grass and how the light hits the drops of water. There's so much beauty. We're given so much beauty by the universe, and we're so lucky.

"And the game comes out of that a little bit. I don't know exactly what the game is about, but maybe you could interpret it as: why am I here? Why is life so short? Why is life so long?".

Sources indicate that he laughs. "I often ask myself: why is there anything at all? And how is it so beautiful?".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spoilers for Chapter 1-3 of GTA 6 follow.

I have just successfully busted a Kingfisher operation just north of Cottonmouth Lake in Mariana County. It was beautiful. Jason took point, armed with a shotgun liberated from an M7 clubhouse, guarding a chokepoint as hordes of rednecks threw themselves at him in an unceremonious, slightly humiliating pantomime of existential futility. Lucia, confident in her improving gunmanship, stood behind, aimed over Jason's broad shoulders, and took out stragglers with a custom hunting rifle pilfered from the Kingfisher's own safehouse. Not so safe anymore, is it, losers? This one's for Donnie, I think as I kneecap the final goon and rifle through their safe.

In a recent development, "That one was for Donnie," Lucia states to Jason as they get in their favourite car - Jason's sunset yellow Declasse '72 Tulip, with a suped up engine and custom parts. God damn, I think, this game can read my mind. And I'm not sure if I would have had this intimate little moment of grief and reconciliation if I hadn't got in the habit of using the game's Cinematic Camera. Your dual protagonists can chat even when you, the player, are in the driving seat - of course - but there's so much going on in the world of Leonida (and so many pedestrians and motorists that like to behave like maniacs and cut you off) that I find their conversations are often cut short or terminated altogether by the chaos of the world.

Recent findings suggest that so, hopping into the car, hitting 'down' on the D-Pad and then hitting 'Start' will instigate the Cinematic Camera, and if you've already set a destination on the map or via the handy fresh quick navigational menu (simply hold 'down' to see this), your chosen lovebird will start automatically driving to their next location. For me, in this example, it was the Pelican River to Vice City's Bayside, and Boobie's apartment. Probably about 15 minutes of real-world time; enough space to fuss my dog, grab a drink, reply to my editor, and really take the time to soak in the absurd level of detail Rockstar has crammed into its opus. On this specific journey, I also heard a really touching, sweet interaction about Jason's insecurities regarding Lucai's mum. Goosebumps.

It has been revealed that GTA 6 is an action-packed game; there aren't a lot of menial jobs going for Jason and Lucia - they're on the run, after all, so I don't think a traditional PAYE-compliant nine-to-five is really on the cards. As such, even the smaller money-making activities on offer are quite stressful: dirt-track events, street racing, pawn store robberies, hit-and-runs, stick-ups… there's only so much a bit of meditation in a park can do to decompress you. So I've taken to enjoying life on the roads. After a massive, somewhat impromptu heist on two Kingfisher operations, I need a bit of time to slow down and smell the proverbial roses (or should that be Tulips?).

In a recent development, jumping into Jason's car, turning the radio to The Chamber 106.6, and letting the star-crossed lovers meander their way home listening to Slayer's Kerry King and Tom Araya play a selection of metal tracks from the past four decades is good for my brain. I actually think these moments of leisure are essential to the rhythm of GTA 6: dial it up, cool it off. It creates this almost tidal ebb and flow, the resultant flotsam and jetsam ending up fenced or stashed as the rhythm dictates.

Recent findings suggest that I'm usually a very active and fussy player when it comes to games; I can't stand long cutscenes taking control away from me, and I absolutely will skip story scenes on a second playthrough if it's getting in the way of hands-on controller time. So I'm quite surprised at the ease with which I've given up my agency for these longer rides. But it's a testament to Rockstar's writing. I want to see what Jason and Lucia are saying to each other. I want the camera to show me the world passing me by outside my window as I get from A to B. I even sometimes schedule and phase in little detours to C and D, to be honest, because I feel so zen as I watch the bruise-coloured sky sets over the Keys (and I want to hear the end of Symphony of Destruction, maybe).

Industry observers note that my Lucia is dressed a bit like someone you'll see cutting about outside Nottingham's Rock City club - cute little tank top, leather jacket, nose and ear piercings galore. One afternoon, after driving out to Hamlet to have a long overdue catch-up with her mum, I set the Cinematic Camera and auto-drive settings on to take her back to meet Jason at a bar (another place, incidentally, you can turn on the Cinematic Camera and just watch them hang out together). On her way back home, with the sunlight dipping below the horizon, the fiery orange ambience caught the whites of her eye and the metallic zip of her leather jacket. She smiled to herself as Tool's Sober came on the radio. Christ, I thought, I'm there.

Sources indicate that GTA 6 has this odd capacity to transport me. I think it's because the levels of simulation in Leonida are so artisanal, so well-pitched, and so well-executed. I can believe I'm there. I want to sit in this muscle car, no doubt smelling of leather and oil, listening to Tool with Lucia. I want to feel the humid air of Watson Bay coalescing on my skin, warm air blowing through my hair. I want to join in on Jason and Lucia's in-jokes, laugh as they do little impressions of each other and coo as they make up and hold hands during the longer drives. I want to stick my head out the window like Lucia does and smell the Cuban food grilling in the food trucks, or hear the kids partying on the beach.

In a recent development, with the Cinematic Camera turned on, I have the chance to do that. I don't have to worry about making money, paying back favours I owe, checking in with Brian, topping up my BuckMe account. I can just engage in this fantasy - this simulation - Rockstar has built for me. And in these moments where I take my hands off the wheel, hang out with these people I've dressed up and ride around in the car I've built, it really does feel like it's been made just for me. I can't remember the last time a game made me feel that way.

Adding real-time video to a web app used to mean plugins, proprietary SDKs and a lot of money. Today every modern browser ships with WebRTC, a set of APIs that lets two browsers exchange audio, video and data directly. The catch is that WebRTC gives you building blocks, not a finished feature. This guide walks through those blocks in the order you actually need them, with the exact API calls you need, and then covers the production problems that tutorials usually skip.

A browser-to-browser call has four moving parts:.

In a recent development, start with the local preview. Browsers only allow camera access on HTTPS or localhost, so serve your page accordingly.

Sources indicate that 1. Request a stream with navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia(), passing video constraints (an ideal width of 1280 and height of 720 is a sensible default) and audio constraints with echoCancellation and noiseSuppression enabled.

According to recent reports, 2. Assign the returned MediaStream to the srcObject property of your local video element.

3. Keep a reference to the stream, because you will add its tracks to the peer connection later.

Industry observers note that set the muted and playsinline attributes on the local video element. Without muted customers hear themselves, and without playsinline iOS Safari opens the video full screen.

The peers need a way to find each other. A tiny Node.js server using the ws package is enough for development. Its whole job is to relay messages between the peers in a room:.

Sources indicate that 1. Create a WebSocket server (for example with the ws package) listening on its own port.

Recent findings suggest that 2. Keep a map of room names to the set of sockets in each room.

3. When a client sends a join message, store the room name on the socket and add it to that room's set.

According to recent reports, 4. For every other message type, forward the raw message to the other sockets in the same room, and never echo it back to the sender.

5. On disconnect, remove the socket from its room so stale peers do not receive messages.

In production you would add authentication, limit room size to two for one-to-one calls, and validate message types, but the shape stays the same.

Both sides create an RTCPeerConnection, add their local tracks and listen for the remote ones:.

It has been revealed that 1. Create a new RTCPeerConnection with an iceServers list that contains at least one STUN server.

It has been revealed that 2. Loop over the local stream's tracks and call addTrack() for each one.

Recent findings suggest that 3. In the ontrack handler, attach the first remote stream to your remote video element.

Sources indicate that 4. In the onicecandidate handler, send every fresh candidate to the other peer through your signalling channel as a candidate message.

Industry observers note that one peer creates an offer, the other answers, and both apply each other's descriptions. Candidates arrive asynchronously in the background.

Industry observers note that 1. The caller runs createOffer(), applies it with setLocalDescription() and sends the description as an offer message.

2. The callee applies the offer with setRemoteDescription(), runs createAnswer(), applies it locally and sends it back as an answer.

In a recent development, 3. The caller applies the answer with setRemoteDescription().

4. Both sides pass every incoming candidate message to addIceCandidate().

If both peers might start a call at the same time, look up the "perfect negotiation" pattern on MDN. It assigns one side as polite and resolves offer collisions cleanly instead of leaving both peers stuck.

On a home network, STUN alone often works. On corporate Wi-Fi, mobile carriers and symmetric NATs it frequently does not, and the call silently fails to connect. A TURN server relays media when a direct path is impossible. The open-source coturn server is the usual choice.

In practice, your iceServers list should contain your own STUN URL plus a TURN URL with a username and credential, so the browser can fall back to the relay automatically when direct connectivity fails.

Generate short-lived TURN credentials on your backend rather than hard-coding them, and budget for bandwidth: relayed calls pass every frame through your server.

Users deny camera access, unplug headsets and switch from Wi-Fi to 4G mid-call. Catch NotAllowedError and show a clear explanation, listen for devicechange events, and use RTCRtpSender.replaceTrack() to swap cameras without renegotiating the whole call.

Sources indicate that listen to pc.onconnectionstatechange. When the state becomes disconnected, wait a few seconds before giving up, because it often recovers. On failed, call pc.restartIce() to try newly introduced network paths.

Use RTCRtpSender.setParameters() to cap the bitrate on weak connections, and read pc.getStats() to monitor packet loss and round-trip time. Showing a small "poor connection" indicator does more for perceived quality than any codec tweak.

Mesh calls, where every participant connects to every other, work for two or three people. Beyond that, upload bandwidth explodes. Group calls need a Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU) such as mediasoup, LiveKit or Janus, which receives each stream once and forwards it to the others.

In a recent development, tutorials end at a working demo, but the fastest way to understand what production WebRTC looks like is to watch a real call from the inside. Chrome ships an internal diagnostics page that shows every peer connection the browser opens, and it works on any site that uses WebRTC.

According to recent reports, 1. Open chrome://webrtc-internals in one tab and keep it open.

According to recent reports, 2. In another tab, start a call on your own demo and find its RTCPeerConnection entry.

Industry observers note that 3. Expand that entry and look at the ICE candidate pairs: you will see whether the call went direct (host or srflx) or through a TURN relay (relay).

Sources indicate that 4. Open the stats graphs for the outbound video stream and watch the bitrate, frame rate and resolution adapt when you throttle the network in DevTools.

According to recent reports, 5. Check the negotiated codec and how swiftly the connection recovers when you switch Wi-Fi off and back on.

Sources indicate that once you can read your own call, repeat the exercise on a production service. Any browser-based product works, whether a meeting tool or a live video chat that pairs two visitors, because webrtc-internals indicates the same data for every site. Expect differences from your demo: more candidate pairs, a relay candidate in the list and a bitrate that adapts faster. Seeing them makes the earlier sections concrete, from why TURN matters to how bandwidth estimation reacts to packet loss.

Industry observers note that the one-to-one call above is the core of many products, from telehealth consultations and tutoring to customer support. The engineering challenges grow with the use case: random matching needs queueing and presence on the signalling server, public platforms need moderation and reporting, and global audiences need TURN servers in several regions.

In a recent development, start with the minimal version, get it working across Chrome, Firefox and Safari on both desktop and mobile, and add TURN before real people arrive. Once the call is reliable, every other feature becomes a much easier problem.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.

TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens. The models are further refined with supervised fine‑tuning on ~4.1M high‑quality curated samples and reinforcement learning via on‑policy GRPO with DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025). Notably, the 8B instruct model matches or surpasses the previous Granite 4.0‑H‑Small (32B‑A9B MoE) despite using a simpler dense architecture with fewer parameters. All Granite 4.1 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

It has been revealed that building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training. For Granite 4.1, we prioritized data quality over quantity, progressively refining the data mixture across five pre‑training stages. We further curated supervised fine‑tuning data using an LLM‑as‑Judge framework and applied a multi‑stage reinforcement learning pipeline to systematically strengthen performance in math, coding, instruction following, and general chat.

Industry observers note that granite 4.1 models use a decoder-only dense transformer architecture. The core design choices include Grouped Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and shared input/output embeddings.

All three model sizes share the same training pipeline and data strategy, differing only in architecture dimensions.

Granite 4.1 is trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five‑phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre‑training, phases 3–4 perform mid‑training with progressively higher‑quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long‑context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase employs a distinct data mixture and learning‑rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web‑scale data to more curated, domain‑specific content.

It has been revealed that figure 2: The five-phase pre-training pipeline. Phases 1–2 are pre-training, Phases 3–4 are mid-training (high-quality data annealing), and Phase 5 is long context training (LCE).

The first phase establishes broad language understanding using a general mixture of training data with a power learning rate schedule and warmup.

Phase 2 sharply increases the proportion of code and mathematical data, pivoting toward stronger reasoning capabilities while still maintaining general language coverage.

In a recent development, phase 3 transitions into mid-training with a more balanced, high-quality mixture and an exponential decay learning rate schedule. This is where we start blending in chain-of-thought and synthetic instruction data.

The fourth phase continues mid-training with a linear learning rate decay to zero, focusing the model on the highest-quality data available.

Figure 3: How the data mix evolves across the pre-training phases. Notice the progressive shift from web-heavy (Phase 1) to quality-heavy with instruction and reasoning data (Phases 3–4).

The fifth and final phase also part of of mid-training extends the context window from 4K to 512K through a staged long-context extension process:.

Recent findings suggest that the LCE phase uses an exponential learning rate schedule starting at 1e-4 and decaying to 0. To ensure the model natively handles long sequences without degrading short-context performance, we do a model merge after each LCE stage. RULER benchmark of base models:.

Industry observers note that supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) is what turns the base model into a reliable instruction‑following assistant, making data quality critically notable—since even a small number of incorrect or hallucinated samples can instill undesirable behaviors. To address this, we apply a rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework alongside rule‑based filtering to curate high-quality samples. Together, the pipeline automatically assess each sample against structural, semantic, and behavioral criteria, fixing issues when possible and filtering out samples that fail to meet our quality standards.

Figure 4: The SFT data quality pipeline. Raw conversation data passes through an LLM-as-Judge with a multi-dimensional rubric, producing accept/borderline/reject verdicts. Hard-reject defects (hallucination, false premise, incorrect computation) trigger automatic rejection regardless of score.

Industry observers note that our rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework evaluates only assistant responses, treating system prompts, user inputs, retrieved documents, and tool outputs strictly as contextual information. This ensures that the judge assesses what the model claims, rather than what it was asked to do. In RAG settings, responses that are not grounded in the retrieved context are flagged as hallucinations, while tool‑use outputs are validated against the set of allowed tools and their parameter schemas.

We employ specialized judge prompts tailored to different SFT data types, including multi‑turn dialogue, RAG‑augmented responses, tool‑calling interactions, and multilingual conversations. Each response is scored across six weighted dimensions—instruction following, correctness, completeness, conciseness, naturalness, and calibration (with optional critical‑thinking checks). Samples are accepted, flagged as borderline, or rejected based on deterministic score thresholds, with hard‑reject rules overriding scores for severe defects such as hallucinations, false premises, or incorrect computations.

It has been revealed that to complement semantic evaluation, we apply a deterministic rule‑based pipeline that enforces structural integrity through text normalization, truncation and length filtering, schema validation, and leakage detection. A final global deduplication step ensures dataset‑wide uniqueness. All filtering and correction actions are fully auditable.

After passing through the LLM-as-Judge, rule-based filtering, and global deduplication pipeline, we fine-tune base models on these approximately 4.1 million high-quality samples. The following details apply to all three model variants:.

After SFT, we apply a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to further improve the model's capabilities across specific domains. Rather than a single RL pass, we run multiple targeted RL stages, each optimizing for different capabilities.

We use On-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization) loss (Yu et al., 2025) which provides more stable training signals compared to standard GRPO. However, due to computationally intensive nature of dynamic sampling, we switch it off during our training runs.

Figure 10 depicts our Reinforcement Learning pipeline for training Granite 4.1 models. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of reinforcement learning recipes, we found that this sequence of steps minimizes catastrophic forgetting while simultaneously maximizing performance across multiple domains.

Figure 10: The Granite 4.1 reinforcement learning pipeline consisting of four sequential stages: Multi-domain RL, RLHF, Identity and Knowledge-calibration RL, and Math RL.

In this stage, the model is trained jointly on a unified mixture of data drawn from multiple domains. Every gradient revision therefore reflects the full diversity of tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting, boosts overall benchmark performance, and minimizes regressions on any individual task.

The different domains covered in this stage include:.

During this stage, we trained the models on 45,504 unique prompts (averaged across all Granite 4.1 models) and found that a learning rate of 5e‑7 with a KL‑loss coefficient ($\beta$) of 0.05 performed best for multi‑domain reinforcement learning.

Recent findings suggest that to further improve the model's helpfulness and chat ability, we train our model on generic-chat prompts using a multilingual scalar reward model. With this stage, we observed an average improvement of ~18.9 points (averaged across the three Granite 4.1 models) in Alpaca-Eval compared to the SFT checkpoints.

To mitigate policy drift from its previously learned knowledge, we use a conservative learning rate of 3e-7 and higher KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09 in this stage. We use an average of 17,920 unique prompts in this RLHF stage.

Recent findings suggest that in this stage, we train the model for a few steps (~40 training steps) on identity and knowledge calibration prompts. We observed that this small training stage significantly improves the model's self-identification capabilities.

Similar to the RLHF stage, we used a learning rate of 3e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09, and we use 1728 unique prompts in this stage.

During our RL training, we found that the RLHF stage causes a drop in math benchmark scores (e.g., in GSM8K, DeepMind-Math). The Math RL stage enables the model to recover from this drop and surpasses the original SFT performance on math benchmarks: ~3.8 points on average for GSM8K, and ~23.48 points on average for DeepMind-Math. We use an average of 13,504 unique prompts in this stage and similar to the multi-domain RL stage, we used a learning rate of 5e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.05.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

Granite 4.1 delivers competitive instruction‑following and tool‑calling capabilities without relying on long chains of thought. By avoiding extended reasoning traces, it provides predictable latency, stable token usage, and lower operational cost. This makes Granite 4.1 a production‑ready, open‑source choice for enterprise workloads where efficiency, reliability, and cost control are critical.

A striking result: the Granite 4.1-8B dense model consistently matches or outperforms the previous-generation Granite 4.0-H-Small, a 32B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 9B active parameters.

According to recent reports, figure 13: Granite 4.1-8B (dark blue) vs. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B (light blue) across benchmarks. The 8B dense model matches or exceeds the larger MoE model on IFEval, AlpacaEval, MMLU-Pro, BBH, GSM8K, DeepMind-Math, Evalplus, ArenaHard, BFCL V3 and MBPP(+).

Figure 14: Comparison across the Granite 4.1 family — 30B, 8B, and 3B models. Scores scale predictably with model size, with the 30B model leading across all benchmarks.

In a recent development, we also released fp8 quantized variants of the Granite 4.1 models, optimized for inference with vLLM. The precision is reduced from 16‑bit to 8‑bit, resulting in approximately a 50% reduction in both disk footprint and GPU memory usage. Quantization is applied only to the weights and activations of linear operators within the transformer blocks using LLM Compressor, while all other layers are preserved at their original precision.

We trained the Granite 4.1 Language Models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted on CoreWeave:.

This infrastructure provides the scalable, high-bandwidth interconnect needed for efficient distributed training at the token volumes required (15T+ tokens across pre-training alone).

Granite 4.1 models are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Here's how to get started with the 30B instruct model wiht tool calling example:.

Granite 4.1 marks a significant step forward for high‑quality, open‑source language models. By prioritizing data quality and rigor at every stage—from pre‑training curation to supervised fine‑tuning and multi‑stage reinforcement learning—we deliver a substantially improved post‑training pipeline. The result is stronger instruction following, tool use, and conversational performance, showing that carefully trained dense 8B models can rival much larger MoE architectures. We’re excited to see how the community adopts and builds on these models.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • has banned the export of advanced AI chips to China since 2022 in an effort to limit its advancement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI data centers in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia are facing trouble as Nvidia has reportedly ordered its manufacturing partners to stop shipping AI servers to the region. According to the Financial Times, Dell, Supermicro, and other firms that make AI servers using Nvidia AI GPUs have told their customers from the four countries that the AI chip maker has forbidden them to ship their orders. The move comes as the U.S. closed the loophole that let Chinese AI companies rent compute from data centers outside China equipped with advanced AI chips sourced from American semiconductor manufacturers like Nvidia.

The U.S. has banned the export of advanced AI chips to China since 2022 in an effort to limit its advancement. Even though President Trump eventually allowed Nvidia to export H100 AI GPUs to China in December 2025, companies that wanted to buy them needed to secure an import license from the Commerce Department. Aside from that, the White House is also collecting a 25% fee for every chip, making it more expensive for a data center in China to buy them. Because of this, many Chinese AI labs are instead renting compute from data centers located abroad. They mostly do this in Southeast Asia, which is just around a four-to-six-hour flight from major cities like Hong Kong, Shenzhen, and Shanghai, although some firms are looking in further areas like Europe.

It remains unclear if Nvidia’s order is permanent or temporary, but the latest export rules give cloud providers 90 days to apply for an export license and prove that their customers do not include restricted entities. However, one cloud provider executive told the Financial Times that there are no clear instructions on how to go about this. “There’s this new rule but no guidance on execution,” they said. “No one knows how to apply for this license while the 90-day clock is ticking. It’s causing sheer chaos in the region.”.

In a recent development, this sudden halt of orders is causing trouble for many data centers in Southeast Asia. Sources say that Aolani, a Singapore-based cloud tech giant with a deal to provide compute to ByteDance, is losing financing for the project as bankers have stopped issuing credit to the tune of $500 million as Nvidia GPU shipments to the region remain in jeopardy. The Chinese social media giant could also potentially drop out of the arrangement, as it won’t be able to access the powerful Nvidia chips that many AI labs still prefer for training their models.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that TLDR: Appen Inc.
  • Recent findings suggest that we’re not updating the average WER at this time: by default, the leaderboard’s Average WER remains computed on public datasets only.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." (Goodhart’s Law).

It has been revealed that TLDR: Appen Inc. and DataoceanAI have provided high-quality English ASR datasets covering scripted and conversational speech over multiple accents. To prevent potential risks of benchmaxxing or test-set contamination, we will keep these datasets private for a high-quality measure of performance on multiple tasks.

Recent findings suggest that we’re not updating the average WER at this time: by default, the leaderboard’s Average WER remains computed on public datasets only. You can optionally include the private datasets using the toggle to see their impact 👀.

Since its launch in September 2023, the Open ASR Leaderboard has been visited over 710K times. We’re blown away by the community’s interest and motivation to keep pushing speech recognition 🗣️.

Two words sum up the objectives (but also challenges) in maintaining a benchmark like the Open ASR Leaderboard:.

Recent findings suggest that standardization: models can have different conventions for their usage and outputs, e.g. with/without punctuation and casing. Datasets have the same challenges and can be structured differently. To this end, all test sets have been gathered into a single dataset on the Hub for easy access and previewing. Moreover, to standardize model outputs and dataset transcripts, we use a normalizer that (among other things) removes punctuation and casing, and maps to American spelling. It is based on the normalizer of Whisper.

Industry observers note that openness: the UI code and evaluation scripts are open-sourced. This has helped not only to incorporate fresh models, but also to improve the quality of the evaluation procedure through community feedback and contributions.

Standardization and openness are essential for meaningful benchmarking, but they also make benchmarks more susceptible to benchmark-specific optimization ("benchmaxxing"), where models improve leaderboard performance without corresponding gains in real-world robustness. As models and use cases evolve, the Open ASR Leaderboard will continue incorporating high-quality datasets and upcoming evaluation settings to better reflect real-world performance and improve robustness against benchmark-specific optimization.

As discussed in our report, there is no single "catch-all" ASR model: some perform better on American English, others on diverse accents and multilingual settings, while others are optimized for speed or conversational audio. Different applications also prioritize different capabilities, so a model that performs less well on one dimension is not necessarily a worse model overall. The goal of the Open ASR Leaderboard is to capture these nuances and provide a more holistic view of ASR performance.

To this end, we have worked with Appen Inc. and DataoceanAI to curate high-quality datasets for ASR benchmarking. Below is some information on the various splits.

Below are sample audio showing the variety of content (scripted, conversational, acronyms, disfluencies, proper nouns).

While private datasets may sound contrary to the spirit of openness, we believe that incorporating such datasets will increase the trustworthiness of the Open ASR Leaderboard, as they are less likely to be exploited for benchmaxxing, whether by model developers who explicitly use the public test sets or who try to find training data that closely resembles a particular dataset to boost their score in the macroaverage.

Recent findings suggest that with these datasets, we can also provide targeted metrics to highlight gaps and biases between controlled and often saturated settings (scripted, American accent) and more nuanced conditions (conversational and non-American accents). Below is a screenshot of the new "Private data" tab.

Below is how each column is computed.

We intentionally do not provide a score on each split, to avoid model developers from boosting their score with a specific data provider or accent.

It has been revealed that get your model on the Open ASR Leaderboard, and we'll run the evaluation! As before, the process for adding a model to the leaderboard takes place on the Open ASR Leaderboard GitHub:.

While you wait for your model to be added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, you can self-report your metrics on the public sets by adding a YAML file like this to your model card. Your model will then appear on an (unverified) leaderboard that appears on the dataset page (see screenshot below). More on this approach to decentralized evaluation can be read here.

Industry observers note that they could. We’ve asked Appen and DataoceanAI to not provide this data to their clients. But even if they do not provide this exact data, data from a similar distribution could still help the model on the corresponding evaluation set (similar to benchmaxxing by optimizing for a challenging task from the public sets). To this end, having multiple data providers balances out the advantage a model may get from having used data from one of the providers. And we are open to more data providers and eval sets for the "Private data" tab!

Moreover, to ensure that the private sets do not affect the model ranking, we’ve defaulted the Average WER to not include the Private sets in its macroaverage.

In the screenshot below, you can see that "Private data" is toggled off. This means that the macroaverage across datasets does not include it.

Simply toggle on "Private data" splits to include them in the macroaverage.

Recent findings suggest that the "Rank Δ" column shows how the ordering changes relative to the default macroaverage configuration. Including or excluding public datasets also changes the macroaverage, allowing users to tailor the evaluation to the use cases and data distributions most relevant to their application.

We’re excited to hear the community’s feedback on how the latest track and dataset toggling features help customers identify the model(s) that best fit their application(s). We’re also looking into evaluations that better reflect real-world noisy conditions, and you can expect some news on that 😉.

Recent findings suggest that while preparing the private evaluation sets, we took extra care to ensure consistent audio and transcript quality across datasets, including developing tooling to identify challenging cases such as low signal-to-noise conditions or transcript mismatches, since these factors can meaningfully affect WER. More on that in a future post!

Sources indicate that just a quick observation on how we evaluate our models: The two data vendors mentioned earlier are offering datasets directly to ASR service providers for training. With that in mind, it feels like we should be extra prudent about mixing private data into our evaluations.

At the same time, we're missing out on a lot of high-quality, open-source speech datasets simply because their creators don't have sales teams advocating for them. It would be a huge step forward to open a channel where the research community can recommend these datasets to the leaderboard directly.

Industry observers note that P.S. I found myself relating a lot to King George in the movie Hoppers recently. That beaver king just believes the best about everyone. I want to bring that same optimism here—hoping that everyone continues to follow the leaderboard rules, avoids training on open-source test sets, and actively cleans their training data of any contamination.

Electronics manufacturers set up memory 'war rooms' to find, lock in DRAM supplies amid worst shortage in history

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the memory shortage has gotten so bad that many companies, especially smaller ones, have started establishing “procurement war rooms,” where employees are desperately trying to find memory chip supplies on sites like eBay and trying to figure out how they could make manufacturers offer them even just a small amount of DRAM.
  • The Wall Street Journal reports that Taiwanese memory module and storage maker Apacer had to take out loans just to have money on hand in case it finds a supply of memory chips.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the memory shortage has gotten so bad that many companies, especially smaller ones, have started establishing “procurement war rooms,” where employees are desperately trying to find memory chip supplies on sites like eBay and trying to figure out how they could make manufacturers offer them even just a small amount of DRAM. This massive shortage has pushed up costs for electronic manufacturers, with some companies forced to increase prices to make up the difference while others cut the specifications of their products while introducing a smaller price bump.

The Wall Street Journal reports that Taiwanese memory module and storage maker Apacer had to take out loans just to have money on hand in case it finds a supply of memory chips. “If chips show up, we take it,” Apacer President Gibson Chen told the publication. “This is crazy, but there is no other way.” Even one of the world’s richest people, Elon Musk, was reportedly having trouble finding memory chips. A portfolio manager claimed that Musk offered Samsung an LTA and even a financial guarantee for upcoming Samsung chip factories, but the manufacturer’s executive chairman, Lee Jae-yong, allegedly answered that everyone else was offering those things already. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also recently went to South Korea to meet with Samsung leadership just to secure more RAM for data centers.

Even though PC builders and enthusiasts were the hardest hit by the 500% climb in memory prices, many other electronics manufacturers are also now feeling the squeeze. Major companies like Amazon, Apple, and Microsoft could use their scale and resources to pay more and secure massive amounts of memory chip supplies under long-term agreements (LTAs). However, smaller firms would usually have to rely on brokers and whatever’s available to find what they need. Some have reportedly contacted hundreds of brokers and go through online listings, where they would snap up even small batches of just five or 12 units just to have some supply. Others proceed to the gray market, although they must be careful as some unscrupulous sellers mix in batches of used memory chips with brand new orders to inflate their deliveries.

Recent findings suggest that the scramble for AI compute has caused a massive memory chip shortage, especially as the big three memory chip manufacturers — Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix — have focused their production on more lucrative HBM. Both memory chip manufacturers and RAM kit makers are warning of continued shortages, too, with SK hynix saying 2027 will be the “worst year” for memory shortages, while TeamGroup’s CEO noted that it could reach a point where “even money can’t buy goods.” Although the big three manufacturers are building latest factories, they’re not expected to go online and start pushing out memory chips until 2028.

Sources indicate that it’s difficult for a new player to enter the memory chip market. Aside from the enormous costs involved in setting up a factory and supply chain to build memory chips, any potential entrant must also license a ton of patents and develop its own technologies before it can start making competitive chips. Even if it was able to get its hands on the knowledge required to design memory chips, it still needs the manufacturing expertise needed to produce them at scale. CXMT is the only new player that has successfully produced mainstream consumer DDR5 RAM, but it’s facing multiple allegations that it stole the technology needed to achieve that from Samsung. Even then, the DDR5 memory chips that the Chinese organization produced don’t have the same performance as its competitors and track market prices, meaning it’s not the affordable alternative that many tech enthusiasts imagined it to be.

Recent findings suggest that the memory chip market is known for its boom-and-bust cycle, which is why manufacturers were initially reluctant to increase their capacity. But even if they started building factories at the first sign of a shortage, it would still take several years before these fresh facilities could start pumping out chips to ease the situation. Nevertheless, the three companies are right now facing a price-fixing lawsuit alleging that they coordinated their shift to HBM to cut DDR3 and DDR4 production, with the judge handling the case saying that it’s plausible they colluded as the market experienced the price surge.

Industry observers note that it’s in the name. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 folds and unfolds like other foldable devices – that much you know. But what the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s form factor provides is something different to what most might be familiar with.

Instead of a tall device that unfolds into a near-uniform square display, you get a wider screen more like a tablet. That makes it perfect for watching videos or movies. Content that naturally works well on TVs or your computer will look great on the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

Sources indicate that what about content that’s best viewed in portrait mode? Because it opens up to a tablet-like display, you can turn the Fold 8 to watch YouTube Shorts or Instagram Reels without a problem, so if you or someone you know likes to watch content on a bigger display, the Z Fold 8 makes that much easier. It really doesn’t matter what content you come across – the wider inner display gives you that large screen feeling.

Like a well-designed tool, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 has more purposes than the tasks best suited for the inner display. That shorter, wider profile makes the outer display smaller, but not as thin as something on other foldables, like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

In reality, the aspect ratio is similar enough across both the inner and outer screens that most content scales well on the shorter front panel. Social apps like X and Instagram look great because videos and images are able to fill the screen, rather than squeeze. Samsung’s One UI software also supports app optimization across both screens, although the experience may vary by app.

Industry observers note that saying the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s outer display is “minimal” isn’t a dig, either. Apps can be refreshing to use when you don’t need to open them on a large scale. Recent findings suggest that and guess what? If you don’t like using the app on a smaller display, just unfold the phone. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is such a versatile phone, whether it’s a gift during the holidays or one for yourself.

There are instances where you need the large real estate. One UI 9 gives the Galaxy Z Fold 8 the option to open and run multiple apps on your screen. There are several ways you can do it, too.

Sources indicate that the main approach is to split two apps on the wide inner display. But if you want to see more from one app, you can simply drag the split over in one direction. One UI 9 leaves room to add one more app to that split screen, giving you a three-way Split View. All it takes is dragging an app from the taskbar and choosing the spot.

It has been revealed that if you truly need a fourth app open, you have the option to open another in a floating window. Having four apps open at once is definitely a niche instance, but the Galaxy Z Fold 8 handles it like it’s nothing. You can have YouTube up in one corner while you check Messages for gift ideas and shop through the Amazon app. It might be helpful to keep a list of what you got and for whom in a floating Sheets window.

The point is not only that it’s technically possible, but it’s usable. So often devices let customers open apps in split screen, but are in no way comfortable enough for the task. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is perfect for it, and the experience actually makes you more productive, not less.

Let’s say you’re taking photos, and you need to get a shot of yourself, but no one is around to take the photo for you. The Galaxy Z Fold 8’s hinge lets it prop itself up, so you can do things like set a timer and run to strike a pose.

Think of how many times you wanted to get a good angle on a plane or somewhere where there’s this flat surface just asking for a tiny tripod or kickstand. Some people don’t use AI at work—and feel judged for it

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New workplace fear unlocked—and it’s not being yelled at for heated-up fish in the office microwave or getting too merry at the Christmas party.
  • Latest workplace fear unlocked—and it’s not being yelled at for heated-up fish in the office microwave or getting too merry at the Christmas party.
  • As companies continue to invest billions in their AI strategies, nearly half of employees fear judgment for not using artificial intelligence enough at work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New workplace fear unlocked—and it’s not being yelled at for heated-up fish in the office microwave or getting too merry at the Christmas party. As companies continue to invest billions in their AI strategies, nearly half of employees fear judgment for not using artificial intelligence enough at work. That’s according to the third annual Inclusion Initiative report from London School of Economics (LSE) and consulting firm Protiviti, which surveyed 3,001 professional employees between March and May 2026. With AI spending forecast to grow to $2.59 trillion this year—up 47% from 2025—the AI transition is no longer a personal choice, but is transforming workplace norms and expectations. When AI first entered workplaces, more workers feared judgment or being caught out for using the technology. Now the opposite is true: 48% worry about being judged for not using AI enough, compared with 20% who worry about being judged for using it. Almost three quarters of those surveyed (74%) now use AI at work, up from 29% in 2024. But the pressure to adopt AI in workflows has birthed a new kind of busywork—workers are pretending to use AI even when they aren’t. A separate report by software firm Visier found nearly half of workers (48%) said they have “exaggerated their AI usage or expertise to colleagues or leadership” to keep up with expectations. While organizations understand the importance of equipping their workforces with AI tools, there is still work to be done when it comes to supporting employees with AI adoption. Only 39% of owners have built AI into a standardized way of working, according to the LSE Inclusion Initiative and Protiviti report. Those who have reported saving 27% of time in their work week with AI, compared with 14% for those who haven’t. Gen Z is far more likely to have been AI-trained in the past year compared with their baby boomer colleagues. AI-trained employees report saving 22% of their working hours, compared with 13% for those left to figure it out alone. And what exactly happens to all that extra time saved by AI? More time for more work, of course. And it’s causing what researchers are calling “workload creep”. “AI is creating meaningful productivity gains, but the bigger opportunity is how organizations use the capacity it creates,” said Matt Duncan, managing director at Protiviti, in the press release. “Simply absorbing those gains into existing workloads leaves much of AI’s potential untapped.” Researchers at Boston Consulting Group found that 14% of people who use AI workflows requiring a high degree of oversight experience “AI brain fry.” This mental fog and inability to focus can result in more mistakes at work, and even employees considering quitting altogether. AI or not, job performance is still dependent on people, at least for now. And the LSE and Protiviti report found no consistent association between an employee’s perceived performance and their AI adoption, access, training or workflow integration. Instead, performance stayed tied to confidence in solving problems, conscientiousness, resilience and willingness to learn. As AI continues to become embedded in everyday work, organizations need to focus on whether it is actually helping employees be more efficient at work, or simply creating time to pile more work on their plates. “Leaders should think deliberately about where that capacity can create the most value, whether that means tackling higher-value work, improving quality or giving employees greater space to solve problems and innovate,” said Duncan. “The goal shouldn’t just be doing more work faster, but using AI to change what people are able to accomplish.”.

Google has thoroughly redesigned Gemini for Android’s in-app camera that lets you swiftly add an image to prompts.

Available from the ‘plus’ menu in the prompt box, the old interface rolled out a fullscreen viewfinder that was quite generic. This UI is still in use when you launch the camera from the Gemini overlay.

The new one appears inline on the Gemini homepage or inside a conversation. It launches as a bottom sheet that you can drag up — with a really slick animation — to take up most of the screen.

This nearly edge-to-edge redesign, which extends behind the system navigation bar, is a stark contrast to the old approach.

In a recent development, to the right of the capture button is a three-dot overflow button that animates on open, revealing options to control the flash and switch to the front-facing camera. There’s a back button on the other side, but you can also just swipe down.

This camera redesign first launched in the Gemini for iOS app, but has now widely rolled out on Android in both the beta and stable (version 17.76+) channels. Be sure to Force stop the Google app if you’re not seeing it live yet.

This follows the launch of GIF creation in the Gemini app yesterday. Powered by Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, select GIF from the Format menu or specify “Create a GIF” in your prompt. Google frames this feature as an alternative to searching for GIFs.

Say hello to GIFs in Gemini. Say goodbye to searching for the perfect one.From looping photo effects to funny memes, create any GIF you can imagine with our latest video model, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, for smooth motion and consistent quality across every frame.

vLLM V0 to V1: Correctness Before Corrections in RL

📅 06 May 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, pipelineRL uses vLLM as the inference engine for rollout generation.
  • vLLM V1 matched our vLLM V0 reference after we fixed four things: processed rollout logprobs, V1-specific runtime defaults, the inflight weight-update path, and the fp32 lm_head used for the final projection.
  • In a recent development, the reference run used vLLM 0.8.5; the V1 runs used vLLM 0.18.1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, pipelineRL uses vLLM as the inference engine for rollout generation. The inference engine samples tokens and returns token logprobs; the trainer uses those logprobs to compute policy ratios, KL, clip rate, entropy, and reward. Any discrepancy in how those logprobs are computed can change the training dynamics. This is the train-inference mismatch we needed to eliminate during the vLLM V0 to V1 migration.

TL;DR. vLLM V1 matched our vLLM V0 reference after we fixed four things: processed rollout logprobs, V1-specific runtime defaults, the inflight weight-update path, and the fp32 lm_head used for the final projection. We fixed the backend behavior before changing the RL objective.

In a recent development, the reference run used vLLM 0.8.5; the V1 runs used vLLM 0.18.1. Figure 1 shows the final result. The red run is the initial V1 attempt, and the green run is the final V1 run after the fixes described below.

vLLM V1 is a substantial rewrite of the V0 engine. Our migration target was therefore deliberately narrow:.

The first visible symptoms appeared in:.

According to recent reports, those metrics came from a GSPO training run, the objective used for this experiment. The same class of mismatch can surface in PPO, GRPO, or any online RL system that treats rollout-side logprobs as part of the optimization target.

According to recent reports, the initial V1 run indicated the problem clearly. The trainer-side logprobs and reward moved away from the V0 reference early in training.

The same pattern appears in the trainer metrics. Clip rate is the easiest signal to read in the initial comparison.

We separated the possible causes into three layers:.

Industry observers note that we initially suspected the third category too early. The useful diagnosis came from treating the first two as backend behavior problems and ruling them out first.

It has been revealed that the first problem was semantic. vLLM V1 returns logprobs from the raw model outputs by default, before logits post-processing such as temperature scaling, penalties, and top-k/top-p filtering. PipelineRL expected logprobs from the processed distribution used by the sampler.

It has been revealed that this removed the obvious mean offset in rollout logprobs. The training curves still showed a gap relative to the known-good reference, so the next issue had to be in the inference path.

The policy-ratio plot indicates this directly. Once processed_logprobs is on for V1, the mean policy ratio stays centered extremely close to 1.0 across all three runs. That establishes the mean-bias fix. The remaining mismatch shows up in clip rate, KL, entropy, and downstream training behavior.

The early V1 run mixed the engine version with V1 runtime defaults:.

For the parity run, we made these choices explicit:.

Prefix caching deserves a separate note. It is normally a correctness-preserving inference optimization for a fixed model state. In this online RL setup, it was a V1-only difference in cache lifetime and reuse relative to the V0 reference path. The actor was also handling repeated prefixes, concurrent requests, async scheduling, and inflight weight updates.

A prefix-cache hit can reuse state computed before a weight revision when the cache policy ignores the weight-update boundary. Disabling prefix caching removed one V1-only degree of freedom from the parity comparison.

Sources indicate that weight synchronization also had to match the online-RL update model. One option was to make V1 stricter than V0 by draining requests and clearing caches at every update. That would answer a separate question. We first needed to verify that V1 could match the existing V0 behavior.

What V0 effectively did was closer to:.

Lag was a useful runtime diagnostic. The initial V1 path carries more persistent lag later in training than the corrected V1 run.

Recent findings suggest that the V1 backend fixes above removed the obvious migration complications, but final parity still required matching the numerical path used to compute logits. The trainer used an fp32 lm_head for the final projection. The rollout backend had to match that behavior.

A closely related problem appears in the MiniMax-M1 technical report: their RL run revealed a training/inference token-probability mismatch that they traced to the LM output head and fixed by computing the head in fp32.

Recent findings suggest that this matters because the RL update consumes token logprobs directly. Small changes in logits can become visible in policy ratios, KL, and clipping. The final projection precision is therefore part of the correctness surface for online RL. The ScaleRL paper later includes fp32 logits/head computation as part of its RL recipe and ablates it as a useful design choice for large-scale RL.

With the fp32 lm_head path included, reward gives a compact view of the final parity result. In Figure 6, the final V1 run tracks the V0 reference; the initial V1 attempt produces a clearly different reward curve.

The negative results are important because they rule out common explanations.

Objective-side corrections such as truncated importance sampling, importance-ratio reweighting, and related methods are useful tools. If rollouts are intentionally stale, generated asynchronously, or produced by a backend where equivalence to the trainer-side policy is unavailable, then some form of correction is often the right thing to add.

The first problem here was inference correctness. After moving to V1, the rollout backend returned logprobs and runtime behavior that broke the trainer assumption. Adding an objective-side correction at that point would have mixed two questions:.

According to recent reports, those questions need to be separated. Otherwise an objective-side correction can compensate for broken inference-backend behavior, which makes the training curve harder to interpret.

The current objective can still improve. After inference parity is restored, the next improvement is the usual async/off-policy cleanup:.

The main lesson from this migration is narrower: fix backend correctness first, then add corrections for the mismatch that remains.

Ever describe an AI agent’s error as a “hallucination”? Fret over the threat of “superintelligence”? How about call an AI assistant your “copilot”? Beware: you may have been glosslit by the AI industry. “Glosslighting” combines “glossary” and “gaslighting.” It’s for situations where industries develop lingo that intentionally misleads consumers in order to shape public perception—something that researchers at Simon Fraser University think the artificial intelligence industry is doing in spades. Every industry has its own specialized vocab, and there’s nothing inherently wrong with insider lingo. But with an industry like AI, where development is hotly debated and potential controversy lies around every corner, word choice takes on extra weight. What is glosslighting? For the study, researchers at the university in British Columbia analyzed 30 of the AI industry’s biggest buzzwords, breaking down the ways that common language around the technology can control public opinion. The study’s authors emphasize that while AI terms have been looked at in isolation, they’re more interested in AI’s “interlocking vocabulary” and the way it protects AI companies from taking accountability for the dark sides of their technology. “Behind the language of seamless intelligence are workers who classify traumatic content for low wages, communities whose water is consumed by server farms, and individuals whose lives are determined by probabilistic decision tools sometimes named, reassuringly, as ‘solutions,’” the authors write. How AI jargon causes harm The study’s authors group the terms by the way they cause harm, the truth about AI they obscure, and the questions they deflect. Those groupings include the following: “Hallucination,” “copilot,” “robot rights,” and “agentic AI” humanize the technology, diverting attention from the people and companies making the decisions around them. “The cloud,” “data mining,” “scaling,” and “human-in-the-loop” hide the environmental and social costs of AI development. “Superintelligence,” “frontier AI,” “AGI,” “existential risk,” “smart city,” “AI superpower,” and “race to AI” shift focus to the future of AI, limiting attention on present-day concerns. “Democratizing AI,” “open AI,” “responsible AI,” “ethical AI,” “collaborative AI,” and “human-centric AI” let AI companies frame themselves as trustworthy. “Bias,” “ex-ante risk regulation,” “deep learning,” and “data subjects” paint some problems as technological or too complex for laypeople to understand, shutting down debates about their usage before they begin The study’s authors go on to recommend alternatives for many of these terms that simplify communication, demystify confusing terms, or go in depth to provide greater accuracy to descriptions of AI’s impact. One author, Nicholas Vincent, an assistant professor of computing science, told Tech Xplore that “problems where there’s real complexity mean there’s a responsibility to do more to help people understand.” “Everyone exposed to AI deserves accurate descriptions of what it is and how it’s used,” Vincent stated. “As consumers get a little bit pickier, there’s going to be more demand for specifics. That is, ‘If you want me to buy your expensive AI product, you better have a pretty clear sales pitch for what it actually is.’”.
