Building Blocks for Foundation Model Training and Inference on AWS

📅 11 May 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For a long time, "scaling" in foundation models mostly meant one thing: spend more compute on pre-training and capabilities rise.
  • Figure: Adapted from "AI's Three Scaling Laws, Explained" (NVIDIA Blog).
  • Taken together, these scaling regimes push the foundation-model lifecycle—pre-training, post-training, and inference—toward convergent infrastructure requirements: tightly coupled accelerator compute, a high-bandwidth low-latency network, and a distributed storage backend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a long time, "scaling" in foundation models mostly meant one thing: spend more compute on pre-training and capabilities rise. That intuition was supported by empirical work such as Kaplan et al. (2020), which reported predictable power-law trends in loss as you scale model parameters, dataset size, and training compute. In practice, these trends justified sustained investment in large-scale accelerator capacity and the surrounding distributed infrastructure needed to keep it efficiently utilized. But the frontier has evolved—and scaling is no longer a single curve. NVIDIA's "from one to three scaling laws" framing usefully emphasizes that, beyond pre-training, performance increasingly scales through post-training (e.g., supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods) and through test-time compute ("long thinking," search/verification, multi-sample strategies).

Figure: Adapted from "AI's Three Scaling Laws, Explained" (NVIDIA Blog).

Taken together, these scaling regimes push the foundation-model lifecycle—pre-training, post-training, and inference—toward convergent infrastructure requirements: tightly coupled accelerator compute, a high-bandwidth low-latency network, and a distributed storage backend. They also raise the importance of orchestration for resource management, and of application- and hardware-level observability to maintain cluster health and diagnose performance pathologies at scale.

Another key trend is the increasing reliance of the foundation-model lifecycle on an open-source software (OSS) ecosystem that spans model development frameworks, cluster resource management, and operational tooling. At the cluster layer, resource management is typically provided by systems such as Slurm and Kubernetes. Model development and distributed training are commonly implemented in frameworks such as PyTorch and JAX. Monitoring and visualization—that is, observability—are often achieved using Prometheus for metrics collection and Grafana for visualization and alerting, positioned as an operational layer atop infrastructure and resource management. Figure 1 illustrates this layered architecture, showing how hardware infrastructure supports resource orchestration, which in turn enables ML frameworks, with observability spanning across all layers.

Figure 1: The layered architecture of open-source software stacks for foundation model training and inference.

This post is intended for machine learning engineers and researchers involved in foundation model training and inference, with particular attention to workflows built atop OSS frameworks. It analyzes how AWS infrastructure—including multi-node accelerator compute, high-bandwidth low-latency networking, distributed shared storage, and associated managed services—interacts with common OSS stacks across the foundation model lifecycle. The primary goal is to provide a technical foundation for understanding systems bottlenecks and scaling characteristics spanning pre-training, post-training, and inference. This introductory post surfaces the overall system architecture, emphasizing the integration points between AWS infrastructure components and OSS tools that underpin large-scale distributed training and inference.

The remainder of this series examines how this layered architecture is realized on AWS, progressing through infrastructure, resource orchestration, the ML software stack, and observability. The following sections preview each layer.

As illustrated in Figure 1, infrastructure is anchored by three coupled building blocks—accelerated compute with large device memory, wide-bandwidth interconnect for collective communication, and scalable distributed storage for data and checkpoints.

In a recent development, accelerated compute forms the foundation of large-scale foundation model pre-training, post-training, and inference. AWS offers several generations of NVIDIA GPUs as part of its Amazon EC2 accelerated computing instances, including the Amazon EC2 P instance family. The P5 instance family includes p5.48xlarge with eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs, p5.4xlarge with a single H100 GPU for smaller-scale workloads, and p5e.48xlarge/p5en.48xlarge variants with NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The P6 instance family introduces NVIDIA Blackwell B200 architecture with p6-b200.48xlarge and Blackwell Ultra B300 with p6-b300.48xlarge. Across these generations, the dominant scaling axes are peak Tensor throughput, HBM capacity and bandwidth, and interconnect bandwidth (within and across nodes).

Sources indicate that as a first-order approximation, peak Tensor Core throughput—measured in floating point operations per second (FLOPS)—helps situate these accelerators on a common axis. The table below summarizes per-GPU peak throughput for dense BF16/FP16 and FP8 Tensor operations, along with HBM capacity and HBM bandwidth, using SXM/HGX-class specifications that align with NVSwitch/NVLink-based multi-GPU nodes.

Sources indicate that note: NVIDIA product tables often report Tensor throughput “with sparsity”; this table reports dense throughput. Where applicable, dense throughput is taken as half of sparse throughput, following NVIDIA’s guidance for HGX-class platforms (NVIDIA). DGX figures are system-level; the B200 HBM capacity and bandwidth values are expressed per GPU by dividing DGX totals by eight (NVIDIA).

Sources indicate that as models scale, step time is often dominated by collective communication and memory movement rather than raw compute throughput, motivating explicit scale-up and scale-out bandwidth accounting. For the multi-GPU instances, GPU communication spans two regimes. Internal scale-up (NVLink/NVSwitch) provides high-bandwidth, low-latency GPU-to-GPU connectivity within a node, enabling collectives such as all-reduce and all-gather to execute without traversing the host networking stack. External scale-out (EFA) provides OS-bypass networking across nodes, which AWS uses as a building block for Amazon EC2 UltraClusters where communication-heavy collectives span thousands of instances. The following table summarizes key specifications across these instance types:.

In a recent development, note: EFA bandwidth is converted from Gbps to GB/s (÷8) for consistency with other bandwidth metrics; see the EC2 accelerated computing networking specifications. NVLink and EFA bandwidth figures are shown as aggregate per-instance values rather than per-link values; see the P5 instance family page and the P6 instance family page for the corresponding intra-node interconnect and networking characteristics.

Sources indicate that elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) is a network interface for Amazon EC2 that provides OS-bypass remote direct memory access (RDMA) capability using the Scalable Reliable Datagram (SRD) protocol. By enabling applications to communicate directly with the network device through the Libfabric API—bypassing the operating system kernel—EFA reduces latency and improves throughput for collective operations in distributed training.

In a recent development, multiple generations of EFA are available on different instance families. Amazon EC2 P5 and P5e instances are equipped with EFA version 2 (EFAv2). EFA version 3 (EFAv3), provided on P5en instances, reduces packet latency by approximately 35% compared to EFAv2. EFA version 4 (EFAv4), available on P6 instances, delivers an additional 18% improvement in collective communication performance relative to EFAv3.

At scale, both distributed training (streaming corpora and writing multi-terabyte checkpoints) and large-scale inference (staging weights and managing KV cache growth) motivate a tiered storage hierarchy—local NVMe SSD for hot data, Lustre for shared high-throughput access, and Amazon S3 for durable persistence.

In this series’ primary multi-GPU instances, local NVMe is provided as instance store (ephemeral) with 30.72 TB raw capacity (8 × 3.84 TB NVMe SSD); see the EC2 accelerated-computing instance store specifications.

Industry observers note that lustre is an open-source, POSIX compliant distributed file system widely used in high-performance computing (HPC) to provide a shared namespace with high aggregate throughput across many clients. Amazon FSx for Lustre provides Lustre as a fully managed service and exposes it as a parallel file system capable of terabytes per second of throughput, millions of IOPS, and sub-millisecond latencies. Data Repository Associations enable integration with Amazon S3, supporting lazy loading of training datasets and automatic checkpoint export for durability.

At cluster scale, these instances are deployed in Amazon EC2 UltraClusters, which provision thousands of accelerated instances as a single, tightly placed cluster within an Availability Zone and interconnect them using a petabit-scale nonblocking network.

Figure: 2nd-generation Amazon EC2 UltraClusters (example P5 UltraCluster).

For workloads with high per-step communication intensity (e.g., expert parallelism in MoE models where all-to-all token dispatch spans many GPUs), the size of the NVLink domain can become a first-order constraint. As an extension of the internal scale-up axis, increasing the NVLink domain reduces how often performance-critical communication must leave the NVLink fabric.

According to recent reports, amazon EC2 UltraServers extend the NVLink domain beyond a single EC2 instance by connecting multiple component instances through a dedicated accelerator interconnect. AWS reports that P6e-GB200 UltraServers are built on the NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 platform and expose up to 72 Blackwell GPUs and 13.4 TB of aggregate HBM3e within one NVLink domain. At larger scales, EFA remains the cross-node fabric for multi-UltraServer jobs, but increasing the intra-domain GPU count can reduce how often performance-critical communication must leave the NVLink fabric.

Industry observers note that these systems are built from NVIDIA Grace–Blackwell superchips, which couple Grace CPU memory and Blackwell GPU HBM via cache-coherent NVLink-C2C, enabling direct access across CPU- and GPU-attached memory without explicit host–device copies. In practice, this can extend the effective memory available to GPU workloads (e.g., by placing colder model state or KV cache in CPU-attached memory) while avoiding PCIe-scale copy overheads, albeit with higher latency and lower bandwidth than local HBM.

Recent findings suggest that the component instance type for P6e-GB200 UltraServers is p6e-gb200.36xlarge, which provides four GPUs and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) v4 networking. The tables below summarize the per-instance and composed UltraServer configurations.

Note: The p6e-gb200.36xlarge EFA bandwidth is converted from the published aggregate EFA networking (4 × 400 Gbps) to GB/s (÷8); see the EC2 accelerated computing networking specifications.

Note: UltraServer EFA bandwidth is converted from terabits per second (Tbps), as reported by AWS, to GB/s (÷8); see the P6e-GB200 UltraServers announcement and the P6 instance family page.

Industry observers note that when training spans hundreds or thousands of accelerators, manual resource management becomes intractable. For example, a training job requiring 512 GPUs must co-schedule 64 eight-GPU nodes (P-instances) simultaneously, and release resources atomically upon completion or failure. Both Slurm and Kubernetes address this challenge through a control-plane architecture: a centralized scheduler maintains cluster state and makes allocation decisions, while worker nodes execute assigned workloads.

Figure 2: High-level architecture of Slurm-based and Kubernetes-based resource orchestration on AWS.

Slurm (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) is the dominant workload manager in high-performance computing, built on a modular plugin architecture that allows the scheduling algorithm, topology model, resource types, and accounting backend to be configured independently. Its scheduling model organizes resources into partitions (logical groupings of nodes), accepts job submissions via sbatch, and debuts parallel tasks via srun with synchronized startup across allocated nodes. Critically for distributed training, Slurm schedules at the job level—allocating entire multi-node jobs atomically before any task launches. A backfill scheduler starts lower-priority jobs in idle slots without delaying higher-priority ones, while a multi-factor priority system weighs fair-share usage, job age, and QOS tiers to order the queue across tenants. Slurm also supports topology-aware placement through plugins that model network switch hierarchies—on AWS, encoding the EFA fabric topology to co-locate jobs on nodes with minimal switch hops—and native GPU scheduling through its Generic Resource (GRES) interface, which tracks GPU types and enforces device affinity.

According to recent reports, AWS provides multiple deployment options for Slurm-based orchestration. AWS ParallelCluster is an open-source cluster management tool that automates the deployment of Slurm clusters on EC2, handling head node provisioning, compute fleet scaling, and integration with shared storage. AWS Parallel Computing Service (PCS) offers an alternative that provides the managed control plane. For distributed training workloads specifically, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod supports Slurm mode with additional capabilities tailored to large-scale training, such as continuous node health monitoring and job auto-resume functionality.

In a recent development, kubernetes takes a declarative, API-driven approach: people specify desired state through resource manifests, and controllers reconcile actual state to match. While Kubernetes excels at model deployment, its native scheduling model exposes several gaps for tightly coupled distributed training. Kubernetes schedules at the pod level; without job-level atomicity, a multi-node training job can partially start—some ranks running while others remain Pending—wasting GPUs or causing deadlocks. Vanilla Kubernetes also lacks batch queue semantics with priority-based backfill, built-in awareness of network fabric topology (NVLink domains, EFA interconnects) for placement of communication-heavy collectives.

Several Kubernetes-native projects address these gaps at different layers. Kueue operates as an admission controller atop the default scheduler, managing job-level gang admission, multi-tenant quotas with hierarchical fair sharing, and priority-based preemption—while delegating pod placement to the underlying scheduler. Volcano and NVIDIA KAI Scheduler take a different approach, replacing or augmenting the default scheduler to integrate gang scheduling directly with topology-aware pod placement—Volcano as a general-purpose batch scheduler, KAI Scheduler with deep NVLink/NVSwitch awareness for GPU-optimized placement. These layers are complementary: Kueue can manage admission and quota policy while passing admitted jobs to a topology-aware scheduler for placement.

For Kubernetes-based orchestration on AWS, Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) provides managed Kubernetes with GPU scheduling via the NVIDIA device plugin. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod also supports EKS mode, combining Kubernetes orchestration with HyperPod's training-specific capabilities. HyperPod EKS extends EKS with features designed for foundation model training at scale. Task governance provides compute allocation and policy enforcement across teams, integrating managed Kueue for admission control and Karpenter for just-in-time node provisioning. Checkpointless training addresses the recovery latency inherent in traditional checkpoint-based fault tolerance. Rather than periodically serializing model state to shared storage, checkpointless training maintains continuous peer-to-peer state replication across GPUs. When a failure occurs, surviving nodes reconstruct the lost state through EFA-based communication rather than reading multi-terabyte checkpoints from FSx for Lustre or S3. Elastic training enables jobs to automatically scale based on resource availability. When additional accelerators become available (e.g., from completed jobs or newly provisioned capacity), elastic jobs can expand to utilize them; when higher-priority workloads require resources, jobs can contract while maintaining training progress.

Distributed training and inference involve multiple software layers that must be correctly configured and coordinated. A useful model treats the runtime stack as five layers, ordered from hardware-adjacent components (which must function correctly for anything to run) to framework-level abstractions (which determine programmer productivity and model throughput): hardware enablement, accelerator runtime and math libraries, communication substrate, ML frameworks, and distributed training/inference frameworks.

Figure 3: The ML software stack for distributed training and inference on EC2 instances.

At the foundation, Linux kernel drivers provide direct hardware access. The NVIDIA GPU driver exposes compute capabilities and supports GPUDirect RDMA for direct data transfers between GPUs and network adapters. The GDRCopy driver (gdrdrv) enables low-latency CPU-initiated copies to and from GPU memory, used by NCCL for small-message transfers. The EFA driver provides OS-bypass networking through the libfabric API, and the Lustre client driver enables POSIX access to FSx for Lustre parallel file systems.

The CUDA platform provides the programming model and runtime for GPU compute. Applications compiled against CUDA can launch kernels on NVIDIA GPUs, manage device memory, and coordinate execution across multiple devices. The current release is CUDA Toolkit 13.x, with support for Blackwell architecture (compute capability 10.x).

In a recent development, modern training and inference performance is increasingly driven by specialized optimization libraries and custom kernels, not just general-purpose vendor primitives. Kernels like FlashAttention fuse attention into a single memory-efficient pass, cutting HBM traffic and improving throughput. Many teams also write shape- and precision-specialized fused kernels (e.g., layernorm/residual/activation, quantized GEMMs, MoE dispatch, KV-cache ops) tuned to their exact models. This is enabled by programmable toolchains such as Triton (Python GPU kernel compiler) and NVIDIA's CuTe (tensor layout and warp-level DSL), with libraries like CUTLASS providing highly optimized GEMM and fusion building blocks. In practice, this kernel and compiler layer often determines end-to-end performance as much as the ML framework.

Sources indicate that multi-GPU training depends on efficient collective communication. NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) implements collective operations—all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-to-all, broadcast, and point-to-point send/receive—with topology-aware algorithms that exploit NVLink for intra-node communication and network transports for inter-node traffic. NCCL dynamically detects the communication topology and selects ring or tree algorithms depending on message size and available bandwidth. While data-parallel and tensor-parallel strategies rely primarily on all-reduce and all-gather, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models with expert parallelism depend on all-to-all collectives to route tokens between GPUs: a dispatch all-to-all sends each token to the GPU hosting its assigned expert, and a combine all-to-all returns expert outputs to the originating GPUs (NVIDIA Developer Blog). Because every GPU exchanges data with every other GPU in the expert-parallel group, all-to-all communication volume scales with the number of experts and can become a dominant bottleneck at high expert-parallelism degrees.

On AWS, NCCL's inter-node communication is enabled through the aws-ofi-nccl plugin, which maps NCCL's transport APIs to libfabric interfaces. This allows NCCL to leverage EFA's OS-bypass and Scalable Reliable Datagram (SRD) protocol without application changes.

For inference workloads, collective operations do not capture all communication patterns. Disaggregated inference architectures—which separate prefill and decode phases onto distinct GPU pools—require efficient point-to-point data movement, particularly for transferring KV cache state between instances. NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) addresses this requirement by providing a unified API for point-to-point transfers across memory tiers (HBM, DRAM, NVMe, distributed storage) and interconnects (NVLink, InfiniBand, Ethernet). NIXL integrates with inference frameworks such as NVIDIA Dynamo and supports backends including UCX and GPUDirect Storage.

The two dominant frameworks for foundation model development are PyTorch and JAX. JAX takes an SPMD (Single Program Multiple Data) approach through XLA, where the same program executes across devices with automatic data distribution and collective lowering. This blog focuses on PyTorch, which sees broader adoption in the open-source ecosystem and forms the basis for the distributed training and inference frameworks discussed below.

It has been revealed that pyTorch provides tensor computation with GPU acceleration, automatic differentiation, and a flexible eager-execution model. For distributed workloads, PyTorch's torch.distributed module provides the core primitives: process groups for collective communication, and distributed data-parallel abstractions including Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) and Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP2). DDP replicates models across GPUs and synchronizes gradients via all-reduce, while FSDP2 shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across workers using techniques from the ZeRO algorithm, enabling training of models that exceed single-GPU memory capacity.

The top layer comprises frameworks that build on PyTorch to provide higher-level abstractions for distributed training and inference at scale. For training, three categories of frameworks address different points in the complexity-performance tradeoff. Below are few examples.

Hugging Face Transformers provides the Trainer class with built-in support for distributed training via Accelerate, which abstracts over DDP, FSDP, and DeepSpeed. This path prioritizes ease of use and broad model compatibility, making it suitable for fine-tuning and moderate-scale training where configuration simplicity matters more than maximum throughput.

NVIDIA Megatron Core targets maximum efficiency at scale, implementing 3D parallelism (tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism) with optimizations including FP8 mixed precision via Transformer Engine. The NeMo Framework builds on Megatron Core to provide end-to-end workflows for pre-training and fine-tuning.

It has been revealed that for reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and related post-training methods, veRL (Volcano Engine Reinforcement Learning) provides a flexible framework that implements algorithms including PPO, GRPO, and REINFORCE++. veRL's HybridFlow architecture allows mixing training backends (FSDP2, Megatron) with inference engines (vLLM, SGLang) in the same job, avoiding weight synchronization overhead by sharing model weights in memory between actor and rollout components.

It has been revealed that for inference serving, vLLM implements PagedAttention, managing the KV cache as paged virtual memory to reduce fragmentation and enable higher batch sizes. SGLang extends this with RadixAttention for automatic prefix reuse across requests, a zero-overhead batch scheduler that overlaps CPU scheduling with GPU computation, and a cache-aware load balancer that routes requests based on predicted cache hit rates. Both frameworks support tensor parallelism for serving models that exceed single-GPU memory, and both integrate with NVIDIA Dynamo for disaggregated serving architectures that separate prefill and decode phases.

Observability is a prerequisite for debugging and operating distributed training systems at scale. When a training job stalls or throughput degrades, practitioners need visibility into whether the cause is hardware failure, network congestion, storage bottlenecks, or application-level inefficiency. At the infrastructure scale discussed in this series—thousands of GPUs, petabits of interconnect bandwidth, and terabytes of checkpoint data—the challenge shifts from simple monitoring to systematic telemetry collection, storage, and analysis. Observability spans three telemetry categories: infrastructure metrics (GPU, network, storage), workload metrics (training throughput, queue latency), and alerting for proactive fault detection.

The de facto standard for observability in Kubernetes and HPC environments combines Prometheus for metrics collection with Grafana for visualization and alerting. Prometheus operates on a pull-based model, periodically scraping HTTP endpoints exposed by metric exporters. Collected metrics are stored in a time-series database (TSDB) and queried via PromQL, a flexible query language for aggregation, filtering, and alerting rule evaluation. Grafana consumes Prometheus as a data source, rendering dashboards and triggering alerts based on PromQL expressions.

For production deployments, Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus (AMP) provides a fully managed, Prometheus-compatible time-series database that scales to ingest millions of samples per second without requiring operators to manage storage, replication, or high availability. Amazon Managed Grafana (AMG) offers a managed Grafana workspace with native integration to AMP and AWS authentication via IAM Identity Center. Together, these services eliminate operational overhead while preserving compatibility with existing Prometheus exporters and Grafana dashboards.

According to recent reports, DCGM-Exporter exposes NVIDIA GPU metrics in Prometheus format, including utilization, memory usage, power, temperature, and hardware health indicators such as ECC errors and XID events. For training workloads, SM activity (DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_ACTIVE) often provides a more accurate measure of compute efficiency than basic utilization metrics.

In a recent development, EFA exposes driver-level statistics (bytes, packets, retransmits, timeouts) that help diagnose collective operation bottlenecks in distributed training. The aws-ofi-nccl plugin bridges NCCL to the libfabric interface, and operators can combine EFA counters with NCCL diagnostics (NCCL_DEBUG=INFO) to isolate network-layer issues.

Amazon FSx for Lustre exposes client-side metrics including throughput and metadata latency, while application-level metrics (step time, tokens per second, loss values for training; TTFT, inter-token latency for inference) can be exported via Prometheus client libraries.

According to recent reports, proactive fault detection prevents hardware concerns from propagating into extended training interruptions. A typical workflow monitors DCGM health metrics and triggers alerts when error counts exceed thresholds. ECC single-bit errors (SBE) may be tolerable in small numbers, but accelerating SBE rates often precede double-bit errors (DBE) or other failures. XID 63 (row remap failure), XID 64 (GPU fallen off bus), and XID 94/95 (contained/uncontained errors) typically warrant immediate node replacement.

The GPU Health - Cluster dashboard (Grafana dashboard ID 21645) provides a reference visualization for common GPU error patterns. The dashboard aggregates ECC errors, XID events, thermal violations, and row remapping status across all cluster nodes, enabling operators to identify failing hardware before it impacts training jobs.

Figure 4: GPU Health - Cluster dashboard showing GPU error patterns and instance reporting.

The shift from a single pre-training scaling law to three complementary regimes—pre-training, post-training, and test-time compute—has not fragmented infrastructure requirements; it has reinforced them. All three regimes demand tightly coupled accelerator compute, high-bandwidth low-latency networking, and scalable distributed storage, differing mainly in workload profile and resource scheduling patterns.

Sources indicate that this post surfaced the four-layer architecture that addresses those requirements on AWS: infrastructure building blocks (EC2 P-instances, EFA networking, and tiered storage), resource orchestration (Slurm and Kubernetes with SageMaker HyperPod), the ML software stack (from kernel drivers and CUDA through NCCL to PyTorch), and observability (Prometheus, Grafana, and GPU health monitoring). Each layer constrains and enables the layers above it—a misconfigured driver or saturated network link can bottleneck an otherwise well-tuned training run just as effectively as a suboptimal parallelism strategy.

Understanding these integration points is the foundation for diagnosing performance bottlenecks and making informed scaling decisions across the foundation model lifecycle.

Keita holds a PhD in Science from the University of Tokyo.

#162727. AI may not be a bubble. But the way we’re financing it might be

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4845 w)

AI may not be a bubble. But the way we’re financing it might be

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4845 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the firm into a leadership crisis.
  • According to recent reports, jensen Huang is back at Nvidia.
  • Investors may be relieved to have Huang back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia. On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the firm into a leadership crisis. Investors may be relieved to have Huang back. But the events of the past two weeks have shown just how much Nvidia—and the wider AI industry—still depends on one man. The board said it had consulted senior U.S. government officials before reinstating Huang and concluded that his return posed no national security risk. Its investigation remains open, however, and Nvidia has confirmed additional measures to address national security and compliance concerns. Huang’s departure also raised questions about Nvidia’s maturity as a corporate institution. In an analysis published shortly after Huang’s resignation, Andy Thurai, founder and principal analyst at The Field CTO, pointed to companies like Apple and IBM that spend years preparing their next generation of leaders. “That separates a mature corporate entity from a founder-led juggernaut,” he wrote. Huang is back, but Nvidia still needs to prepare for a future without him. Meanwhile, another major artificial intelligence company was making history on Wall Street. Anthropic, the maker of Claude, went public on November 19, pricing its shares at $83 in one of the largest initial public offerings in history. At that price, every one of an estimated 96% of the company’s employees held equity worth more than $1 million, according to data from Hill.com reported by CNN. The stock opened at $111.50 before closing its first trading day at $97.17. Investors who bought at the IPO price made money, but those who bought when trading opened were already sitting on losses. Both developments come at a pivotal moment for the AI industry. Billions of dollars continue to pour into the sector, but how much money are the companies receiving those investments actually making? And how long will investors be willing to wait? Judah Taub, managing partner at Hetz Ventures, thinks investors need to separate their excitement about AI from their assessment of the businesses behind it. “AI isn’t a bubble. But the way we’re financing AI might be,” he tells Fast Company. “The internet wasn’t a bubble, but many internet companies were. AI will be exactly the same.” AI could transform entire industries and create enormous economic value. But there’s no guarantee that the companies spending billions to make that transformation possible will benefit most from it. Much of that value could instead go to businesses that find the most profitable ways to use the technology. THE MONEY BEHIND THE AI BOOM Anthropic’s IPO illustrates the extraordinary sums flowing into the AI industry. The company closed the offering on November 20, raising approximately $93.5 billion, including proceeds from shares sold by existing shareholders. Of that, $91.6 billion went to Anthropic before fees and expenses. The company also secured a separate $26 billion investment from Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, and an affiliate of TSMC, the Taiwan-based chipmaker. Notably, several of those investors also supply the computing power and infrastructure Anthropic needs to operate. AI developers need vast amounts of computing power, while chipmakers and cloud providers need customers willing to pay for it. Both sides benefit. But if a supplier gives its customer the money to buy its products, how do investors know how much of that demand would have existed otherwise? Such circular financing deals linking AI developers, chipmakers, and infrastructure providers have become increasingly common among the industry’s biggest players. “Nvidia has been selling the picks and shovels of the AI gold rush,” Taub indicates. “But when the shovel manufacturer starts financing the gold miners, investors should ask whether they’re measuring demand for shovels or demand for financing.” Isabelle O’Keeffe, a London-based deep tech investor, worries that the infrastructure buildout could outpace demand for AI products. “The circular financing works as long as real customer demand is pulling it through,” she says. “The risk is when the infrastructure gets built faster than end customers are paying for it.” That could leave cloud providers servicing debt on underused data centers and model developers struggling to meet their spending commitments. Anthropic’s IPO filings detail approximately $900.9 billion in compute and related commitments extending over many years. Though some arrangements are conditional and the money isn’t due all at once, the figure illustrates how much future demand the company is betting on. In a recent analysis for Fast Company, Mark Sullivan showed how Anthropic is pursuing more efficient computing techniques and developing infrastructure that could reduce its dependence on outside cloud providers. The company also needs to attract more customers, expand beyond its strength in coding, and find profitable ways to serve users as its models become more sophisticated—all of which could become increasingly difficult if competitors offer similar capabilities at lower prices. Complicating matters is that some of Anthropic’s competitors also control much of the infrastructure it needs to grow. “The hyperscalers sit on both ends of Anthropic’s supply chain: They control the route to market, and they ration the physical compute required to serve it,” Thurai wrote in his analysis of the company’s IPO filing. “The revenue growth is real, but so are the costs,” O’Keeffe says. She isn’t particularly alarmed by Anthropic’s first day on Wall Street, interpreting the stock’s retreat from its opening price as a sign that investors are becoming more discerning. “I’d read it as selectivity, not rejection,” she says. For other AI companies considering an IPO, O’Keeffe believes the lesson is to price their stock sensibly, demonstrate improving margins, and avoid relying on overly optimistic revenue projections to justify their valuations. Now that Anthropic is public, investors will gain regular insight into the financial performance of one of the world’s leading AI developers. Other AI companies looking to raise money may find their prospects increasingly tied to Anthropic’s performance. THE BILL IS COMING DUE Investors aren’t the only ones scrutinizing AI spending. So are the businesses buying the technology. Kevin Kiley, CEO of the enterprise AI management company Airia, says businesses are changing how they evaluate the technology. A year or two ago, executives faced pressure from boards and investors to adopt AI more rapidly. Some companies celebrated employee usage figures without assessing whether the tools actually improved their work. Many bought AI tools before figuring out what they needed them for or how much money they could save. “The bills are coming in, and executives are asking more pointed questions,” Kiley says. “Are we improving productivity? Are we reducing operating costs and risk? How is this investment contributing to revenue and the bottom line? The focus is shifting from input to output.” Businesses are becoming more selective about the applications they fund, and executives want to understand which departments are consuming AI resources and what they’re getting in return. The difficulty is that measuring AI returns remains a challenge. Employee usage can increase even as savings or productivity gains remain elusive. Kiley says some companies are spending more on AI even as models become cheaper to use. As organizations expand their deployments, AI agents take on more work, call additional services, and process more information. What looks like a simple request to an employee could involve dozens of separate model calls, each potentially incurring a cost. Some of that expense could be avoided. Kiley notes that organizations frequently use powerful, expensive models for routine tasks that smaller systems could handle. Airia’s internal data suggests that 89% of common enterprise AI tasks don’t require the capabilities of frontier models, though that estimate hasn’t been independently verified. The company has also encountered agents that process more information than necessary, repeatedly call external tools, or get stuck performing the same actions. For an enterprise with thousands of employees using AI daily, even small amounts of unnecessary computing can quickly become expensive. Airia says its testing has produced cost reductions exceeding 50% through better model selection and workflow design, without sacrificing quality. Actual savings will vary by workload. But identifying those opportunities requires companies to understand where their AI spending goes—something Kiley believes many organizations still struggle with. “Making a model 20% smarter doesn’t necessarily make an employee 20% more productive,” he tells Fast Company. This could become a problem for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. If smaller, cheaper models can perform a growing share of everyday business tasks, how much more will customers be willing to pay for each new generation of frontier models? Companies that help businesses deploy, manage, and integrate AI could capture more of the economic value. Airia operates in that market, so Kiley has a commercial interest in that outcome. He also expects demand for AI governance, security, and cost management to grow. “I expect a more selective but healthier market, where organizations focus their resources on AI applications delivering measurable returns and scale back those that aren’t.” WHO GETS THE VALUE? Some of the biggest winners of the AI boom may turn out to be companies that have no intention of selling AI software. Michael Heltzen, CEO of the biotechnology company eXoZymes, sees opportunities in pharmaceuticals, materials, energy, and manufacturing, where AI could help develop products that are difficult or expensive to produce through conventional methods. “There’s a fundamental difference between generating financial activity and excitement around future potential, including hype-driven sales, and creating genuine, lasting economic value for shareholders,” he says. “The AI industry is doing plenty of the former. Now it needs to prove the latter.” His company combines AI with laboratory experimentation to develop enzymes for manufacturing valuable molecules. While its commercial ambitions still need to be judged against measurable results, the approach illustrates how businesses could use AI to create entirely new products rather than simply making existing operations more efficient. “Our measure of value is simple,” Heltzen says. “Can we make something highly valuable that only we can make?” Taub at Hetz Ventures argues that investors would benefit from distinguishing between three markets within the AI economy: compute, or spending on the infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI; intelligence, or what customers will pay to use AI models; and outcomes, or the economic value created when AI performs useful work. “These markets are connected, but they are not interchangeable,” he says. Consider a data center that generates billions of dollars in equipment sales and construction spending before anyone knows whether its computing capacity will generate enough revenue to justify the investment. Equipment suppliers may have already made money, while the data center operator still has years of expenses to recover. Further down the chain, the companies paying for that computing power have their own investments to justify. For Matt Calkins, CEO of the AI automation company Appian, creating more value from AI will require making the technology dependable enough for businesses to use in their most vital operations. “The top job of the AI industry today is not to drive blockbuster IPOs but to do the hard work of making AI useful in the biggest organizations for the biggest jobs. The AI value proposition isn’t complete. We need to focus more on safety and reliability,” he says in written commentary. A tool that saves employees hours of work during a demonstration may prove less economical once the costs of checking its output, correcting mistakes, and maintaining the system are factored in. We’re already seeing a version of this with AI-generated software. Developers can produce code faster than before, but companies still need people and systems to maintain it, investigate failures, and keep applications running. And even if AI companies get pricing and reliability right, they still need to build products people want. During a conversation at Dubai Future Week last week, Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at MIT, described what he called “the bubble of people creating technology.” He argued that AI developers can become disconnected from public concerns and the ways people experience their products. That presents a business risk, too. Companies could spend billions developing capabilities that impress researchers and investors but have limited appeal to the customers expected to pay for them. WHAT A CORRECTION COULD CHANGE A slowdown in AI funding could be good news for startups that have learned to do more with less computing power. Those struggling to retain customers or generate healthy margins, meanwhile, could find it increasingly difficult to raise money. O’Keeffe, the deep tech investor, believes such a shift could benefit companies building applications on top of existing AI models. “For the application layer, a reset would be healthy,” she says. “It clears out the me-too products and makes everyone focus on efficiency and real customer ROI.” But there’s a potential downside. Developing frontier AI models requires enormous capital, often years before a company can expect meaningful returns. If investors become reluctant to finance those efforts, the advantage could shift further toward tech giants with the cash and infrastructure to fund research themselves. Ironically, greater financial discipline could give the biggest technology companies even more control over the AI industry. Businesses might have thousands of AI applications to choose from, yet many could depend on models developed by the same handful of companies. Still, history offers some reassurance that a financial correction need not spell disaster for AI itself. Taub points to railroads, electricity, and the internet, each of which attracted extraordinary investment. Many of the businesses financing those technologies failed or disappointed their shareholders, but the infrastructure they built supported economic activity long afterward. AI may produce a similar outcome, creating opportunities for businesses that don’t even exist today while leaving some early investors with substantial losses. “We should be careful not to confuse a correction in AI valuations with a correction in AI’s potential,” Taub warns. Huang’s return may restore some confidence in Nvidia’s leadership, and Anthropic’s IPO has provided the company with a huge infusion of capital. Over the coming quarters, Anthropic’s earnings, the performance of infrastructure investments, and the AI contracts businesses choose to renew could tell us much more about where the industry is headed. For much of the boom, the industry has measured its ambition in chips purchased, data centers announced, and billions raised. The challenge now is turning those investments into enough paying customers, useful work, and profits to sustain the businesses behind them. Some of the companies spending the most today may discover that they financed the future without securing much of its rewards.

Nothing confirms ‘aggressive’ smartphone release schedule for 2027 with US focus

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alongside a teaser for the fresh Ear (note) recorder, Nothing CEO Carl Pei has confirmed the company’s plans for a major 2027 in terms of smartphone releases, as well as a focus on the US market.

Speaking to Bloomberg, Carl Pei indicates that Nothing right now has “tens of millions of devices in use,” and that there are big plans for 2027.

In a recent development, this includes “more attention” to the US market for Nothing, with the US being Nothing’s fastest-growing market for audio devices. In 2026, Nothing debuted its Ear (3a) earbuds, multiple CMF-branded devices, and two pairs of over-ear headphones including its high-end Headphone (1) Pro in September, all of which are sold in the US (and on sale during Black Friday).

Pei further noted that Nothing would have a more “aggressive” smartphone release schedule in 2027. Previously, it was said that Nothing would launch six new smartphones next year, following just three new smartphones in 2026.

Pei stated Nothing now has “tens of millions of devices in use” across its smartphones, earbuds and other products. The organization is also planning to devote more attention to the US market, while pursuing a more aggressive smartphone release schedule next year than it did in 2026.

The manufacturer remarked it has generated more than $2 billion in revenue since its first product release in 2022 and that the US is its fastest growing market for audio gear.

Industry observers note that nothing doesn’t have a strict schedule for new product launches, but Nothing Phone (4a) debuted in March 2026, with Phone (3) launching in the Summer of the year prior. With six new devices supposedly in the works, it’s anyone’s guess as to when they might release.

Sources indicate that email remains an important communication channel for web applications. From account verification and password resets to product announcements and customer notifications, many applications depend on email to keep customers informed.

Recent findings suggest that for developers, however, implementing email functionality involves more than connecting a service and sending a message. A reliable email system needs to handle authentication, dynamic content, delivery failures, user preferences, event tracking, and integrations with other application components.

Industry observers note that using an email service provider (ESP) can simplify this process. Most modern providers offer REST APIs, SMTP relays, templates, automation features, and reporting tools that developers can integrate into existing applications.

This guide explores the technical considerations involved in building email integrations, including API-based sending, webhook handling, automation workflows, and deliverability.

There are two common ways to connect an application to an email delivery service: SMTP and REST APIs.

SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is a standard protocol used to transfer email messages between servers. Developers can connect an application to an SMTP server using credentials and configuration settings.

In a recent development, REST APIs provide another approach. Instead of communicating through an email server protocol, an application sends HTTP requests to an endpoint. The provider processes the request and returns a response.

Both methods can support transactional and application-generated emails, but their implementation differs.

An application already supports SMTP configuration.

Developers want a relatively straightforward integration.

Existing frameworks or libraries provide built-in SMTP support.

An application needs programmatic control over email operations.

Developers want structured responses and error handling.

Email functionality needs to integrate with other application services.

The system requires event tracking or additional API capabilities.

The right approach depends on the application's architecture, expected email volume, and integration requirements.

An API integration allows an application to trigger emails in response to specific events.

For example, an ecommerce application might send an order confirmation after a successful payment. A SaaS application could send an account verification message after registration.

A typical integration follows this process:.

The application detects an event.

The backend prepares the recipient and message data.

The backend authenticates with the email provider.

The provider processes the request.

The application records the response and handles any errors.

Consider a Node.js application that needs to trigger an email campaign through an API.

Some platforms, including Mailmodo, provide REST API functionality for triggering campaigns and integrating external applications with email workflows.

The following example demonstrates the general structure of an HTTP request using a campaign-triggering endpoint:.

Industry observers note that this example uses the documented Mailmodo trigger endpoint and request structure. The campaign ID and API key must be replaced with the values from the relevant account.

Notice that the API key is loaded from an environment variable rather than written directly into the source code.

According to recent reports, this is an vital security practice. Credentials should never be exposed in frontend JavaScript, public repositories, or client-side application bundles.

Not every email provider offers the same integration capabilities. Developers should evaluate providers based on their API documentation, authentication methods, supported endpoints, event notifications, and integration flexibility.

For example, Elastic Email provides a REST API that developers can use to send emails and manage different email operations from an application.

Industry observers note that its API uses HTTPS requests and API-key authentication. Developers can use the available endpoints to send messages, manage campaigns, retrieve information, and configure webhook notifications.

When evaluating an email API, consider these technical requirements:.

Authentication: Check how API keys are generated, stored, restricted, and rotated.

Documentation: Look for clear endpoint descriptions, request examples, response formats, and error codes.

SDK availability: Official libraries can reduce the amount of integration code required.

Permission management: Separate credentials for sending emails and accessing account information can reduce unnecessary exposure.

API limitations: Review connection limits, request timeouts, rate limits, and account-level restrictions before deploying an integration.

A provider with extensive features is not necessarily the best option for every project. The key consideration is whether its API supports the application's actual requirements.

Recent findings suggest that sending an email is only one part of the communication process. Applications may also need to know what happens after a message is submitted.

This is where webhooks become useful.

A webhook allows an external service to send an HTTP notification to an application when a particular event occurs.

Depending on the provider, events may include:.

For example, an application could receive a delivery-failure notification and update the corresponding email record in its database.

A basic Express.js webhook endpoint might look like this:.

Industry observers note that this is a simplified example rather than a complete provider-specific webhook implementation. A production endpoint should validate the provider's signature or other authentication mechanism and follow its documented payload structure.

It should also handle duplicate events safely. Webhook providers may retry notifications when an application does not respond successfully.

An idempotent event handler prevents the same notification from creating duplicate database updates or triggering repeated actions.

Email automation connects application events with predefined communication sequences.

Instead of manually sending every message, developers can create workflows that respond to user activity.

Consider a SaaS application with the following registration process:.

The backend stores the new user.

A verification email is triggered.

If the user does not complete onboarding, a follow-up message may be triggered.

A simplified workflow can be represented as:.

In a production application, email delivery should generally be handled through a background job queue rather than blocking the registration request.

A queue also makes it easier to retry temporary failures, manage sending volume, and prevent email delays from affecting the main application.

Developers should consider tools such as Redis-backed queues or framework-specific job processors when building larger systems.

According to recent reports, automation platforms can also help manage more complex journeys. For instance, a developer can connect application events to an external email workflow instead of implementing every communication sequence independently.

The key is to keep business logic in the application while using the email service to manage message delivery and relevant campaign operations.

A successful API response does not necessarily mean that an email has reached the recipient's inbox.

Email deliverability depends on several technical factors, including domain authentication, sender reputation, message quality, and recipient engagement.

Developers should pay attention to the following configurations.

Sender Policy Framework identifies the mail servers authorized to send messages on behalf of a domain.

A correctly configured SPF record helps receiving servers evaluate whether an email originates from an authorized source.

DomainKeys Identified Mail adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages. Receiving servers can use the corresponding public key in DNS to verify the signature.

In a recent development, domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance builds on SPF and DKIM. It allows domain owners to publish policies for handling messages that fail authentication checks and receive reports about authentication activity.

These three mechanisms should be configured carefully, especially when an application sends emails through multiple providers.

According to recent reports, email systems generate useful operational data. However, developers should avoid treating every available metric as an accurate measure of user engagement.

For example, open tracking can be affected by privacy features and automated image loading. Click tracking may also include automated security scans.

More reliable application-level signals can include:.

These events can be connected with email campaign data to understand how communication affects application activity.

Developers should also maintain a clear separation between email delivery records and user account records. This makes it easier to investigate delivery challenges without unnecessarily modifying customer data.

When collecting engagement information, applications should follow applicable privacy requirements and respect user communication preferences.

Before deploying an email integration, developers should review the following areas:.

API security: Store credentials in environment variables or a dedicated secrets manager.

Domain authentication: Configure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.

Error handling: Account for failed requests, invalid recipients, and temporary provider errors.

Background processing: Use queues for asynchronous email delivery.

Webhook validation: Verify incoming notifications and handle duplicate events.

Monitoring: Track delivery failures, bounce rates, and application-level outcomes.

Testing: Test email templates across different clients and devices before production deployment.

These practices help create an email system that is easier to maintain, troubleshoot, and scale.

Email integration is an important part of modern application development, but a reliable implementation requires more than connecting an SMTP server or calling an API endpoint.

Developers need to consider authentication, asynchronous processing, webhook security, automation logic, domain configuration, and event monitoring.

Recent findings suggest that REST APIs are useful for applications that need programmatic control over email operations, while SMTP remains a practical option for systems that already support standard mail-server connections. Webhooks add another layer by allowing applications to respond to delivery events and update their internal records.

By choosing an integration method that fits the application architecture and following sound security and deliverability practices, developers can build email functionality that supports both immediate communication needs and long-term application growth.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few months ago, I got a DM on LinkedIn from someone wanting to interview me for a feature she was writing. At the end of the interview, I asked her how she found me. She replied, “ChatGPT.”  If you’re running a solo business, you’ve probably thought about how people find you online. Maybe you even track the information by asking or through a “How did you find me?” question on your website. Many people now ask an AI chatbot for a recommendation, the same way they’ve typed questions into Google for years. No matter how you feel about using AI tools personally, AI search is something that may have more and more of an impact on your business over time. AI as the newly introduced recommendation engine For a long time, getting found online meant search engine optimization (SEO), or showing up in Google results by publishing content like a blog. The newer version is AEO (answer engine optimization) or GEO (generative engine optimization). The idea is that AI tools might “find” you the way Google once did. AEO and SEO share the same fundamentals. AI tools pull from publicly available information on the Internet, so the more you put out there, the easier you are to find. In BrightLocal’s 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey, 45% of consumers stated they used ChatGPT or another AI tool to get recommendations for local businesses. A year earlier, it was 6%. That’s a substantial jump in a single year. The survey looked at local businesses, so it may not line up exactly with the work you do, but directionally it suggests that more and more people are turning to AI search to find what they’re looking for. Make sure you have a consistent online presence Like Google, AI tools look for an authoritative answer to whatever question someone asks. SEO has long focused on ranking in Google by following a set of “rules.” To me, AEO feels more like a wide-open, unclaimed field. No one quite understands it yet, though many people are trying to influence the AI search results. You can’t control the algorithms or LLMs, but you can control some of the narrative when Google Search or AI search finds you. AI tools piece together a description of you from all of these sources. Your website Your website is an obvious source for who you are and what you do. Your About and Products/ Services pages are good places to start. Make sure they’re up to date with the information you’d want someone to know or find. From there, you might add content that answers the questions potential clients are likely to ask. My website includes an FAQs section to help the algorithms and LLMs understand me better. Content also increases the likelihood that you’ll appear in search results, AI or otherwise. A blog works, and so does a publicly available newsletter. Case studies and testimonials help too, especially when they include client names and outcomes (with permission, of course). Your content on other sites Content on other sites gives AI tools something to cite when it answers someone’s question. It might be a podcast episode where you were a guest, or an article you wrote for someone else’s website. YouTube videos and social media posts count as well. Claim your business profile Google Business Profile is the original way to claim your business and correct its information. It’s worth setting up if you serve a local area, but for many online service providers (like me) it wasn’t necessary. In November 2026, OpenAI rolled out a beta of Businesses in ChatGPT, which lets a business claim and manage its listing. It’s in beta and open to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the U.S. Once your business is verified, you can upgrade its details. You’ll even be able to see how often ChatGPT mentions your business in its answers and how many people click through to your website. A LinkedIn Tech giant Page works for a one-person business, too. I have one, and it demonstrates up when people search on LinkedIn. AI is one more way people ask for information I’ll admit: I immediately claimed my business profile in ChatGPT when I heard it was available. It only took a few minutes to verify my website and identity, and then I could see what ChatGPT “knows” about me. I also plan to track how many times ChatGPT mentions me (currently sitting at 19). Word of mouth still keeps my pipeline full, because people know the type of work I do. But I can’t ignore that people are also turning to AI chatbots for recommendations.

#162723. Breaking: Unlocking asynchronicity in continuous batching
