Breaking: Introducing the Ettin Reranker Family

📅 19 May 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4147 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today I'm releasing six new Sentence Transformers CrossEncoder rerankers, state-of-the-art at their respective sizes, built on top of the Ettin ModernBERT encoders, together with the data and full training recipe that produced them:.
  • The models were trained with a distillation recipe: pointwise MSE on mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v2 scores over cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-v1-data, which is a subset of lightonai/embeddings-pre-training mixed with a reranked subset of lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning.
  • Our six rerankers paired with google/embeddinggemma-300m on MTEB(eng, v2) Retrieval.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today I'm releasing six new Sentence Transformers CrossEncoder rerankers, state-of-the-art at their respective sizes, built on top of the Ettin ModernBERT encoders, together with the data and full training recipe that produced them:.

The models were trained with a distillation recipe: pointwise MSE on mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v2 scores over cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-v1-data, which is a subset of lightonai/embeddings-pre-training mixed with a reranked subset of lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning.

Our six rerankers paired with google/embeddinggemma-300m on MTEB(eng, v2) Retrieval. See Results for five more embedder pairings.

In a recent development, if you're new to rerankers and want the "why" first, jump to What is a reranker, and why pair one with an embedder?. If you just want to plug a model in, jump to Usage. If you want to train your own, jump to Training.

According to recent reports, I bootstrapped the training recipe below with the latest train-sentence-transformers Agent Skill shipped in Sentence Transformers v5.5.0. Install it with hf skills add train-sentence-transformers [--global] [--claude] and ask your AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, ...) to fine-tune a SentenceTransformer, CrossEncoder, or SparseEncoder model on your data.

Sources indicate that A reranker (a.k.a. pointwise cross-encoder) is a neural model that takes a (query, document) pair and outputs a single relevance score. Unlike an embedding model, which encodes the query and document separately and computes their similarity from the two embedding vectors, a reranker lets the two texts attend to each other through every transformer layer. That joint encoding is more accurate but also more expensive: the model has to be run once per (query, document) pair rather than once per text.

It has been revealed that because cross-encoders are too expensive to run over a full corpus, the common production pattern is retrieve-then-rerank: a fast embedding model retrieves the top-K candidates (cheap), then a cross-encoder re-orders just those K with high accuracy. The total cost stays bounded while the final ranking is much closer to what an exhaustive cross-encoder pass would produce.

Throughout this blogpost I'll use "reranker" and "cross-encoder" interchangeably.

The released models are normal Sentence Transformers CrossEncoder models, so you can use them with just 3 lines of code:.

For a query and a list of candidates, you can also use rank to get back sorted indices and scores:.

You can swap cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-32m-v1 for any other size to trade quality for speed. All six accept up to 8K tokens of context (useful for long-document reranking) thanks to ModernBERT's long-context pre-training.

According to recent reports, it is recommended to install kernels and set model_kwargs={"dtype": "bfloat16", "attn_implementation": "flash_attention_2"} for the highest throughput. See the Speed section below for more details, but in general you can expect a 1.7x-8.3x speedup over default loading depending on model size and sequence length.

A complete example with a fast embedder for retrieval and the reranker for the final ordering:.

Sources indicate that this is the same shape used by most modern search systems. The retriever decides what enters the funnel, the reranker decides what wins.

All six rerankers share the same architecture and differ only in their backbone size. The backbone is one of the six Ettin encoders from Johns Hopkins University's Ettin suite. These are ModernBERT-style models with unpadded attention, RoPE positional encodings, GeGLU, and 2T tokens of open-license pre-training, supporting up to 8192 tokens of context.

Sources indicate that on top of each encoder, the reranker uses a 4-module classification head that mirrors ModernBertForSequenceClassification but is built from Sentence Transformers' modular components. The underlying Transformer is a plain AutoModel rather than AutoModelForSequenceClassification, which lets us use sequence unpadding for variable-length inputs for Flash Attention 2. At medium-document sequence lengths this is a 1.7x-8.3x speedup over fp32+SDPA depending on model size (see Speed for the full benchmark):.

According to recent reports, in my ablations, CLS pooling outperformed mean pooling. That was a little surprising. ModernBERT uses global attention only every third layer and the other two-thirds use local-window attention that cannot reach CLS from distant positions. Empirically, those few global layers carry enough signal to make CLS the better pooling choice.

All six models are released under the Apache 2.0 license, matching the Ettin encoders.

I ran each released model through the full MTEB(eng, v2) Retrieval benchmark (10 tasks, top-100 reranked) using MTEB's two-stage reranking flow, pairing each reranker with six embedding models that span the speed/quality spectrum:.

Sources indicate that the dashed retriever-only line in each chart below is the headline number to beat. Anything below it means the reranker actively hurts the pipeline on average:.

Sources indicate that mean NDCG@10 over the 6 embedder pairings, sorted descending. Our six models are in bold, and the teacher mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v2 is underlined.

† Capped to max_seq_length=8192 (the 4B Qwen3-based rerankers don't fit on a single H100 80GB at native context). Native-context evaluation is likely higher.

Sources indicate that nanoBEIR is a fast 13-dataset subset of BEIR that uses 50 queries per dataset against up to 5000 documents each. NanoBEIR is what metric_for_best_model was set to during training (see Evaluation), and what I used to guide the experimentation.

The smallest model I'm releasing, our 17M, beats the 33M ms-marco-MiniLM-L12-v2 by +0.051 NDCG@10 (0.5576 vs 0.5066) on MTEB and +0.038 (0.6746 vs 0.6369) on NanoBEIR at roughly half the parameter count. The 32M beats the 568M BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 by +0.025 (0.5779 vs 0.5526) on MTEB, a 17x parameter gap. If you've been using one of the legacy MiniLM rerankers as the default in your retrieve-then-rerank stack, swapping in our 17M (or 32M) is a low-risk drop-in replacement, with a noticeable quality bump on both benchmarks.

Recent findings suggest that moving up the table, our 150M is the strongest reranker I tested in the under-600M range on MTEB, edging out the recent Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B (596M) by +0.005 (0.5994 vs 0.5940) and beating every BAAI bge-reranker variant by 0.03 to 0.05. The 68M is also worth a mention: at 0.5915 it lands almost exactly on Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B (0.5940) while using a ninth of the parameters.

Recent findings suggest that at the top of the released range, our 1B model closely tracks its teacher. It comes within 0.0001 of the 1.54B mxbai-rerank-large-v2 on MTEB (0.6114 vs 0.6115) and within 0.008 on NanoBEIR, despite distilling from a model 54% larger than itself. The distillation effectively closes the gap to the teacher, which is what I was hoping to see going into this release.

The overall strongest reranker in the comparison is Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-4B at 0.6367 MTEB, +0.025 above our 1B model. Closing that gap from the current recipe would likely require distilling from a stronger teacher (our teacher itself sits below Qwen3-Reranker-4B). For most retrieve-then-rerank workloads, our 1B at a quarter of the parameters (see Speed) is a much more practical pick.

Quality numbers are only half of what matters for a reranker. The other half is whether its latency fits inside the budget you have between retrieval and showing results to the user. Let me walk through what I measured.

I benchmarked all six released models against thirteen public rerankers (strong baselines up to about 1B parameters) on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB. The queries and documents come from sentence-transformers/natural-questions at its natural document-length distribution: most NQ answers are short, some are long. Documents are truncated at max_length=512 to avoid giving the older models an unfair advantage. Each model uses its best supported attention implementation: Flash Attention 2 wherever the architecture supports it (BERT, XLM-RoBERTa, ModernBERT, Qwen2), SDPA where it doesn't, and eager for DeBERTa-v2 (which currently has neither FA2 nor SDPA support in transformers).

In a recent development, for every model an auto-batch search starts at batch size 8 and doubles until the GPU runs out of memory. At each batch size I run three timed passes and keep the median throughput, so a single unlucky run doesn't drag the number around. The reported throughput is at whichever batch size won.

Sources indicate that table 1. Throughput in pairs per second, all in bfloat16. Our six rerankers are in bold.

Our 17M is the fastest reranker in the whole comparison, at 7517 pairs per second. That's almost twice the throughput of ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 (3817) and faster even than the smaller ms-marco-MiniLM-L4-v2 (4029). And as you saw in the MTEB table earlier, our 17M is also more accurate than every MiniLM variant. If you're currently running a MiniLM cross-encoder, swapping to our 17M is a one-line change that improves both your latency and search quality.

It has been revealed that our 150M is an even more interesting comparison, because there are two direct architectural peers at exactly 150M parameters: Alibaba-NLP/gte-reranker-modernbert-base and ibm-granite/granite-embedding-reranker-english-r2. Both are built on the same ModernBERT-base backbone. Our 150M runs at 3237 pairs per second, while the two peers come in at 1418 and 1404 respectively, for a 2.3x speed gap.

Industry observers note that all three 150M models use Flash Attention 2, but the two peers load through AutoModelForSequenceClassification, which keeps the inputs padded. So attention itself runs the FA2 kernel, but the rest of the model is still doing dense compute on padding tokens that don't contribute anything. Our modular Transformer module (see Architecture Details above) propagates unpadded inputs all the way through the model, so every layer only spends compute on real tokens. That's the difference between getting some of FA2's benefit and getting all of it.

According to recent reports, at the bottom of the table, our 1B model hits 928 pairs per second, which is 2.4x faster than the 1.54B teacher mxbai-rerank-large-v2 (387 pairs per second) while matching its MTEB score within 0.0001. The teacher is Qwen2-based with a prompt-template overhead per pair, so the distilled student inherits the teacher's calibration and judgement but skips all the runtime baggage. This is honestly the most satisfying single number in the whole release for me.

One unfortunate note: the DeBERTa-v2-based mxbai-rerank-{xsmall,base,large}-v1 series ends up much slower than the rest of the table because DeBERTa-v2 right now supports neither Flash Attention 2 nor SDPA in transformers. The 70M mxbai-rerank-xsmall-v1 runs at 2636 pairs per second, about half the throughput of our 68M at almost the same parameter count. The models themselves are perfectly fine, they just don't get to use modern attention kernels.

If you're self-hosting on a consumer card rather than a datacenter GPU, here's the same throughput sweep on an RTX 3090. Same benchmark setup as Table 1: bfloat16, best-supported attention per model, three-trial median throughput at the largest batch that fits.

Our 17M is still the fastest model in the table at 9008 pairs per second, actually higher than its H100 number, which suggests that at tiny sizes raw compute isn't the bottleneck and the H100's extra muscle doesn't translate. The middle of the table reshuffles a bit, with the MiniLM rerankers overtaking our 32M and 68M, and the 1B slipping behind mxbai-rerank-base-v2 (189 vs 221 pairs per second). Our 150M model still holds a solid lead over the two 150M ModernBERT-based peers, and the teacher-replacement story still holds, with our 1B at 2.7x the throughput of the 1.5B mxbai-rerank-large-v2 (189 vs 69 pairs per second).

On CPU, we can't take advantage of bf16, Flash Attention 2, or unpadding, so the latency story is a bit simpler: the higher the parameter count, the slower the model. The 17M model is considerably faster than ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 (267.4 vs 143.9 pairs per second) and even faster than the smaller ms-marco-MiniLM-L4-v2 (206.2). As expected, our 150M model lands alongside the two 150M peers (14.0 vs 14.5 and 14.7 pairs per second) now that unpadding no longer applies. If you're CPU-bound, our 17M and 32M are the practical picks.

It has been revealed that to explain where the speed comes from, the next table sweeps fp32+SDPA, bf16+SDPA, and bf16+FA2 for our six models using the same bench config. The FA2 column is split in two: one with the inputs still padded (what a wrapped model would see) and one with unpadded inputs (what our modular Transformer actually does). The rightmost column is what our models use by default when FA2 is enabled.

Table 2. Precision and attention ablation for the six released sizes at max_length=512 on natural NQ documents. Each cell demonstrates pairs / second with the multiplier relative to fp32+SDPA in parentheses, and peak GPU memory on the second line. The rightmost column (in bold) is the configuration our models use by default when FA2 is enabled.

Recent findings suggest that the total speedup from bf16+FA2 w.o. padding over the fp32+SDPA baseline grows sharply with model size, from 1.71x on the 17M to 8.26x on the 1B. Most of that growth comes from bf16 alone: the fp32+SDPA to bf16+SDPA step gives the 17M only a 1.03x speedup but gives the 1B a full 5.60x speedup, also due to the lowered memory cost allowing for bigger batch sizes. In short, bfloat16 is the biggest single contributor to the overall speedup.

Unexpectedly, turning on FA2 while the inputs are still padded is actually slower than bf16+SDPA at every size in the release. The FA2 kernel prefers an unpadded format, and when you feed it padded inputs you pay the bookkeeping overhead of converting between formats while still spending compute on the padding tokens themselves. So the bf16+FA2 w. padding column is roughly what you'd measure if you swapped sdpa for flash_attention_2 in model_kwargs without changing anything else about the model loader. This is the situation that gte-reranker-modernbert-base and granite-embedding-reranker-english-r2 from Table 1 are in.

Industry observers note that lastly, going from bf16+FA2 w. padding to bf16+FA2 w.o. padding is worth between 1.78x (1B) and 2.45x (68M) of additional throughput, and it also cuts peak memory considerably, allowing for higher batch sizes.

According to recent reports, so my recommendation is simple: enable bf16 and FA2 together. The six Ettin rerankers will use unpadded inputs by default, since that's what the modular Transformer module from the Architecture Details section is set up for. The full snippet is the same as in the Usage section above:.

Use pip install kernels to install FA2. It ships pre-built kernels for a wide range of GPU architectures, CUDA versions, and operating systems.

One caveat for other CrossEncoders: the full speedup is only available for models built with a modular Transformer like the Ettin rerankers. Applying the same two flags to a CrossEncoder that loads through AutoModelForSequenceClassification lands you in the slower bf16+FA2 w. padding column of Table 2 instead.

It has been revealed that the training script below started as the output of the latest train-sentence-transformers Agent Skill, shipped in Sentence Transformers v5.5.0. If you use an AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, ...), you can install the skill and ask it to fine-tune a SentenceTransformer, CrossEncoder, or SparseEncoder model on your data. The skill carries version-aware guidance for base model selection, loss and evaluator choice, hard-negative mining, distillation, LoRA, Matryoshka, multilingual training, and static embeddings, plus template scripts for each model type.

According to recent reports, A prompt like "Fine-tune a cross-encoder reranker on (query, document) pairs from my dataset, mine hard negatives, and push to my Hub repo" will produce a runnable script you can then iterate on. That's how I started working on the recipe below.

In a recent development, all six rerankers were trained with the same single-stage recipe. Only the learning rate and the per-device batch size vary per model size. The full training script is ~150 lines and uses one published dataset.

The recipe converged after a single sweep across model sizes. Each size's learning rate was tuned by a small grid search on a ~15% subset of the final training data, and the resulting LRs transferred cleanly to the full-data runs without re-tuning. No per-size tuning beyond LR was needed.

Most published reranker recipes train on human-labeled relevance triples (a query, one positive document, and optionally hard negatives) with a contrastive, pointwise, pairwise, or listwise loss like MultipleNegativesRankingLoss, BinaryCrossEntropyLoss, RankNetLoss, or LambdaLoss, respectively. See my earlier Training and Finetuning Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost, for example.

But this approach has a few practical and theoretical drawbacks. First, positives need to be human-labeled, which is expensive and slow to scale across many domains. Second, the model only ever sees a label for the small subset of (query, document) pairs that someone went through. Especially after hard negative mining, you end up with a lot of false negatives, e.g. as shown in Hard Negatives, Hard Lessons. Third, the binary nature of this labeling doesn't match reality, where some documents are simply more relevant than others.

According to recent reports, I took a different route here: pointwise MSE distillation from an existing strong teacher reranker. The setup is simple enough to describe in three lines:.

I've released the training data as a single Hugging Face dataset, cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-v1-data, assembled from two sources. Each source is kept as its own split so the provenance is transparent:.

Total: ~143M (query, document, score) triples, plus a held-out 5K-row eval split (the tail of quora) that drives the in-training eval loss.

Most hyperparameters are constant across model sizes:.

Only the learning rate and global batch size very per model size.

global_batch_size is per_device_batch_size x world_size x gradient_accumulation_steps. On a single 8-GPU node, the 1024 global batch for 17m means per_device=128. On 8 nodes, it means per_device=8. The training script computes per_device_batch_size from global_batch_size // world_size so the same script works at any node count. The global batch size could be made more consistent, but I found that the above values worked well and didn't want to retune them just for the sake of consistency.

I monitored NanoBEIR mean NDCG@10 during training (eval every 5% of steps) and used it as the metric_for_best_model for load_best_model_at_end. NanoBEIR is fast, so I could afford it 20 times per training run. After training, I evaluated both the best checkpoint (according to NanoBEIR) and the last checkpoint on the full MTEB(eng, v2) Retrieval benchmark. The final release checkpoint was the one that did best on MTEB. The NanoBEIR-preferred checkpoint won for all sizes except 68m, where the last checkpoint was slightly stronger.

It has been revealed that the complete script (what every released model was trained with) is a single file. Only ENCODER_SIZE changes per run, and everything else is automatic:.

For multi-node training (anything past 17m/32m), launch the same script with torchrun:.

According to recent reports, the ettin-reranker-v1 family, trained with a single simple recipe, is state-of-the-art at every released size up to 1B parameters. Pointwise MSE distillation from a strong teacher onto a broad-domain and retrieval-specific mix scales cleanly from 17M to 1B parameters, with only the learning rate and per-device batch size changing between sizes.

Every ettin-reranker-v1 model beats the ms-marco-MiniLM-L*-v2 family by a comfortable margin on MTEB and NanoBEIR. cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-150m-v1 is the strongest mid-tier reranker I tested in the under-600M range, cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-400m-v1 lands within 0.0024 of the 1.54B teacher's MTEB score, and cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-1b-v1 matches that teacher within 0.0001.

Recent findings suggest that if you build something on top of these, please let me know! I'd genuinely love to see what people do with them, and if you manage to train better rerankers using the released data, even better. The recipe is intentionally simple, partly so that there's plenty of headroom for someone else to improve it. Train a stronger teacher and the same script can keep producing better students.

I'd like to thank the Ettin team (Orion Weller, Kathryn Ricci, Marc Marone, Antoine Chaffin, Dawn Lawrie, and Benjamin Van Durme) for building the base encoders that these rerankers are built on, the LightOn team (Antoine Chaffin, Raphael Sourty, Paulo Moura, and Amélie Chatelain) for their work on the training data collection, and the Mixedbread AI team (Xianming Li, Aamir Shakir, Rui Huang, Tsz-fung Andrew Lee, Julius Lipp, Benjamin Clavié, and Jing Li) for their work on the teacher model.

If you use the ettin-reranker-v1 family or any of the released artifacts, please cite this blogpost:.

If I understand well, you are mixing lightOn hard negatives data (with Jang et al. stratified sampling) with broader lightonai/embeddings-pre-training - which (i think) doesn't include mined negatives.

Correct on all counts. They're different data formats initially. I took:.

Yes, I did try various mixes. Specifically, I tried multiple approaches for the second subsampling (256 -> 64), e.g. grabbing 16 random docs, grabbing top 8 + 8 random, top 16 + 16 random, top 16 + 16 uniformly sampled, top 32, top 64, and what worked best for me: 32 top + 32 uniformly subsampled.

Sources indicate that I also tried different mixes of the pre-training data vs the embeddings-fine-tuning data. As you can see https://huggingface.co/datasets/cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-v1-data#lighton-pre-training-32-configs, I limited the largest sources from embeddings-pre-training to 5M and smaller ones to 2.5M, but during my tests I also tried limiting the largest to 1M and the smallest to 500k. Expanding to the larger number of rows was beneficial. I might also benefit from going larger, but that was exceeding my training time goals. I only experimented with the number of embeddings-fine-tuning data by updating its sampling (e.g. the top 64 has 2x as much fine-tuning data as the top 32 test).

Sources indicate that I ended up not wanting to do too many experiments on the data mixture, as I was wary that I might start to overfit on my evaluation benchmark (NanoBEIR), which would only result in better NanoBEIR scores but worse overall MTEB scores. So I didn't do too much.

In ST, you advise to discard Arguana and Touché when using Nanobeir13, I guess it works best with those at the end ?

Sources indicate that in truth, I probably should not have excluded these 2 from the default CrossEncoderNanoBEIREvaluator, as people might run the dense and reranker evaluators side by side and expect to be able to compare them, which you now sadly can't do. But in short: At the time, my opinion was that Arguana and Touche2020 didn't really match the usual usage for rerankers. For example, in ArguAna the query is just a big paragraph, and in Touche the documents are a bit vague (i.e. not as confident information sources but instead opinions). I think these might make them less suited as benchmarking datasets for reranker models, and I suppose also less interesting as training datasets for training rerankers. In the blogpost, I included them, as I want the scores to be easier to compare to the dense NanoBEIR13 scores from a standard embedding model.

According to recent reports, the discussion about keeping rerankers usable and avoiding overfitting to NanoBEIR is valuable. For deployment comparisons I'd also like to see quality and p50/p95 end-to-end latency at a fixed candidate count, plus a lexical-recall ceiling. We recently evaluated batched semantic judgments on a narrow BM25 candidate pool and reported server and client timings separately: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). We haven't tested Ettin on that set, so this is not a model comparison. Are there published CPU latency measurements for the smaller Ettin variants at a fixed batch size?

According to recent reports, A few years ago, renting a VPS meant signing up to be a part-time sysadmin. You’d SSH into a blank Ubuntu prompt and lose a Saturday to Nginx configs and firewall rules before writing a single line of your actual project.

In 2026, three things have changed. What we build has changed: AI coding tools turn weekend ideas into working apps, and AI agents need a machine that stays on after your laptop closes. Who runs servers has changed: you can now ask an AI agent in your terminal to set up a reverse proxy, close a port or work out why something broke. And what servers cost has changed: the AI boom is soaking up the world’s memory supply, and hosting prices are rising with it.

So I bought the smallest Hostinger VPS plan, deployed a Node.js app in Docker, and handed the DevOps work to Hostinger Agent, the AI assistant built into the dashboard.

Below is what that felt like step by step and whether it’s worth locking in a price before they climb further.

Most VPS hosting for developers now falls into four buckets. They all run on the same kind of machine; what changes is how much RAM you give them.

Apps built with AI coding tools. Claude Code and Cursor get you to a working Node.js or Python app fast, then leave you wondering where to put it. A VPS gives you one fixed monthly bill instead of usage-based pricing. If you want push-to-deploy, Hostinger offers Ubuntu templates with Coolify or Dokploy preinstalled.

AI agents and automations that run 24/7. For most people, a “VPS for AI” means a CPU box that never sleeps, not a GPU. Think n8n workflows, a scheduled scraper, or your own agent in a Docker container. Hostinger even has an “Ubuntu 24.04 with Claude Code” template: SSH in, run claude /login, and the agent keeps working after you close your laptop.

APIs, backends and databases for side projects. A Postgres instance, a Redis cache and a small API behind a reverse proxy fit comfortably on a mid-sized strategy. You pick the versions, the extensions and the backup schedule.

Client sites and stores. Freelancers outgrow shared hosting when one client needs a custom PHP extension or a WooCommerce store starts to crawl. A VPS with cPanel or Plesk, or a WordPress or WooCommerce template, keeps client work isolated and under your control.

If you’d rather not build anything from scratch, the Docker Manager catalog listed 1,017 one-click templates when I checked, including 93 under AI/ML and 162 under Developer tools.

According to recent reports, for this Hostinger VPS review, the question I cared about was simple: how long from “Choose initiative” to an app on the internet? On KVM 1, the entry plan, it was about 12 minutes. Here’s each step with rough timings.

I went with KVM 1: 1 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 50 GB NVMe storage and 4 TB of bandwidth. On the Black Friday deal it costs $6.49/mo, paid upfront as $155.76 for 24 months, and renews at $11.99/mo.

It has been revealed that you choose the server’s location and what to install during checkout, alongside your billing details. The location picker shows estimated latency for each data centre; mine showed about 80 ms.

Industry observers note that install options come in three tabs: Plain OS, Control panel and Applications. I picked plain Ubuntu 26.04 LTS to see how much work the AI would take off my hands. A daily backup add-on is offered, but weekly backups are already included.

The five-minute estimate was about right. The “you’re ready” screen then gives you two ways in: the VPS dashboard, or a pre-filled ssh root@ command. It also offers a free domain for a year to use as the server’s hostname.

The overview shows the OS, plan, CPU, RAM, disk and bandwidth at a glance, with Docker Manager, Backups & Monitoring, Security and DNS Manager in the side menu.

Every server also gets a hostname under hstgr.cloud (mine was srvXXXXXXX.hstgr.cloud), which came in handy later for SSL. I’ve masked my hostname as srvXXXXXXX throughout and blurred IP addresses in the screenshots.

Plain Ubuntu doesn’t ship with Docker. Open Docker Manager in hPanel and it installs Docker for you with one click. From there you can deploy apps from a Compose file, a repository URL or the one-click catalog.

According to recent reports, click Web console and you’re logged in as root in a browser tab, with Hostinger Agent in a panel beside it. You don’t need an SSH client or keys. The login banner flagged 33 pending updates, 23 of them security fixes; more on that later. A quick docker --version confirmed Docker 29.9.3 was ready.

Here’s the whole app: a tiny HTTP server with a health check, and a Dockerfile on Node.js 24, a supported LTS line.

Then build it, run it and check it:.

Industry observers note that the build took 8.3 seconds, including pulling node:24-alpine, and the health check answered straight away. The --restart unless-stopped flag brings the container back after a crash or reboot, which I tested later.

That’s a working app, but on plain HTTP, on a high port, with no TLS. Getting it production-ready is the DevOps part I handed to the AI.

An AI-managed VPS isn’t the same as a traditional managed VPS. You still get a self-managed server with full root access, but Hostinger Agent does the work you’d normally do yourself. Agent (previously called Kodee) is an MCP-powered assistant that lives in the dashboard and beside the AI web terminal, and it’s included at no extra cost. You can also connect Claude or Cursor to your server through Hostinger’s MCP server.

I gave it three tasks in plain English.

My prompt: “Check that Docker is installed, then set up a reverse proxy with a free SSL certificate so my demo-app container (port 3000) is served at https://srvXXXXXXX.hstgr.cloud.”.

In a recent development, it started by looking around: the Docker and Compose versions, which ports were in use, whether a web server was already running, and the OS release. Then it installed Caddy from Caddy’s official repository, configured the proxy and made sure ufw allowed web traffic.

Industry observers note that it read Caddy’s logs to confirm the Let’s Encrypt certificate, which arrived in about 6 seconds. Finally it tested its own work: HTTPS returned 200, and plain HTTP returned a 308 redirect. The whole task took about two minutes.

To give it a real fault, I ran docker stop demo-app and reloaded the site. Then I asked why it was returning a 502 and to fix it.

Industry observers note that in a single command, it checked the container state (Exited (137)) and searched Caddy’s logs, where it found connect: connection refused on port 3000. It restarted the container, confirmed /health and HTTPS were back, and even pointed to my docker stop in the terminal history. It also explained that --restart unless-stopped covers crashes and reboots, but not a manual stop.

A tip it didn’t mention: exit code 137 means Docker had to force-kill the container, because Node running as PID 1 ignores SIGTERM. Add --init to docker run for clean, instant shutdowns.

In a recent development, this was the most impressive answer. ufw already allowed only those three ports, but Agent noticed port 3000 was still reachable from the internet, because Docker-published ports bypass ufw rules.

Recent findings suggest that it recreated the container bound to 127.0.0.1:3000, so the app is only reachable through Caddy, and confirmed with an external port check. It left DNS, time sync and Caddy’s local admin port running, explaining that stopping them would break DNS and time sync.

Then I asked it to reboot the server. First it checked that Docker and Caddy start on boot and that the container’s restart policy was set, then it rebooted. The site came back over HTTPS without any help from me.

Nothing I asked for was destructive, so Agent just got on with it: the firewall change, the container rebuild and the reboot all ran without a confirmation prompt.

Sources indicate that the Agent panel says so upfront, noting that terminal commands can run without one. For destructive actions such as reinstalling the OS or restoring a backup, Hostinger’s FAQ says Agent always asks for confirmation first.

One thing worth knowing: to close port 3000, Agent removed and recreated my container. That was harmless for a stateless demo, but a container that keeps data without a volume would lose it. Take a snapshot before big jobs, and keep the panel in view.

So 4 GB is plenty for one or two small apps. Move to 8 GB on KVM 2 once you add Coolify, a database, or n8n with its own Postgres, because those are the services that eat memory.

Finding a cheap VPS got harder in 2026, because memory got expensive. AI data centres are buying up DRAM, and hosts are passing the cost on. In April 2026, Hetzner raised cloud server prices by up to 37%, citing hardware costs, then raised prices again in June. #162709. AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year.
  • Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
  • The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss.

According to recent reports, the results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

Sources indicate that using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

Recent findings suggest that another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.

The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

Sources indicate that "Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," mentioned Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops.".

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict.

Sources indicate that sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

According to recent reports, immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially notable.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

Industry observers note that because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

In a recent development, "One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late.".

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening.

It has been revealed that doctors at the moment rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

According to recent reports, but obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

Sources indicate that the approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer mentioned. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things.".

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns.

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

According to recent reports, the researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

"Good AI starts with good data," noted Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a substantial part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today.".

Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

Recent findings suggest that "It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer noted. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line.".

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments.

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Industry observers note that obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

Industry observers note that these longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

According to recent reports, rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to upcoming insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most vital contributions to medicine, opening upcoming directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer mentioned, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before I introduced my own tech giant, I worked as a web developer for a New York media company. One of my colleagues was a coding savant. They could build a webpage in mere hours, an incredible feat in the early aughts. They could identify bugs and rapidly come up with smart solutions. But they also frequently disappeared in the middle of the workday and took personal days with little to no notice. My colleague was reliable in their work, but not dependable day-to-day. Employees—and organizations—need both to provide real value. In today’s fast-changing tech landscape, customer expectations are evolving. Customers expect businesses to be reliable and digital experiences to work as promised. At the same time, they’re becoming wary of the tech race. In a recent survey of about 3,500 U.S. consumers about their digital lives, 77% said tech companies focus more on outpacing the competition than on solving real user problems. What separates leading organizations in the AI era is not reliability alone, but dependability at every step. Here’s how leaders and organizations can deliver on that promise. Make every customer experience consistent Having a product or service work the way you need it to is vital. No doubt, customers take note. In the above-mentioned survey, three-quarters of consumers reported that new tech features improved their lives and that digital experiences were becoming more personalized. At the same time, fewer than 30% said they strongly agree with that sentiment. The takeaway for businesses: There’s room for improvement. Where can businesses identify those areas for improvement? One strategy is ensuring that the entire user experience is 24/7 consistent. Every interaction along the customer journey, from initial inquiries to troubleshooting, should provide the same level of care and attention. Artificial intelligence can help make that possible. Customized AI agents, for example, can respond to common inquiries around the clock. When faced with more complex or nuanced challenges, they can escalate the matter to human representatives. This ensures customers can connect with your company whenever they need to, and without requiring employees to be always on. Consistency also means ensuring customers receive the same information across channels, whether they’re perusing the website, DMing with a chatbot via an app, or speaking with an employee on the phone. For customers, the result isn’t just a reliable product or service—it’s feeling heard and seen. That’s where dependability makes a difference. Customers build trust when every interaction feels responsive and aligns with what the organization has promised. Ensure every interaction feels like your brand Every interaction between customers and your company is an opportunity to build a relationship—or weaken an existing one. Especially in the age of AI, your company’s voice has to be cohesive, whether customers are chatting with an employee or a chatbot. As noted in Harvard Business Review, chatbots are becoming the frontline of customer interactions—and they can shape how customers perceive your brand, from its personality and values to its approach to customer service. What’s more, the HBR article highlights research showing that people who interacted with a warm, supportive AI companion felt closer to the chatbot than to colleagues, acquaintances, and even friends. People of a more task-oriented assistant, on the other hand, felt less connected to it than to their human relationships. The implication for brands: How AI communicates impacts the customer experience, as well as the kind of relationship customers believe they have with a company. For starters, customer-facing AI tools should reflect your brand identity. With a chatbot, for example, you can begin by defining its personality; whether it’s a supportive coach, an empathetic companion, or a sophisticated advisor. Decide the kind of information it handles and when conversations should be handed off to a human. AI-powered chatbots should do more than just sound like your brand. They should deliver the kind of relationship that reflects your company’s mission and values. Anticipate customer needs and act on them In the AI era, one of the biggest competitive advantages is anticipating customers’ needs, sometimes even before they’re aware of them. Consider a large language model like ChatGPT, which predicts what you might need next, encouraging users to continue engaging with it. For instance, you prompt ChatGPT to generate an outline; it does, then asks whether you’d like a draft introduction as well. Whether or not you say yes is your choice, but the option is there. Today’s companies can leverage AI to anticipate needs, streamline service, and resolve issues faster. AI-powered platforms like Chorus.ai can analyze customer interactions, synthesize sentiments, and flag recurring pain points. Then, your employees can better understand the customer experience and focus on developing solutions. Looking forward, AI-powered tools like Thematic can identify emerging trends and themes, helping companies evolve their products and services to remain competitive. As the founder of a company that began with online forms and has continually expanded its offerings over the past two decades, I know firsthand the importance of adapting to changing needs and spotting market opportunities. Importantly, AI is not error proof. Humans should always be kept in the loop to review decisions that impact the customer experience. Be transparent about AI use and jump in if and when AI falls short. That kind of behavior builds dependability and, on the customer side, reinforces loyalty.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the AI market and its developments have continually garnered opposition from several areas of society, to the point where protests are now frequent. On the day of Anthropic's IPO, Nov. 19, there were protests in multiple locations. As of right now, there's a fellow by the name of Elliot Callender on his third day of hunger strike in front of Anthropic's San Francisco offices, protesting against the manufacturer's use of RSI, or AI Recursive Self-Improvement.

It has been revealed that for now, he seems gung-ho about the effectiveness of his hunger strike, remarking that "It would be bad press for Anthropic if I had to go 40+ days to pressure them," and noted that he intends to protest with OpenAI once he's done with Anthropic. He also urges California residents to ring up Governor Gavin Newsom and request a legislative session on the topic of RSI.

Callender just had a fellow protester join him now, too, though they might have a hard road ahead changing the hearts of CEOs who believe your ownership of RAM is a bad thing, and that immersive video games would be excellent entertainment for those unemployed due to AI.

RSI is an AI training method wherein a model is put to work to improve itself repeatedly in a test-feedback-improve loop, purportedly making for much faster evolution compared to normal methods. It's a safe bet that most every frontier lab is using it, and Anthropic in particular has remarked that Claude wrote 90% of its own code back in September.

Many AI opponents consider that the field is moving too fast, for several reasons. The first claim is that there's not enough time or oversight to ensure the proper testing and safety of the developed models. Others consider that the economic impact is too violent and coming in too fast and would broadly prefer a slowdown. Some also consider that reaching some sort of general intelligence (AGI) is feasible and see that as a doomsday scenario best left to cinematic productions.

Industry observers note that such treaties are viewed with skepticism at best, considering how physically invisible model training is, requiring just data centers with the appropriate hardware. If the current U.S.-China-Nvidia situation surrounding high-end AI accelerators is any illustration, it's arguable if there's truly any international interest in controlling frontier AI development to begin with, much less choosing how quickly it's performed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Okay, so here’s the deal (literally): last year’s Moto G Stylus (2025) is on sale right now on Amazon for just $199, and if you desperately need a digital writing tool with your phone, it’s a good buy.

It has been revealed that that is the short answer; the long answer is a little more complicated, as due to some challenges with the 2026 model, you are missing out on exactly…nothing. Yes, at under $200, you are getting essentially the same phone because Motorola decided that, due to RAM and storage shortages and price hikes, the newer model would forgo any major upgrades. The 2026 model starts at $499, so if you had your eye on it, yeah, it’s a silly way to waste $300 in our opinion.

In a recent development, it has the same Snapdragon 6 Gen 3 processor, 8GB RAM, and 128GB storage. There’s a 120Hz display too and the good news is you get a microSD card slot to expand the storage if you desperately need it. Other notable features include a 5,000mAh battery, 68W wired charging, 15W wireless charging, a 50MP camera setup, and, as of writing, it should be due for an Android 16 upgrade.

According to recent reports, the star of the show of the Moto G Stylus (2025) is the stylus. It boils down to this: if you want a phone that isn’t a Galaxy Ultra, then this is the only other line that makes sense for document signers.

However, there are better deals out there. I think the Galaxy A56, at just $299, is an incredible offer right now and way more deserving of your hard-earned cash. Even so, if you want clean software or that stylus, the Moto G Stylus (2025) at $199 is at least an option especially for a family member or a backup to your existing phone.

Tech Report: Julia Fox wants to pay women back for splitting bills on dates with men

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women are fed up with being asked to split the bill on first dates.
  • Women are fed up with being asked to split the bill on first dates.
  • It has been revealed that if you’ve been dating in recent years, you’re aware that it’s a dumpster fire of an ordeal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women are fed up with being asked to split the bill on first dates. And now, Julia Fox, the actress and activist, is coming to the rescue. If you’ve been dating in recent years, you’re aware that it’s a dumpster fire of an ordeal. Between conversations on dating apps that never go anywhere, unsolicited nudes, and a slew of unoriginal conversationalists, the only consistent thing about modern dating is low effort. When it comes to women who are actively dating, it’s one of their biggest complaints—especially when it comes time to pay the tab. While it was once a standard practice in heteronormative romantic connections for men to pay the bill on a first date, women have been getting vocal about the fact that chivalry seems to be very, very dead. And they are over it. The frustration comes as the cost of dating seems to be rising in lockstep with men’s perceived low effort. According to fresh research from the dating platform Seeking, 61% of Gen Z women have been asked to split the bill on a first date. That’s more than twice the rate of boomer women (27%) who have been asked to do the same. Meanwhile, 75% of women say they appreciate it when a man pays (like . . . duh?). The gap could explain, in part, why so many women say they’ve given up on dating. According to a Pew Research Center study published in 2023, fewer than 35% of single women say they’re seeking romantic relationships, compared with 54% of single men. Enter the Anti 50/50 Campaign, a movement led by Fox that aims to address one of women’s biggest gripes with modern dating. The campaign allows women who’ve been asked to go halfsies on a date to apply for reimbursement. All they have to do is create a profile on Seeking’s website, share the details of the experience, and upload a receipt of the date’s bill. Those who are selected will be reimbursed up to $50. The $50,000 reimbursement fund will be open until February 10, 2027, or until all the money has been claimed. “I think we need to get over the idea that women should have to justify what they want out of dating,” Fox noted in a press release. “I’m all for women being independent, but that doesn’t mean we have to entertain low-effort men who think splitting a check is the height of romance. If you’re going to court somebody, COURT THEM.”  The campaign certainly aims to raise awareness about a common pink flag. But it also speaks to the fact that women don’t earn as much on the dollar as men. So many modern men seem to have forgotten that there’s still a glaring pay gap that hurts women’s financial stability. According to a recent report from the Center for American Progress, the pay gap has barely budged since the year 2000. In 2025, women workers made $13,760 less annually than men. Women who worked full-time earned around 84 cents for every dollar made by male counterparts. “We’re giving women their money back while encouraging men to lead with generosity,” says Dana Rosewall, CEO of Seeking. “Somewhere along the way, the patriarchy convinced women that splitting the bill was empowerment, when really it just made being cheap socially acceptable.”  In other words, if men are wondering whether or not women notice or appreciate it when they offer to pay for a first date, the short answer is: Yes, they do. It’s not just about money. It’s about effort, and not glossing over what may be easy for men to miss, but women surely don’t: that financial equality hasn’t quite arrived, no matter how hard women have worked to tip the scale.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 🧠 Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/olmoearth | 📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth_v1_1 | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/olmoearth_pretrain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

🧠 Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/olmoearth | 📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth_v1_1 | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/olmoearth_pretrain.

We released OlmoEarth (v1) in November 2025. Since then, partners have applied it across a wide range of tasks, from tracking mangrove change to classifying drivers of forest loss to producing country-scale crop-type maps in days, scaling deployments to national, continental, and global areas. Every release moves us closer to our mission: bringing state-of-the-art AI to organizations and communities working to protect people and our planet.

When OlmoEarth processes satellite imagery to make predictions across tens to hundreds of thousands of square kilometers, efficiency shapes what’s possible. Over the full lifecycle of running OlmoEarth – data export, preprocessing, inference, and post-processing – compute is by far the highest cost. A more efficient model means we can support more partners on the OlmoEarth Platform, and that anyone running OlmoEarth on their own can leverage this technology faster and at lower expense.

That’s why we built OlmoEarth v1.1: a latest family of models that cuts compute costs by up to 3x while maintaining OlmoEarth v1's performance on a mix of research benchmarks and tasks we’ve constructed with partners.

It has been revealed that the OlmoEarth models are transformer-based models, one of the dominant architectures in machine learning today. To process remote sensing data, we first convert it into a sequence of tokens the model can ingest.

Sources indicate that two important levers control efficiency in transformer-based models: model size (this is why we release a family of models, so users can pick the size that fits their compute budget) and token sequence length. Compute costs scale quadratically with the token sequence length, so even small reductions can meaningfully cut the cost of running the model.

Recent findings suggest that MACs, or multiply-accumulate operations, estimate the computation needed for one model forward pass; lower MACs generally mean cheaper, faster inference. The y-axis is inverted because lower average rank is better. Labels show model family and size. All plotted points use the pasted MAC/rank values.

This raises an notable question for transformer-based remote sensing models: what should a token represent?

Take Sentinel-2 imagery, a common modality we process. A Sentinel-2 input will be some tensor with a height and width (H, W representing the latitudinal and longitudinal pixels), a temporal dimension T, and 12 Sentinel-2 channels ([H, W, T, D=12]).

It has been revealed that at the moment, we split the data into resolution-based patches. Concretely, this means that we will pick some spatial patch size p, and split our overall Sentinel-2 image into patches of size p x p:.

For each patch, we create a token per timestep per resolution. So a Sentinel-2 input with 2 timesteps yields 6 tokens per patch (2 timesteps x 3 resolutions, 10m, 20m, and 60m).

In total, a[H, W, T, D=12] Sentinel-2 input will yield H/p x W/p x T x 3 tokens.

Using a unique token per resolution is a common technique when processing Sentinel-2 data—Galileo and SatMAE both take this approach, and SatMAE indicates significantly better results when doing it. However, it is not universal: CROMA is a model that only uses a single token for all bands, regardless of resolution. Because token counts compound multiplicatively, collapsing resolutions into a single token produces three times fewer tokens and material savings across pretraining, fine-tuning, and inference.

Naively combining the tokens in this way leads to significant performance drops, including a 10 ppt drop on m-eurosat kNN (a common benchmark task for remote sensing models). We hypothesize that separating Sentinel-2 bands into different tokens makes it easier for OlmoEarth to model notable cross-band relationships.

Industry observers note that merging tokens without impacting performance required us to modify our pre-training regimen. We describe those changes in detail in our paper.

The result is a model family that does more with less. At every size, OlmoEarth v1.1 runs up to three times cheaper than OlmoEarth v1, making frequent, planet-scale map refreshes more affordable for every team running OlmoEarth. If you're using a model from the original OlmoEarth family, try OlmoEarth v1.1. It provides similar performance to OlmoEarth v1 while requiring one third of the compute, though we have seen some regressions (see our technical report for more details). If it works for your task, you should see a significant speedup during fine-tuning and inference.

Sources indicate that pretrained remote sensing models have many degrees of freedom, which makes them hard to study. When performance shifts, is it the architecture, the dataset, or the pre-training algorithm?

We train OlmoEarth v1.1 on the same dataset as OlmoEarth v1, so any differences between the two isolate the effect of methodological changes. We hope this advances understanding of scientific principles when pretraining models for remote sensing.

Check out the OlmoEarth v1.1 weights and training code, including the weights for our Base, Tiny, and Nano models.

Breaking: How to navigate the holiday party season while sober

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • When Tat Read decided to give up alcohol four years ago to support a family member who was struggling with addiction, she knew that her career would present some obstacles.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Being in the industry that I’m in, I’m always at parties; I’m always at dinners,” claims the 45-year-old communications professional.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when Tat Read decided to give up alcohol four years ago to support a family member who was struggling with addiction, she knew that her career would present some obstacles. “Being in the industry that I’m in, I’m always at parties; I’m always at dinners,” notes the 45-year-old communications professional. “My job is about bringing people together. And when people are brought together, there’s always alcohol on the table.” Read, who says she was never much of a drinker to begin with, started limiting her consumption to a drink or two at work-related events about five years ago. As a mother of four, however, she found that even a small amount was more trouble than it was worth. “My kids are really young. I have to be up early in the morning, and it was starting to affect my sleep,” she says. “It just had downstream impacts that I really wasn’t appreciating.” Read says her colleagues supported her decision to give up alcohol completely, but says it’s still hard to navigate professional situations with upcoming people, like networking events. “I had trepidation about being fully sober because I knew it was an awkward conversation to have,” she says. “Sometimes I will hold a glass of sparkling water instead of champagne to not feel like I need to explain myself.” Read isn’t the only one who occasionally finds strategies to avoid conversations about her sobriety. According to a recent survey by the Boca Recovery Center, which operates addiction treatment centers in Florida, Indiana, Massachusetts, and New Jersey, 39% of Americans who abstain from alcohol hide their sobriety at work and 30% fake it to blend in—like drinking sparkling water from a champagne flute. And 13% have skipped a work event, celebration, or date to avoid the topic altogether. Given that more than half of sober Americans have been questioned, pressured, or teased about their decision not to consume alcohol, according to the survey, it is perhaps no surprise that 58% hide it from at least some people in their lives, and that 13% haven’t told anyone. “The holidays make this harder, as events tend to be based around drinking,” says Alison Tarlow, a licensed clinical psychologist who is the chief clinical officer at Boca Recovery Center. “Those hiding their sobriety are managing a drink, an excuse and a conversation all at once—which is socially exhausting in a setting that is supposed to be fun and relaxed.” Stigma remains even as more Americans go sober More Americans are choosing to go alcohol-free for a wide variety of reasons, though taboos related to addiction and mental health remain. According to the survey, one in four Americans have experimented with alcohol-free or reduced-drinking challenges; half of these cite physical or mental health-related reasons, compared with 10% who were recovering from addiction. Against this backdrop, younger generations appear less likely than others to hide their sobriety. According to the survey, only 5% of Gen Z keep it a secret, compared with 12% of millennials and 20% of Gen Xers. But these younger Americans also face the most outside stigma, as 68% of sober Gen Zs have faced questioning, pressure, or teasing compared with 49% of older sober Americans. “Telling people tends to involve fielding questions, which is generally off-putting to those who made such a personal decision,” says Tarlow. “Sobriety is a complex and sensitive decision, and people want to choose who hears about it and when.” Navigating the holiday party season without alcohol The holidays can be an especially challenging time for those who are looking to stay sober. Between personal and professional events, family and financial obligations ramping up, and work responsibilities starting to dwindle, many are left without some of the support systems, practical reasons, or reminders that help them maintain sobriety. Though they may feel judged for ordering an alcohol-free alternative, 93% of Americans say they would not think less of a coworker who skips alcohol at a work event, according to the survey. “The judgment sober people anticipate is usually harsher than what their peers tend to think,” says Tarlow. While colleagues may ask questions, she emphasizes that those who choose sobriety don’t need to explain themselves. “’I’m not drinking tonight’ is perfectly fine,” Tarlow says. “These events are meant to be fun, so focus on enjoying yourself, not others’ expectations. But, if pressure builds, there’s no shame in taking a break or leaving.” Coming up with excuses for not drinking can be exhausting and dishonest, says Phillip Barbb, an executive coach who specializes in sobriety. “You don’t want to feel like you have to have 25 conversations where you’re lying at the holiday party,” he says. “Creating this false narrative for yourself can weigh on you, because you’re building a gap between yourself and others.” Instead, Barbb, who has been sober for almost 19 years himself, suggests preparing a short explanation in advance that feels authentic and genuine, like, “I’m doing it for health reasons,” or “I decided I wanted to try not drinking this holiday season.” Some may also find it helpful to create a practical reason for staying sober to help them through workplace holiday events, like being a designated driver or making an early-morning commitment for the following day. Those trying to stick to their sobriety goals can also enlist the support of a colleague, date, or friend, though Barbb warns that these people shouldn’t be made responsible for someone else’s choices. “It is no one else’s responsibility to keep me sober or to keep me out of bad situations,” he says. “What I do think is cool is saying, ‘I want to go to the event, I don’t want to drink, so I may have a moment or two where I need to pull you aside to just talk or vent.’” How employers can offer more inclusive holiday parties for sober staff With so many Americans experimenting with sobriety—and so many hiding it from their colleagues—organizations will inevitably blueprint holiday parties for attendees who are abstaining from alcohol, whether the organization knows it or not. So it’s important for employers to consider ways they can make the environment more inclusive for workers who don’t want to drink. When a holiday party’s primary activity is consumption, it can make those who are going sober stand out. That is why employers are encouraged to include other activities, like bowling, an escape room, or mini golf. Choice of venue can also play a role, as an event held at a bar or club may create more anxiety—and discourage more from attending—than one held at an activity venue or restaurant. “If you’re hosting an event, you do have a responsibility to offer more than just beer and wine so that people can feel comfortable,” Barbb adds. “If you’re offering signature drinks, do a version without alcohol.” Workplace cultures are often set at the top, meaning it’s up to leaders to model responsible behavior and signal inclusivity for sober attendees. “It’s not anybody’s job—nor is it their right—to pry into the lives of their employees. But you should still make sure that you’re creating environments that are safe for people to be in,” Barbb says. “For executives and leaders, your responsibility for your people continues even outside of work hours.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on sale at Amazon during this year's Black Friday sales event is the 20TB WD Elements external HDD storage drive at $549.99, its lowest price of the year so far. The original listing price for the ample storage drive is $879.99, although it has been on sale for much less previously. Currently, you're getting a $330 discount on that listed price. At a price-per-gigabyte level, the drive works out to 2.75 cents per GB.

Traditional HDDs are much slower than modern SSDs, but beyond the speeds, the main difference is price. You can buy much larger amounts of storage in the HDD form factor than the more expensive SSDs. If you need a lot of room for your files, or want to back up your data for cold storage, then 20TB can hold a fair amount of files, from video to photos to plain old system backups.

In a recent development, this 20TB WD Elements external drive is mains-powered, with a 5Gb/s Micro-USB Type B to USB 3 Type-A interface to connect to your PC. It's not a lightning-quick transfer rate, but it gets the job done and is perfectly fine as long as you're not in a hurry.

The WD Elements 20TB external HDD operates over USB 3.2 Gen 1 via a Micro B USB-B to USB-A, includes an AC adaptor, comes preformatted for Windows, and includes a two-year limited warranty.

In a recent development, the unit is not too large, with a height of 6.53 inches, a depth of 5.30 inches, and a 1.89-inch width. So, it shouldn't take up too much room on a desk. Also, it's been a popular trend to shuck these external drives and use the HDD internally in your PC or place in a NAS, but not all drives are made equal, and some even have custom power connectors, so you'd definitely want to do some research, check out what's inside first, and be aware that it will 100% void any warranty if you're going to take the risk.

Industry observers note that with storage prices at all-time highs, finding deals on large-capacity drives is rare. So if you're in the market for a 20TB upgrade, then is a good deal to put on your radar.

In a recent development, what happens when the world’s most valuable technology company becomes a target for foreign intelligence? That question has taken on fresh urgency at Nvidia, where allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Jensen Huang, its founder, sparked an independent investigation and contributed to his temporary departure as CEO. The unfolding controversy has brought fresh attention to the high-stakes struggle for technological power. From the inner workings of the CIA to China’s pursuit of American technology, these eight books explore the world of spies and secrets, where information can be every bit as valuable as the technology itself. The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and the World’s Most Coveted Microchip By Stephen Witt How did Nvidia become one of the most powerful companies in the world? Stephen Witt tells the remarkable story of Jensen Huang and his rise from ambitious entrepreneur to the man at the center of the AI revolution. It’s a revealing look at the company whose chips have become some of the most coveted technology on the planet, and why control over them matters far beyond Silicon Valley. The Great Heist: China’s Epic Campaign to Steal America’s Secrets By David Shedd & Andrew Badger The battle for technological supremacy isn’t always fought in laboratories or boardrooms. Sometimes, it’s fought in the shadows. Drawing on decades of intelligence experience, David Shedd and Andrew Badger expose China’s sweeping campaign to steal American innovations and secrets, revealing how espionage has become a powerful weapon in the struggle for global dominance. Listen to our Book Bite summary, read by David and Andrew. Buy the book on Bookshop or Amazon. Spies, Lies, and Algorithms: The History and Future of American Intelligence By Amy Zegart Forget what Hollywood has taught you about spies. The real world of intelligence is stranger, more complicated, and increasingly shaped by technology. The Stanford scholar Amy Zegart takes readers inside the CIA and America’s intelligence agencies to reveal how espionage actually works, why intelligence failures happen, and how the digital revolution is rewriting the rules of spying. Listen to our Book Bite summary, read by Amy. Buy the book on Bookshop or Amazon. The Secret Life of Secrets: How Our Inner Worlds Shape Well-Being, Relationships, and Who We Are By Michael Slepian Not all secrets are matters of national security. The psychologist Michael Slepian draws on years of research to explore why we keep secrets, what they do to our minds, and how the things we conceal can shape our relationships and our sense of self. Listen to our Book Bite summary, read by Michael. Buy the book on Bookshop or Amazon. Sell Like A Spy: The Art of Persuasion from the World of Espionage By Jeremy Hurewitz What can a CIA operative teach you about winning someone’s trust? Quite a lot, it turns out. Jeremy Hurewitz reveals how techniques borrowed from the world of espionage can help anyone become more persuasive. The result is a fresh perspective on the competition reshaping the global balance of power. Listen to our Book Bite summary, read by Dan. Buy the book on Bookshop or Amazon.
