📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the U.S. retail industry’s version of the Super Bowl is here with the arrival of Black Friday, an occasion that sellers online and in stores seize to drive year-end sales. This year, the day once considered the holiday shopping season’s unofficial kickoff might look to spectators more like the fourth quarter of a football game.Brands and retailers have promoted steep discounts under the Black Friday banner all month, and some began rolling out deals before Halloween. But enough die-hard traditionalists hit the shops as soon as they can after Thanksgiving that the day remains the year’s biggest for foot traffic at physical stores, according to Sensormatic Solutions, a retail technology company.“Black Friday is still the day for in-store shopping,” mentioned Grant Gustafson, Sensormatic’s head of retail consulting and analytics.Stores also have kept drawing a majority of holiday season spending, although e-commerce captures a bigger share every year, according to U.S. Census data. Industry analysts expect the trend to continue; consumers spent $82.5 billion online from November 1 to November 22, a 9.1% increase from the comparable three weeks last year, according to research by Adobe.Retailers and consumers are giving Black Friday 2026 some other twists. The day’s evolution into a multiweek event has encouraged shoppers to stock up on discounted household basics while checking off their holiday lists, retail analysts said. Artificial intelligence and cost concerns are influencing how, where, when and on what consumers spend, retail analysts said.“It’s not just a moment where shoppers are buying gifts,” said Caila Schwartz, a retail and consumer insights leader at Salesforce. “They’re also buying things that they need, and so that’s going to help drive up a lot of the spend.”Here’s more on the emerging trends for Black Friday and holiday shopping overall: Low views of the economy aren’t expected to dim holiday sales This year’s holiday shopping takes place in a U.S. economic environment marked by voter frustration over gasoline prices fueled by the U.S. war with Iran, and high inflation overall.Analysts and economists scrutinize retail spending on the five days that begin with Thanksgiving Day and end on Cyber Monday for clues about consumers’ financial staying power and commercial prospects heading into the upcoming year.Retail sales were up and down all year as filling up a car and other nonnegotiable costs took more out of household budgets. Commerce Department figures for October showed Americans pulling back on buying books, clothes, sporting goods, and other items.The good news for retailers is that consumer confidence jumped this month as U.S. gas prices continued a steady decline.The National Retail Federation estimated that higher prices would account for about half of the 4.1% sales growth it expected in stores and online in November and December. The group forecast U.S. shoppers collectively spending $1.01 trillion. Black Friday still might have bigger discounts despite early deals U.S. retailers have broadly held the line on prices instead of making big increases across the board, and offered solid discounts that persuaded customers to shop earlier, industry analysts said.Salesforce, which tracks digital spending at a range of retailers, including grocery stores, said November discounts before Black Friday were 8% bigger than last year’s. Early promotions pushed average selling prices of physical merchandise 1% below last November’s prices, Salesforce said.Retailers nonetheless were likely to reserve their best prices for Thanksgiving Day and Black Friday, Vivek Pandya, director of digital insights at Adobe, said.For example, discounts on TVs are expected to average 23% on Friday compared with 11% during the first 22 days of the month, according to Adobe. Shoppers are buying household items along with holiday gifts The deepest discounts between this past Tuesday and Monday were expected on clothing, home goods, and health and beauty, Salesforce said. The company said it expected health and beauty products to average 33% off.With Black Friday commencing well before the day itself, some consumers apply seasonal bargains to last long after the holidays by filling their cupboards with toiletries and clothes they would typically buy at another time, according to analysts.Online sales of personal hygiene products were 40% higher from November 1 through November 22 compared with the October average, according to Adobe’s data. Sales of household cleaning products spiked 33% and clothing basics by 27% during the same time frame, Adobe said.“Usually, when you think of holiday shopping, it’s premium handbags and jewelry and those types of items, but we’re fast seeing shoppers also use this season to stock up on the essentials,” Pandya said. AI tools may be persuading customers to do more online shopping Consumers are using AI-powered shopping tools to help them compare products and prices, particularly as inflation and paying more for gasoline have made them more attuned to price tags, Pandya said.Traffic to online retail sites from links in AI-powered tools more than doubled this month compared with November 2025, Adobe said.A belief that e-commerce sites will offer “the best value possible” has contributed to shoppers’ doing more of their holiday period spending online instead of in stores, Pandya said. —Anne D’Innocenzio, AP Retail Writer.

The U.S. retail industry’s version of the Super Bowl is here with the arrival of Black Friday, an occasion that sellers online and in stores seize to drive year-end sales. This year, the day once considered the holiday shopping season’s unofficial kickoff might look to spectators more like the fourth quarter of a football game.Brands and retailers have promoted steep discounts under the Black Friday banner all month, and some began rolling out deals before Halloween. But enough die-hard traditionalists hit the shops as soon as they can after Thanksgiving that the day remains the year’s biggest for foot traffic at physical stores, according to Sensormatic Solutions, a retail technology company.“Black Friday is still the day for in-store shopping,” said Grant Gustafson, Sensormatic’s head of retail consulting and analytics.Stores also have kept drawing a majority of holiday season spending, although e-commerce captures a bigger share every year, according to U.S. Census data. Industry analysts expect the trend to continue; consumers spent $82.5 billion online from November 1 to November 22, a 9.1% increase from the comparable three weeks last year, according to research by Adobe.Retailers and consumers are giving Black Friday 2026 some other twists. The day’s evolution into a multiweek event has encouraged shoppers to stock up on discounted household basics while checking off their holiday lists, retail analysts said. Artificial intelligence and cost concerns are influencing how, where, when and on what consumers spend, retail analysts said.“It’s not just a moment where shoppers are buying gifts,” said Caila Schwartz, a retail and consumer insights leader at Salesforce. “They’re also buying things that they need, and so that’s going to help drive up a lot of the spend.”Here’s more on the emerging trends for Black Friday and holiday shopping overall:.

It has been revealed that this year’s holiday shopping takes place in a U.S. economic environment marked by voter frustration over gasoline prices fueled by the U.S. war with Iran, and high inflation overall.Analysts and economists scrutinize retail spending on the five days that begin with Thanksgiving Day and end on Cyber Monday for clues about consumers’ financial staying power and commercial prospects heading into the latest year.Retail sales were up and down all year as filling up a car and other nonnegotiable costs took more out of household budgets. Commerce Department figures for October showed Americans pulling back on buying books, clothes, sporting goods, and other items.The good news for retailers is that consumer confidence jumped this month as U.S. gas prices continued a steady decline.The National Retail Federation estimated that higher prices would account for about half of the 4.1% sales growth it expected in stores and online in November and December. The group forecast U.S. shoppers collectively spending $1.01 trillion.

U.S. retailers have broadly held the line on prices instead of making substantial increases across the board, and offered solid discounts that persuaded customers to shop earlier, industry analysts mentioned.Salesforce, which tracks digital spending at a range of retailers, including grocery stores, said November discounts before Black Friday were 8% bigger than last year’s. Early promotions pushed average selling prices of physical merchandise 1% below last November’s prices, Salesforce said.Retailers nonetheless were likely to reserve their best prices for Thanksgiving Day and Black Friday, Vivek Pandya, director of digital insights at Adobe, said.For example, discounts on TVs are expected to average 23% on Friday compared with 11% during the first 22 days of the month, according to Adobe.

Sources indicate that the deepest discounts between this past Tuesday and Monday were expected on clothing, home goods, and health and beauty, Salesforce mentioned. The manufacturer said it expected health and beauty products to average 33% off.With Black Friday commencing well before the day itself, some consumers apply seasonal bargains to last long after the holidays by filling their cupboards with toiletries and clothes they would typically buy at another time, according to analysts.Online sales of personal hygiene products were 40% higher from November 1 through November 22 compared with the October average, according to Adobe’s data. Profiling in PyTorch (Part 1): A Beginner's Guide to torch.profiler

📅 29 May 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you are trying to squeeze more tokens per second out of a Large Language Model (LLM), shave milliseconds off inference, or just understand why your training loop runs slower than the spec sheet promises, the path eventually runs through profiling.
  • Sources indicate that the catch is that profiling has a steep on-ramp.
  • This is the opening post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What you cannot profile, you cannot optimize.

Whether you are trying to squeeze more tokens per second out of a Large Language Model (LLM), shave milliseconds off inference, or just understand why your training loop runs slower than the spec sheet promises, the path eventually runs through profiling.

Sources indicate that the catch is that profiling has a steep on-ramp. The traces are dense walls of colored rectangles. The events carry intimidating names. Most tutorials assume you can already read them. So even when we know we should be profiling, opening a trace can feel like a chore best left for later (or for someone else). This post, and the series it kicks off, is our attempt to lower that on-ramp.

This is the opening post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.

Sources indicate that we document the journey from a beginner's point of view. No prerequisites apart from basic PyTorch. Treat this as a leisurely read with some "Aha!" moments. The structure of the post is intentionally question-led: we open a trace, ask "wait, why is that happening?", and chase the answer until something clicks. By the end you should know:.

Before we begin, two definitions that will make everything below read better:.

You don't usually have to write GPU kernels yourself; when you use a PyTorch operation, it is automatically translated to one or more kernels that do the job on GPU.

With those two ideas in your back pocket, let's start asking questions.

Here is the entire script that we use for the post: 01_matmul_add.py. We recommend opening this script in a separate tab and walk through the code step by step. We use the NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU to run the scripts. It is really easy to setup a GPU on the Hugging Face infrastructure and experiment with the scripts using the Dev Mode with Spaces. One could also run the scripts with the Hugging Face Jobs pipeline.(Note: The traces in this blog were generated using PyTorch 2.13. If you are using a different version, some trace details like CompiledFxGraph might differ or be absent.).

Sources indicate that as correctly quipped by Dr. Sara Hooker, just as we are primarily made up of water, Deep Neural Networks are primarily made up of matrix multiplies. As fundamental as they are, it would be a shame to start our profiling journey with anything else.

Sources indicate that the matrix addition along with the matrix multiplication mimics how weights and biases interact in a neuron. This addition (pun intended) will help us understand how it paves the way for compilation later in the post.

Industry observers note that to profile, we will be using the torch.profiler module. The steps involved are:.

The profiler exports two distinct artifacts:.

It has been revealed that let's see the two in action with our first execution. (Here is the entire 01_matmul_add.py script).

It is recommended to run this script on a machine with a GPU.

If you run the above script (on a GPU machine) you will find a folder traces/01_matmul_add with the two artifacts:.

The .txt file holds the profiler table. Upon opening the file, as shown in Figure 1, one would be greeted with a substantial table with the first column consisting of the events that were triggered inside the scope of profile.

The other columns are related to the time the event takes on the CPU or GPU or any other device(s) specified in activities within torch.profiler.profile. Look at which events take the most amount of time, and try to intuitively understand if that event should in fact take that time. It is also important to look at the column "# of Calls" which dictates how many times the event was triggered.

While we are at it, let's also talk about "Self CPU/CUDA" vs "CPU/CUDA total". The "Self" columns measure time spent only inside the event itself, excluding its children. The "total" columns include the event and all of its children together. So if you look at the "CPU total" of matmul_add, it consists of the time it took on self plus the children events it triggered. This is an important nuance to note.

If you look at the last two lines out of the table you would notice that the profiler tells us that.

The CPU time is in ms while the GPU time is in us. To put things in perspective, the time spent on GPUs (the kernel ampere_bf16_s16816gemm...) is less than 1% of the time spent on the CPU (the matmul_add operation). The GPU stays idle most of the time, which is an immediate red flag. The reason this happens is that the GPU can compute a small matmul very promptly, so our code spends most of the time preparing the kernels, launching them on the GPU, sending the data to multiply and gathering the results. This concept is known as an overhead-bound algorithm.

The easiest way to move out of this regime is to use bigger matrix multiplications.

The last two lines in Figure 2 are:.

Both times are in ms, which means we have materialized more GPU time just by increasing the size of the matrix multiplications. If you look at Figure 2 you would also notice that the most CUDA time is now taken by the GPU kernel (ampere_bf16_s16816gemm_..) and not by the CPU operation that debuted it (matmul_add). This means that we were indeed able to move from overhead bound to compute bound.

We now move into visualising the dispatch chain, which lives inside the .json artifacts. You can upload them to Perfetto UI and see the traces, or you can use uvx trace-util -f traces -b /traces to generate the Perfetto links directly.

In Figure 3, we see the profiler trace for the matrix multiplication and addition. Here the bar width indicates the duration of an event, the vertical nesting is the call hierarchy, the CPU lane denotes the events that happen on the CPU, while the GPU lane reveals the actual kernel executions. One might also notice the empty spaces which are the waiting or idle time.

The script was run with default configurations which are:.

Industry observers note that with Perfetto we suggest using the keyboard for quicker access to the trace. One could use "W A S D" for navigating the trace.

Recent findings suggest that there are two lanes in Figure 4, one for the CPU activity and one for the GPU activity. In the CPU lane one would notice three profile steps (starting from ProfilerStep#2). This comes from the schedule.

In a recent development, the wait skips noisy initializations (ProfilerStep#0), warmup runs through the profiler without recording (ProfilerStep#1), and active is what shows up in trace. One can find the schedule being used in the script here.

Let's put on our detective hats and investigate the trace and ask some questions.

According to recent reports, in Figure 5, we notice that ProfileStep#2 takes more time compared to the other steps, and upon looking closely you would see a similar pattern with the matmul_add annotation as well. The smoking gun is inside the annotation, not the annotation itself:.

In a recent development, that ~228 µs shown in Figure 6 is the "dead window" between entering record_function("matmul_add") and PyTorch actually dispatching aten::matmul. This can happen for multiple reasons, including workspace allocations, cuBLAS (NVIDIA’s proprietary, GPU-accelerated library for performing fundamental linear algebra operations) heuristics, or lazy module loading. We can either look away or run some more warmup steps before we profile (which is the standard).

In terms of profiling, warmup is when you run the events a couple of times before actually profiling it. The pre-work done by the GPU (including the above pointers) are one time efforts which we do not want to profile. In our example, we have two warmup stages, one where we actually loop over the function before entering the profiler, and two inside the profiler which is achieved by the warmup argument. In this section, we have enabled the actual iterations along with the schedule.

Perfetto Trace for 64x64 with Warmup.

In a recent development, in Figure 7 we see that each profile step takes a similar time, but this does not mean we were able to optimize the one time overheads. We warmed up the runs so that the overheads were not profiled. We think that closing this section abruptly without a hint to solving this would do injustice to the reader, so here is a link to read about further optimizing launch overheads.

According to recent reports, in Figure 8, we see that the CPU and GPU lanes have an offset of around 2.5 ms: this is the delay after the CPU submits the CUDA kernels and the time they actually start executing. One might think the warmup stage combined with the schedule's wait and warmup should keep a GPU busy and would diminish the offset.

To uncover what is really happening, let's change our schedule a little:.

Industry observers note that figure 9 shows us that there is an Activity Buffer Request in the GPU lane before any operation. Let's zoom in a little more.

Sources indicate that upon zooming into the GPU trace, we notice that the matmul and add kernels for ProfileStep#0 (the CPU trace of which is not visible in the Figure) happen one after the other, while the kernels for ProfileStep#1 have a window in between. The best explanation for this is that there was an overflow of buffers, and another buffer request (a request to allocate some memory on the GPU VRAM) was issued during the kernel execution.

The best way to rule out other possibilities is to profile for more iterations and see whether a similar window appears in other parts of the trace. To do that we run with active=20.

In a recent development, as shown in Figure 11, we see a similar trend in ProfileStep#1. This is aligned with our previous findings, and we can safely conclude that it was indeed another buffer request.

Industry observers note that in Figure 12, we see the nested CPU calls. This is an crucial visualization, where one gets to understand what a chain of dispatch really looks like.

According to recent reports, we begin with ProfileStep# which encapsulates the profiling step. Due to us annotating the step, we see the matmul_add row. The matmul_add consists of two aten calls, one for matrix multiplication and one for matrix addition.

The aten::matmul is the ATen-level dispatch that those user-facing PyTorch matmul calls land on. aten::mm is the 2D matrix-matrix multiply backend.

Industry observers note that it is very interesting to note how PyTorch calls aten::bmm (batched matrix multiplication) if we add the batch axis to our matrices. Let's take a detour and see the aten::bmm in action.

In a recent development, in Figure 13, upon adding the batch axis to the inputs, aten::matmul now encapsulates a bunch of other prerequisite CUDA runtime calls along with aten::bmm (instead of aten::mm). This also hints at the heuristics that cuBLAS needs to do in order to dispatch the right (most suitable) kernel for the program.

In the rest of the post, we will be working with simple 2D matrices, unless otherwise mentioned.

We notice that for aten::mm there are two CUDA Runtime calls, namely cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor (boxed in Figure 14) and cudaLaunchKernel, while for aten::add there is only the cudaLaunchKernel.

According to recent reports, cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor is a planning call and is purely CPU side. It asks: "given a kernel function, a chosen block size, and a chosen dynamic shared memory size, how many blocks of this kernel can simultaneously reside on one SM (Streaming Multiprocessor)?".

This begs the question, why do we need planning for matmul and not for add?

To understand this, we have to look at the kernel's resource footprint. If you click on the GPU kernels, you will be able to inspect the resource footprint for the respective kernel.

In Figure 15, we note that for matrix multiplication the registers per thread and shared memory are dynamic (based on the size of the matrix). cuBLAS ships hundreds of kernel variants, and each has a heuristic-driven launch path that needs runtime information about hardware capacity. The occupancy query is part of that heuristic. Conceptually, we can think of GPU-accelerated matmuls as working on independent tiles: how many tiles we use and how substantial each tile needs to be depends on the matrices and the hardware. Modern algorithms are way more complicated than that, but this is still a good reference framework.

Industry observers note that from Figure 16 we see that the footprint of addition says 32 registers and zero shared memory. That fits trivially. There's nothing to query, because no hardware resource is going to limit occupancy. The kernel is, by design, resource-light.

Sources indicate that you can use this as a quick diagnostic when reading any trace. Scan the CPU lane for cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor. Each occurrence flags a "heavyweight, adaptively launched" kernel, usually a GEMM (GEneral Matrix Multiplication), conv, or similar. The kernels without a preceding occupancy query are the elementwise/reduction crowd that PyTorch introduces mechanically.

cudaDeviceSynchronize blocks the CPU until all GPU work on this device finishes. The profiler emits this sync at the end of the active window to flush events. Without it, kernel timings would be missing.

A 1.78 ms sync covering 26 µs of real GPU work tells you this run was 98% idle. That's the textbook overhead-bound symptom.

We already know from the profiler table analysis (above) that providing bigger matrices to our algorithm moves it out from the overhead-bound region to being compute-bound.

Let's run the command and dive deeper into the traces.

In a recent development, in Figure 17, we notice that the matmul kernel for ProfileStep#3 takes longer on the GPU than the other steps. This is particularly interesting to note, because the other kernels introduced were the exact same, which means there were no cuBLAS heuristics involved. There are no scheduling gaps, the CPU debuts are normal, and it is not a profiler artifact.

This trace in Figure 17 makes a useful point that's easy to miss in idealized examples: kernel runtimes are not constants, even on the same hardware environment running identical code on identical data.

Recent findings suggest that let's make this more concrete by modifying the script a little. We run the iteration 20 times, capturing each of the steps.

It has been revealed that figure 18 reveals a similar finding. While each kernel was the exact same, they time differently. The different compute times can be blamed on a bunch of reasons:.

Sources indicate that A reader who only saw the average would conclude that a matmul took ~1 ms (mean of 5 = 1084 µs); a reader who looked at the trace would see that the matmul takes ~580 µs except when the GPU throws a fit. Those are very different mental models, and only one of them is correct.

Working with torch.compile has always amazed us. One writes normal eager PyTorch code, but PyTorch tries to capture tensor-heavy regions, turn them into graphs, optimize them, and run generated code. The default backend is usually TorchInductor, and the broad pipeline is:.

In this section, we talk about compilation and look at the profiler traces.

The args.compile flag triggers the following code:.

In Figure 19, we see the upcoming CPU rows named Torch-Compiled Region: 0/0 which points us to the compiled functions being used.

Looking at Figure 20 we ask the question, did we actually fuse the multiplication and addition operations together into one?

According to recent reports, this is operator fusion at the graph level. Inductor took our torch.add(torch.matmul(x, w), b) and rewrote it into a single aten::addmm(b, x, w) call. The vital thing to note here is that it did not produce a new fused CUDA kernel. The actual GPU work is still ampere_bf16_s16816gemm_bf16_128x256_ldg8_f2f_stages_64x3_nn, the same cuBLAS kernel eager mode used. So the "fusion" here is at the dispatcher level, not at the kernel level.

PyTorch provides the torch.addmm function that does what we did in two steps, that is multiply and add. We encourage the reader to look at the traces of this function and comment your observations in the comments below!

Recent findings suggest that while we know in theory what happens when we compile our functions it is equally notable to see it in action. Let's look at the CPU-side hierarchy which reflects torch.compile's runtime architecture.

TorchDynamo Cache Lookup is where Dynamo checks that the current call still matches what was compiled with the same input shapes, dtypes, devices, and tensor metadata. If anything mismatched, Dynamo would recompile. This cost is paid every call, even after compilation.

Torch-Compiled Region is the wrapper that "enters" the compiled version. AOTDispatcher Runtime Wrapper Prologue is AOT Autograd's runtime wrapper. Even though we don't need gradients here, AOTDispatcher is always in the stack handling tensor metadata, view tracking, and would set up the backward pass if requires_grad were true.

It has been revealed that ## Call CompiledFxGraph is where the actual generated code runs. The string after "CompiledFxGraph" is the content hash of the FX graph. It's the same across all three active steps, confirming cache hits.

You can find the generated code on disk under /tmp/torchinductor_/fxgraph keyed by this hash, useful when you want to read the Triton/C++ that Inductor actually produced.

Sources indicate that looking at the traces in Figure 21, we were really happy to notice only one cudaLaunchKernel per step. This observation was directly contradicting what we were seeing in the GPU trace. There were still two kernels being launched per step, namely the Memcpy DtoD (Device -> Device) and the GEMM. Going back to the CPU trace, we noticed that we had completely missed the cudaMemcpyAsync dispatch.

addmm computes out = α·A·B + β·C, and cuBLAS's GEMM-with-bias-add epilogue writes into a destination buffer that needs to already contain the bias. An epilogues can be thought of all the operations that happen after a GEMM. In the world of deep-learning we constantly come up with GEMM-Epilogues like activations, bias addition, normalization and many more. This is why there are cuBLAS GEMM-with- kernel variants.

If you use different modes for torch.compile you would notice different kernel variants being debuted. You can try it for yourself and add a comment below about your observations!

So Inductor-generated code does:.

Industry observers note that the result is mathematically still the same. The bias add isn't free, as we pay a memcpy upfront plus a slightly more expensive GEMM epilogue.

The fusion one might have hoped for, where x·w + b (here out = α·A·B + β·C) collapses into a single kernel with no extra memory traffic, isn't what happened. Inductor preserved the two memory-touching operations, it just relabeled the bias copy as a memcpy and the addition as a GEMM epilogue.

According to recent reports, A truly fused implementation would skip the memcpy. That's what FlashAttention-style hand-written kernels do, and what Inductor can do via Triton codegen, but for a 4096×4096 bf16 matmul, Inductor evidently decided "use cuBLAS, do the bias via epilogue setup" was the best path.

This is the easiest thing to miss when comparing an eager and a compiled run:.

torch.compile is roughly 2× more expensive on the CPU per step. That's because every call walks the full Dynamo > AOTAutograd > Inductor stack, on top of the same aten::addmm dispatch we have anyway. The compile pipeline is built for ML models with dozens of ops where the per-call overhead amortizes (for a single op it's a tax).

torch.compile has a mode argument. It is for the reader to take home as an assignment to read the documentation and come up with a mode that could take the CPU overhead down. 🤗.

Recent findings suggest that A quick reference for the patterns we walked through. The idea is: if you see this in a trace, this is what it usually means.

According to recent reports, we started with a tiny matmul + add and used it as an excuse to learn how to read a PyTorch profiler. Along the way we picked up a few mental models that travel well to bigger workloads. This was the first stop in the Profiling PyTorch series. In the posts that follow, we will gradually leave this two-op toy behind and walk up the ladder of complexity, looking at larger building blocks and, eventually, real models.

Thanks to Noe Flandre, Suvaditya Mukherjee, and Vidit Ostwal for their reviews on the early draft of the post!

Recent findings suggest that the blog post was polished using an LLM. This in no way means that we have let an agent run in the background and let it generate the blog. Some of us in the team are non-english speakers and think LLMs (which are mostly trained in the English Language) can rectify silly grammar mistakes or rephrase sentences that sound less intimidating and cleaner. Hope this helps with the idea of "why should I read, if this was LLM generated". 🤗.

Thanks a bunch for this blog post series -really much needed! Especially the Trace reading cheatsheet sections are very beneficial.

There are some parts I have been thinking about:.

In a recent development, firstly, thanks for the questions. To answer 2 you are right, the context manager should take care of it, but I personally like putting an extra sync to be sure. You can omit it in your own scripts.

Coming to 1, this was really interesting, I had to go back to docs to get more idea. You are right with your observation about cudaMemcpyAsync vanishing and only one kernel launch ..._ldg8_relu_f2f_stages_64x3_nn. It turns out that the latest kernels is a relu family kernel, which does the EPILOGUE properly where it falls under the contract of using a bias and broadcasting it across rows. Previously the bias was 2D and did not fall under the correct EPILOGUE contract, and hence there was an extra cudaMemcpyAsync.

It has been revealed that thanks for the kind words! Glad you liked it.

Good read! Helped introduce me to the world of GPUs and lower level stuff. While I understood the shape of things, it made me realise I have a lot of gaps in my knowledge wrt to this aspect of ML.

It would be great if the PyTorch version that was used was mentioned here as well. I was stuck because my trace was not displaying CompiledFxGraph. It worked on Colab but not on my local machine. I was using PyTorch 2.8.0, which does not show CompiledFxGraph in the trace.

It has been revealed that ah! This is an vital pointer I missed in the blog. I was using 2.13 throughout the post. Thanks for catching it. Do you mind sending a PR to the blog (github.com/huggingface/blog) and I could merge it! 🤗.

‘It was the talk of the playground’: Google’s AI features blocked by LA school officials

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2363 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that school districts are taking steps to block Google’s artificial intelligence features and are considering dropping Google products entirely unless the company gives them a permanent AI workaround, pitting them against the tech giant whose Chromebook computers and learning tools are deeply embedded in America’s classrooms.In a major step, Los Angeles school officials have quietly disabled AI-generated summaries, known as AI Overview, in Google searches on school-issued devices.
  • Industry observers note that school districts are taking steps to block Google’s artificial intelligence features and are considering dropping Google products entirely unless the organization gives them a permanent AI workaround, pitting them against the tech giant whose Chromebook computers and learning tools are deeply embedded in America’s classrooms.In a major step, Los Angeles school officials have quietly disabled AI-generated summaries, known as AI Overview, in Google searches on school-issued devices.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that school districts are taking steps to block Google’s artificial intelligence features and are considering dropping Google products entirely unless the company gives them a permanent AI workaround, pitting them against the tech giant whose Chromebook computers and learning tools are deeply embedded in America’s classrooms.In a major step, Los Angeles school officials have quietly disabled AI-generated summaries, known as AI Overview, in Google searches on school-issued devices. The move makes Los Angeles Unified the largest district to sideline the company, which has remarked it will not separate its search product from AI tools for education.The LA district, which enrolls half a million students, has made no formal announcement, and the move caught parents and students by surprise, said Bridie Lee, a leader of Schools Beyond Screens LA, which has pushed for screen-time limits and tech oversight in the district.The group had several members who weighed in at a meeting of the Los Angeles school board’s A.I. committee on Friday, Nov. 13. By that Monday, AI Overview was gone.“It was the talk of the playground,” Lee said.Google is the dominant provider of education technology for America’s classrooms. Beyond its low-cost Chromebooks, the most widely used student laptops, Google’s suite of education apps like Google Docs and Classroom has become integral to classwork, homework and communication among students and teachers.But concerns about AI’s impact on learning have ignited a battle between schools and Google. In September, the country’s two largest school districts — Upcoming York and LA — announced one-year moratoriums on student use of generative AI, and Google has said it’s not possible to take AI out of its search products. Schools are considering other internet search providers.LAUSD said in a statement it temporarily suspended AI Overview to ensure student experiences are “age-appropriate and safe.” It also said it continually evaluates its digital safeguards, including third-party tools. It was likely using such a tool that it was able to disable AI Overview.Schools Beyond Screens LA asked parents to send videos of what laptop screens looked like and received clips showing that AI Overview was no longer an option in Google search on district devices. Then activists reached out to the district, which confirmed AI Overview was disabled. Lee said they had no other details on how it was done or how long it is intended to stay disabled.“We’re thrilled LAUSD did this,” said Lee. “AI is seeping into everything. It’s dangerous. It’s hurting learning. And it’s a corporate overreach into public schools. It’s Massive Tech attempting to strongarm tech policy without anyone’s consent.”Other districts, such as Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia, have developed plug-ins to remove AI summaries for students searching on Google, according to multiple published reports. Google is increasingly at center of school tech backlash Schools are seeing growing backlash against technology, starting with cellphones and screentime and now focusing on AI, amid concerns that students are using AI to think for them.The Mountain View, California-based company in August found itself at the center of controversy. That’s when it said it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students using Google Classroom, its learning management system. Weeks later, New York City and LA schools banned generative AI. In New York, the ban applies to all elementary and middle school students, and in Los Angeles all students K-12 are banned from using AI on school devices. Both districts said the ban would allow officials to develop AI policies this academic year.Then, in early November, Google backtracked. It published a blog post saying it would instead turn off Gemini and all search tools by default for K-12 schools in the coming months. Administrators would have to turn on each tool if they wanted students to access them.Google said this was to give schools more choice. But the choice to turn off AI altogether is not there.While the blog post does not explicitly say search can’t be used without AI, Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times: “Search and AI are deeply integrated.” If schools ban AI, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”The integration of AI in search isn’t new. Google introduced AI Overview in 2025, and anyone who uses Google search will get AI answers to many search results. Google insists AI Overview is an integral part of its search product now and cannot be separated.Earlier this month, hundreds of Google employees signed a petition asking the company’s leadership to allow schools to turn off AI features “without disrupting their ability to use search as a whole.”“The way the decision has been reported in the press is poor, and makes Google, and our Education and Search products as a result, look like we’re punishing schools for not using AI,” the petition said. “Many students, educators and parents have concerns about AI in the classroom, as is shown by many school districts who have placed moratoriums or bans on such technology. It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products.” Google has made some changes — but not enough, activists say Google says it hears parents’ and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to “shortcut learning” and that it shares the same goal: helping students learn. But what many parents and teachers want — the ability to bypass AI entirely and allow students to use Google search like it was in, say, 2024 — is not something Google offers. This has forced districts across the U.S. to choose between restricting students’ access to AI and maintaining access to the popular search engine.Instead of offering an AI-free search product for schools, Google announced a pilot “guided learning” tool that walks students “step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers.”“We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers,” the company said in a statement.Presently, Google search offers AI Overview, which contains summarized answers resulting from general searches, and AI Mode, which is a chatbot interaction. Guided learning, which is not yet available, will walk people through steps intended to support critical thinking to get to the answer.LA schools had already disabled Google’s AI Mode at the beginning of the school year on school-issued student devices, said Jack Kelanic, the district’s chief information officer, during a school board committee meeting on artificial intelligence last week. Educators and staff still have access.“We understand this as a deeper embedding of AI into the education suite,” Kelanic said. He added, to applause, that the district is not bound to Google’s products if officials determine the changes are not in line with the district’s priorities.“We have choices,” Kelanic said. “We can change the default search engine literally overnight.” The Associated Press’ education coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wyze is today launching the Window Bird Cam, a new $70 camera that has a bird feeder and can identify bird species, keep a log, and more.

The Wyze Window Bird Cam comes in two parts. There’s a stick-up camera that mounts to the inside of your window with a shade to reduce reflections, similar to the Wyze Window Cam that launched last year. The other half mounts to the outside of your window with suction cups and includes a tray for birdseed.

The idea here is to attract birds direct to the camera’s view, with Wyze further adding a latest “Bird Watch” feature to its app which can identify bird species and keep a log of what species have stopped by and how many birds are using the feeder.

It has been revealed that the camera’s lens is tuned for focus distances of around 4-6 inches and has a higher frame rate of 30fps. The feeder tray has drainage and there’s an add-on perch for $15 extra.

“Bird Watch” is free for 3 months, but costs $6.99/month (or $69.99/year) after that. Free users still get live view and bird detection, but no species ID, a limited log, and no cloud recordings of bird visits (there is a microSD card slot for local recording).

  • One user details the app version on their Pixel 11 Pro XL – version 21.46.522.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Users are seeing the option to mute a video appear in the YouTube app on Android, but it isn’t showing up for everyone.

In a recent development, screenshots of a new video control button have started appearing on Reddit over the last week. The posts haven’t exactly begun hot debates, but it’s an interesting UI change. A mute button now sits next to the fullscreen option in the left section of the video player. Tapping it does nothing other than cut audio, until it’s tapped again to unmute.

One user details the app version on their Pixel 11 Pro XL – version 21.46.522. They also note that other devices they’ve checked on the YouTube app versions don’t appear to show any sort of mute button in the UI. Without many comments on either post, it’s hard to nail down just how wide this rollout might be.

In reality, this seems like a very small UI design test for the YouTube app. YouTube will often select a small number of users to push experimental features to while they polish them further before release. Unlike features that Premium users get to test, these are locked.

It’s not necessarily a massive change, but it’s sort of a confusing one. One wonders why a mute button is necessary. It also adds another button to accidentally hit when trying to tap the fullscreen option.

What do you think? If you’re seeing a mute button in the YouTube app, let us know your thoughts and what kind of phone you’re using.

Beyond LLMs: Why Scalable Enterprise AI Adoption Depends on Agent Logic

  • Numerous studies have cited the overwhelming failure of AI pilots, while others have also highlighted the need for AI to operate at the core of enterprise workflows to enable scalable adoption.
  • Possess a plethora of APIs, databases and servicesC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, guides have aided humanity throughout history. Prehistoric civilizations understood that the sun and the moon could be used to navigate vast distances on land and the high seas. Over time, various journeys facilitated the production of maps for better planning and faster travel time to repeat destinations. Centuries later, the introduction of the compass enabled seagoers to achieve greater accuracy in seeking unexplored destinations. And today, GPS navigation apps guide our every journey. In today’s world of agentic AI, AI agents, admittedly, have the potential to enable scalable AI adoption, transforming industries as we know them. However, an intelligent guide, agentic logic, is needed to realize this potential by fueling high agent quality, cost-effectiveness, and consequent end-user trust.

Enterprise Workflows & Use Cases.

Numerous studies have cited the overwhelming failure of AI pilots, while others have also highlighted the need for AI to operate at the core of enterprise workflows to enable scalable adoption. [1] [2] To better understand this phenomenon and the associated assertion, some analysis of enterprise workflows is required. These workflows are:.

A. Dynamic and long-runningB. Possess a plethora of APIs, databases and servicesC. Oftentimes are constrained by business policies and/or regulations.

It has been revealed that for an agent to function effectively, given these above characteristics, naturally demands an expanded model context, which state-of-the-art frontier LLMs certainly possess, but at what tradeoff? Increased hallucinations, token consumption? Further, can LLMs be equipped with an intelligent guide, GPS, to enable agentic AI execution at the core of the workflow, driving more desirable outcomes? We tested these hypotheses by designing and building agents, equipped with pertinent agent logic, for IBM offerings fully considering the above characteristics. These offerings pertain to some of the most challenging tasks confronting subject matter experts who own various stages of the enterprise software delivery lifecycle for mission critical workloads including:.

According to recent reports, before examining each of these domains in detail, let us define what characterizes agent logic. Agent logic is software primitives, such as knowledge graphs, algorithms, program analysis libraries, which operate at the agentic layer (within an agent harness) and can intentionally steer the LLM in the direction of the enterprise workflow, reducing the context space. In so doing, have strong tendency to drive more performant outcomes in a more cost-effective manner. Let us now examine how agent logic is able to achieve such outcomes in each of the above four domains.

IBM watsonx Code assistant for Z (WCA4Z), used to accelerate mainframe application development and modernization with AI and automation, is equipped with an App Insights agent for application understanding - one of the primary focus areas of enterprise clients running mission critical workloads on IBM mainframe. This agent leverages deep static analysis across the application and stores a pre-indexed representation in a database schema that spans hundreds of interrelated tables with complex semantics, allowing the agent to retrieve precise, structured already available information; thereby improving answer accuracy, reducing token usage, and minimizing back-and-forth interactions with the language model (Mistral Medium 250B in this instance). This approach when applied to multiple mission-critical legacy systems (up to 1M lines of code and 1K programs) maintains marginally superior app understanding performance with ~30× lower token consumption than a baseline frontier LLM-only approach.

In a recent development, aster is an IBM proprietary program analysis and data pre- and post-processing-based library utilized for agent-based generation of unit, integration, API and change-based tests; which from analysis of multiple developer communities achieves higher developer ratings compared with various open-sourced tools or developer-written tests. Based on the latter and superior line, branch and method coverage benchmarks compared with similar open-sourced tools (integration tests) and zero-shot LLMs and coding agents (unit tests), all tested on open-sourced applications, we have been running Aster in pre-production mode on 75+ java IBM CIO applications (up to 560+ classes and 67K+ lines of code) with Devstral 24B model. Steady-state results to date yield +20% - 45% improvement in line, branch and method coverage coupled with superior performance on a subset of these apps compared with state-of-the-art coding agent with orders of magnitude lower token consumption (up to 15×). The rationale for these results is that the program analysis output (used to prompt and “focus” the LLM) coupled with sub-agents for augmenting coverage and remediating runtime and compilation errors enable a more performant outcome with significant cost reduction.

Industry observers note that while LLM context for app-related use cases as described in 1 and 2 are “restricted” to the app source code, for runtime management of apps on deployed infra, the underlying IT full stack comes into play. Here we define a knowledge graph (KG) encompassing entities (microservices, database/middleware services, MELT etc.) coupled with embedded (“tribal”) knowledge from domain experts. With such a graph and bounding the LLM to local bound reasoning for non-deterministic outcomes, an observability-driven approach is used to achieve reduced context space spanning the IT stack and underlying app source code (if relevant) for incident root cause analysis (and other use cases). With this approach, leveraging the equivalent Instana data model, we have seen the proprietary Instana “I3” (intelligent incident investigation [8]) agent achieve up to 4.0× improvement over ReAct agent with GPT-5.1 as measured using ITBench [9]. With Gemini 3 Flash the ReAct agent performance improves to within 17% lower than the I3 agent while consuming 1.6× more tokens, We have extended this approach to source code with agents for code analysis (leveraging program dependency graphs) and bug remediation (leveraging inference scaling), also tested on ITBench, illustrating superior performance for the source code analysis and bug remediation agents (Gemini 2.5 Flash) over state-of-the-art coding agent both for finding the culpable microservice (3.0×) and bug repair (1.6×) while consuming respectively 3.7× and 5.9× less tokens. This multi-agent system was announced at IBM Think as part of the newly unveiled IBM Concert Platform for shift-left IT Operations and is also being piloted internally with IBM CIO. [10].

Enterprises face increasingly complex and fragmented compliance requirements, forcing teams to spend considerable time manually creating controls, assessments and remediation plans. No centralized knowledge exists and fixes are written manually, which introduces a risk of errors and security gaps. Because compliance work is complex and multi-step, it requires coordinated policy-driven automation across specialized agents rather than manual effort or simple AI prompts. Our multi-agent system automates compliance by algorithmically decomposing complex tasks into coordinated steps, using adaptive planning, dynamic decomposition and workflow sequencing with continuous feedback to iteratively identify fixes and expand assessments. It is 1.3 – 2.0× more performant than prior agents (Claude 4 Sonnet) using fixed planning strategies, as also measured using ITBench. This approach transforms compliance into a continuously guided self-correcting process and dramatically improves outcomes, especially in complex scenarios, boosting success rates from single digits to as high as +80% (Claude 4 Sonnet). This multi-agent system and 16K+ digitized controls mappings were unveiled as part of IBM Sovereign Core at IBM Think, integrated with monitoring, drift detection, providing automated evidence generation, ensuring audit evidence stays securely within customer control. [12].

Recent findings suggest that the above examples illustrate the impact of agent logic in reducing LLM context and guiding the LLM to traverse the core of the workflow in a highly performant and cost-effective manner. Additionally, we have employed similar approaches to two case studies, one with a configurable generalist agent and runtime (CUGA) in the healthcare domain and another for the condition-based maintenance for physical assets with IBM Global Real Estate.

Case Study 1: Configurable Generalist Agent (CUGA) Healthcare benchmark - algorithmic policy enforcement. [13].

The following health insurance customer care example is a compact illustration of why agentic systems outperform LLM-only conversational models in regulated environments. CUGA’s (configurable generalist agent) policy system implements policy-as-code for agent governance, which is enforced at runtime independent of model prompts and without fine-tuning. Our experiments show that the agent’s policy system closes large gaps in task correctness, enforcing structured workflows, safe intent handling, reliable tool usage, and controlled output formatting across all model families (Claude Opus – 4.5, GPT OSS 120B and GPT – 4.1) with accuracy improvements ranging from 15% to 26%. Authority is enforced through least-privilege disclosure, explicit compliance rules, and human escalation paths. Intelligent actions are proposed, while authority is exercised by policy and oversight mechanisms. Reasoning is autonomous; decision rights are constrained. CUGA is also a key component in the IBM Think Sovereign Core launch.

Industry observers note that case Study 2: Condition-based Maintenance of Physical Assets for IBM Global Real Estate - directed acyclic graph. [14],[15].

Recent findings suggest that enterprise maintenance systems collect copious amounts of asset data but are unable to effectively combine them, demanding experts to manually piece together fragmented signals and make decisions without unified, evidence-based insights. Our recently debuted Maximo Condition Insights [16] agent analyzes large-scale asset data across thousands of assets and locations (sensors, work orders, failure modes and events analysis), using structured evidence and validation loops to reliably identify challenges, prioritize actions and support decision-making with consistent, traceable insights. We have piloted this agent (using GPT OSS 120B) internally with IBM Global Real Estate (GRE), reducing asset analysis time from 15-20 mins to 15-30 sec (a 97% improvement) and increasing asset review coverage from ~1% to ~30% spanning over 120 sites and 6K physical assets. Using AssetOpsBench, the Condition Insights agent reduced unsupported claims by 57%, cut verbosity by 35%, improved rule compliance by 30%, maintained near-zero contradictions, and lowered token usage by on average 77%, while slightly increasing diagnostic specificity. This agent, equipped with a directed acyclic graph, provides structural engineering and operational context to reduce unsupported reasoning under naive prompting, while constraint-aware prompting markedly improves rule adherence, reduces verbosity, and lowers overall token consumption without introducing instability.

In a recent development, summary and References: We have benefited from guides for centuries, which have simplified and enhanced our lives. As technology has evolved, so have the guides we use, enabling us to do more and further shrink our global village. With the arrival of this agentic AI era, as we seek to further enhance society in part through economies of scale, we should continue this trend and fully leverage agent logic to simplify model context and intelligently traverse enterprise workflows at the core; only then will scalable adoption at optimal operating costs be truly feasible.

Kioxia's 3rd-gen XL-Flash hits Optane-class 3-microsecond read latency with 70% higher density

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Kioxia Corporation showcased a prototype of its fresh XL-Flash Generation 3 technology, next-generation low-latency, high-performance flash memory, at its KIOXIA Forum in Tokyo.
  • The low-latency XL-Flash fills “a newly introduced memory tier” to bridge the gap between DRAM and regular flash memory, in a way that can complement or replace some DRAM to help drive down costs, especially in AI servers and data centers.
  • The first generation was SLC with under-5 µs reads, arriving in 2019.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Kioxia Corporation showcased a prototype of its fresh XL-Flash Generation 3 technology, next-generation low-latency, high-performance flash memory, at its KIOXIA Forum in Tokyo. The flash, which uses CMOS directly Bonded to Array, or CBA, for better power efficiency and storage density, is about 135% more efficient with 70% higher bit density than Gen 2, and its 3 µs average read latency is less than 10% of that of Kioxia’s standard BiCS8 TLC. Samples are due March 2027, and Kioxia named its GP2 enterprise SSDs, rated for more than 18 million 512-byte random read IOPS, as its first product using it.

The low-latency XL-Flash fills “a newly introduced memory tier” to bridge the gap between DRAM and regular flash memory, in a way that can complement or replace some DRAM to help drive down costs, especially in AI servers and data centers. This has some similarities to Optane, which used 3D XPoint instead, as a storage class memory (SCM) option to reach higher IOPS. Intel and Micron’s 3D XPoint stored bits as changes in the cell material’s resistance rather than as trapped charge like NAND, and Intel exited the Optane business in 2022. The XL-Flash NAND is built on BiCS flash technology, but it’s tuned for low read latency and high write endurance.

The first generation was SLC with under-5 µs reads, arriving in 2019. By 2022, Gen 2 added 2-bit MLC as an option for lower bit cost, trading some like-for-like performance for better price-to-density. Gen 3 is reported to use SLC, and its 3 µs average read latency challenges the first gen’s sub-5 µs rating while being more than ten times faster than the 40 µs of standard BiCS8 TLC. This is within the same ballpark as Optane SSDs. The flash also reportedly has SLC endurance at 150,000 to 250,000 P/E cycles, at least 50x standard TLC, running at a 4.8 Gb/s interface speed.

under 5 µs (SLC), under 10 µs (MLC).

Recent findings suggest that XL-Flash achieves lower latency, in part, by using more, smaller planes (16 per die, with a 4KB page, on earlier generations), which is common with SLC and low-latency flash, and especially helps with smaller I/O. Kioxia’s GP drives target 512B accesses rather than the typical 4KB, a pattern that matches developments in enterprise storage requirements for AI and other emerging workloads that involve constant fine-grained memory lookups. 3D XPoint would outmatch it for write performance, though, due to not needing to erase for new data.

The newer gen is able to maintain high levels of performance at much higher density thanks to CBA bonding, where Kioxia makes the logic CMOS wafer and flash memory-cell wafer separately and later bonds them. This technology also improves the efficiency of 512-byte reads, by Kioxia’s own tests, which matches the design intention of the forthcoming GP2. Kioxia hasn’t disclosed full details on the flash, such as layer count.

Industry observers note that the GP2 Super High IOPS SSD will be Kioxia’s first product to use the latest flash, promising high levels of performance, including up to 28 GB/s sequential reads, if it can saturate PCIe 6.0 x4 as expected. Kioxia’s 2.5x IOPS number, versus “typical TLC-based SSDs,” comes from a comparison to its own CM10 drives, for 512B I/O. Endurance will also be excellent at up to 50 drive writes per day, which is within the ballpark of Optane storage.

Kioxia is considering E1.S and E3.S form factors, and the drive will support direct liquid cooling, which is increasingly necessary for certain data centers, including GPU-heavy ones where the GP2 is likely to operate.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

These drives will serve as a flash tier to help get more out of a GPU’s HBM, and Kioxia first demonstrated the GP series with Nvidia earlier this year. Offloading memory by any means possible is becoming a strategy with AI, even at the enthusiast level, due to high memory demands and how the technology and its KV caching work.

While the flash should sample to select customers before the end of the first quarter of 2027, Kioxia only promises GP2 evaluation samples to select customers by the end of that year. Exact specifications for the drive may differ, but what is clear is that later GP drives will target up to 100 million random-read IOPS that Kioxia and Nvidia have been working toward for AI servers. Kioxia revealed its XL1 series of CXL memory expansion modules on XL-Flash in August, and it “will continue to leverage the speed, power efficiency, and endurance of XL-FLASH” for emerging data center needs.

For centuries archaeologists have attempted to learn the origins of what we believe was known as Bleak Friday. Theories have long-pointed toward some sort of national purge day, in which citizens of the United States were encouraged to murder one another in the pursuit of widescreen televisions. But more and more evidence is being unearthed that it might have been a day of mourning due to not knowing which indie game to play next. To prevent a repeat of such a tragic era of human history, we atÂ Kotaku 3000 are introducing preventative measures, and have compiled together 12 completely excellent lesser-known indie games to keep the bleakness away.

Recent findings suggest that or indeed, I asked developers to email me about their recently released or upcoming games that aren’t getting any attention, so I could stick them on the front page of the site while the bosses are distracted by sales. 12 such games went up on the site yesterday, and here are 12 more! I really cannot get over the incredible variety, originality and excellence on display here. Some are already out and can be bought, and the rest deserve a place on your wishlist.

Developer: Pandan Games Release date: Q2 2027 Steam.

An indie game inspired byÂ Ratchet & Clank is a tall order, but it really looks like Pandan Games could do it.Â GearGrit is a third-person platformer where you play as Tansy Geargrit, escaping from prison for crimes she maybe only committed some of, and attempting to unearth a giant government conspiracy.

Thematically it looks to be of an Agatha Christie era, with all sorts of crime reconstruction, interviewing, information gathering, and all that good stuff. There is a demo, although no release date yet.

Developer: Sebastian Gioseffi Release date: Out now Steam.

And toggles! And an option for “cursorphobic buttons.” There’s also an option for “looming figure” which seems a bit unsettling. And apparently a way to get a flight sim HUD. It looks wonderfully bonkers, and you can buy and play it right now.

Developer: Mothman Mothman Studios Release date: Out now Steam.

I suppose you could argue thatÂ PokÃ©mon Snap is a form of cryptid cam game, butÂ CryptidCam is the real thing. This super-cute game is about taking photos of sweet little woodland oddities, including the likes of the Loch Ness Monster, bigfoot, and the Loveland Frogman (my upcoming obsession), as well as just gorgeous beasties with extra horns. Do that while waiting for next year’sÂ Gift of the Primordials, a turn-based puzzle game about…balancing soil nutrients? No, come back, it looks really good! It’s about building habitats for fantasy wildlife through puzzle mechanics based around judicious placement of plants. I’m still not selling it well. Watch the trailer. And playÂ Batbarian.

Developer: Sunna Entertainment Release date: TBA Steam.

Surely this can’t be the first time someone’s thought to crossÂ Tetris with a platform game? But I’ve certainly never seen it before. And hot-damn, check out the animation work in the trailer above. This just looks phenomenal, with multiple characters and loadouts, buildingÂ Tetrisy towers in order to attack enemies, build combos and gather fresh skills. There’s a demo to check it out right now, but no sign of a release date yet.

“Flash is fragile,” says the blurb forÂ Ad Iterum, “but you can hack it.” Eek. This top-down turn-based roguelike looks gloriously macabre, with wonderful pixel art, as you descend through dungeons mutating your own body through the devouring of your enemies. It’s about seeing how far down you dare go, before attempting to return to the surface with your ill-gotten gains, with unique combinations of mutations defining each run through the procedurally generated world. And it’s out next week!

According to recent reports, as we all know, the way through the underworld is not via well-timed combat, but through the rolling of dice.Â Lovers Die is a Yahtzee-inspired roguelite, rolling dice to eliminate categories as you build up attacks. I adore the art here, those crunchy pixels and the wonderful way descriptive text is presented. Also, why aren’t more dicebuilders based on Yahtzee?! This is a darker, more adult game that the art might initially suggest, and looks compelling. We have to wait until next year to play it.

Developer: Fe Angelo, 2dchaos Release date: TBA Steam, Itch.

Oh my goodness, you have to check out how this third-person survival horror uses color. It’s stunning. I mean, everything about the art is stunning.Â NechromiaÂ is about escaping a gothic castle built of someone else’s memories, with only a lantern to protect you. This looks so incredibly promising, and there’s a demo available on the Itch page for the game.

Developer: Dagada’s Team, Matthieu Lu Release date: TBA Steam.

Industry observers note that gosh, this immediately induced some nostalgia.Â Dagada’s Story looks deeply reminiscent of the Atari/Amiga era of 16-bit platformers, complete with a mascot-like main character. You play as Dagada and his flying chum Naou, able to control each separately in order to solve puzzles, with the goal of saving the harmony of an alien mountain in order to repair Dagada’s spaceship and get home. It looks very charming, and there’s already a demo to check out.

Developer: Stellar Cartography Interactive Release date: Out now Steam.

Recent findings suggest that is it OK to decide you already like a game entirely based on the pun in its title?Â Prophet MarginÂ is part city builder, part board game and part strategy, all about creating trade routes that please the gods. The emphasis is on calm, meditative play, with lots of deep thinking and methodical planning, as well as appeasing the deities of each resource. It came out just a few weeks ago, and for those who’ve discovered it is proving very well-received, although the unfortunate closure of the intended publisher means it’s not yet found enough eyes.

Developer: Goloso Games Release date: TBA Steam.

It has been revealed that one-person team Goloso Games made 2021’s excellentÂ Inspector Waffles, a great point-and-click adventure that is well worth your time. Their next game isÂ Antenna Dilemma, a newly introduced adventure featuring C432632, a grey cube who discovers there’s more to reality than his sofa and TV. It looks superbly bizarre, and there’s a demo out there already if you want to find out more.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, today we’re releasing Mellum2, an open Mixture-of-Experts model optimized for low-latency text-and-code workloads.
  • Recent findings suggest that in our technical report, we evaluate Mellum2 across code generation, reasoning, science, and math benchmarks.
  • The MoE architecture keeps total model capacity high while activating only a subset of parameters for each token.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today we’re releasing Mellum2, an open Mixture-of-Experts model optimized for low-latency text-and-code workloads. Mellum originally started as a code completion model. With Mellum2, we extend that foundation to a broader set of natural language and software engineering tasks while keeping the model focused on efficient inference and deployability. Modern AI systems increasingly rely on multiple model calls: routing, retrieval, summarization, planning, validation, and tool use. Many of these operations are latency-sensitive and do not require the largest available model. Mellum2 targets these workloads.

Recent findings suggest that in our technical report, we evaluate Mellum2 across code generation, reasoning, science, and math benchmarks. Mellum2 is competitive with similarly sized open models while delivering more than 2x faster inference, making it suitable for high-throughput production workloads. Model architecture Mellum2 is a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

The MoE architecture keeps total model capacity high while activating only a subset of parameters for each token. This makes inference more efficient and helps reduce serving cost for real-time workloads. Mellum2 is intentionally focused on text and code rather than multimodal tasks. This specialization keeps the model compact and efficient for software engineering workloads.

Mellum2 works well as a lightweight routing and orchestration model in multi-model systems, including prompt classification, tool selection, and intermediate control-flow steps.

The model is well suited for latency-sensitive retrieval pipelines, including context compression, summarization, and retrieval post-processing.

Mellum2 can be used for agent subtasks such as planning, validation, transformation, and context preparation, reducing the need to invoke larger models for intermediate operations.

Because Mellum2 is open and efficient to serve, it can be deployed in self-hosted environments involving proprietary code or internal data.

As AI systems mature, the most effective architectures are becoming less monolithic. A single frontier model can be powerful, but production systems often need several specialized components working together: retrievers, routers, code-aware models, validators, tool callers, and larger reasoning models. We think of Mellum2 as a “focal” model: a fast, well-scoped model optimized for high-frequency tasks inside larger AI systems. The goal is not to replace every model in the stack. The goal is to make the stack faster, cheaper, and easier to control.

If you are building AI systems for software engineering – inside an IDE, in a RAG pipeline, as part of an agent workflow, or on private infrastructure – Mellum2 is ready to try.

It has been revealed that I tried it on Opencode. I asked it to load the same codeatlas.md than I use in Opencode with Luna 6. It seems it understands it but as soon I ask for changes in natural language it fails. Not useful for natural language project development.
