💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re looking for a decent replacement for an older phone or a backup, and the Pixel 10 looks eerily similar to the Pixel 11, is it still worth it?
  • Sources indicate that one of the best things about the Pixel 10 is that it looks almost identical to the Pixel 11; in some cases, it’ll work with the accessories for the newest phone – but check that before you try.
  • In a recent development, that doesn’t matter to most people, but it could be important to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re looking for a decent replacement for an older phone or a backup, and the Pixel 10 looks eerily similar to the Pixel 11, is it still worth it? Well, of course it is, but let’s get into why in this deep dive.

Sources indicate that one of the best things about the Pixel 10 is that it looks almost identical to the Pixel 11; in some cases, it’ll work with the accessories for the newest phone – but check that before you try. So that means you’re not getting a majorly out-of-date design.

In a recent development, that doesn’t matter to most people, but it could be important to you. Pixelsnap magnetic accessories still work, and while the Pixel 11 trimmed down the camera bar to an all-glass visor, the overall footprint is virtually identical.

Using the same formula might be stale to some people, but it works, so why change it for the sake of it?

Recent findings suggest that I’d argue that the best news is that this finally shows Google is confident, given its success with the Pixel 9 and 10 design. The firm may make changes in the future, but it’s a fairly solid design that feels great after they settled on a physical form factor that works after years of fiddling, and it’s no secret that the goal is to make the switch from iOS to Android as “easy and painless” as possible. A familiar design goes a long way to calming the nerves of a potential switcher. The Pixel 10 is a perfect example of this philosophy. The Pixel 11 essentially proves that too.

It has been revealed that over a year on from release, there don’t seem to be any major or widespread reports of complications on the Pixel 10. I’d say that is a good omen, as people will often know within that timeframe if there are quality control issues and problematic hardware faults.

In a recent development, that mentioned, the only problem I think you have to deal with is the base 128GB storage configuration. It’s not insignificant, but still not going to be tons of room for everything. If you take lots of photos and download loads of things locally to your device, then maybe go for the 256GB model.

One of the weirdest things about the Pixel 10 was that after the Pixel 11 launched along with all other supported handsets, it had a newer version of Android than the latest phone.

Yes, you read that correctly: the Pixel 10 had QPR1 before the Pixel 11.

Recent findings suggest that the entire experience is just more of the same goodness that started with the addition of Material 3 Expressive last year. Android 17 keeps improving; the quality-of-life changes make for a really compelling experience that, while taking some cues from iOS, hasn’t gone full Liquid Glass. Google hasn’t quite kept the day-one update promise like the old days of Pixel, but you still have the cutting edge of the software. Even the Galaxy S26 series isn’t running a release this new and probably won’t for a while.

It has been revealed that rambler has even been added recently, so there is a function bleeding down from the Pixel 11, and there are loads of other quality-of-life changes and features that came with Android 17 QPR1 thrown in. Any bugs that might have been there, however limited, have been addressed in the year the phone has been around.

With the Pixel 10, you may miss out on some of the extra Gemini Intelligence perks or a couple of visual gimmicks like the Pro’s HiLight glow, but none that is yet groundbreaking enough to be drastically upset about.

In a recent development, sure, the competition might offer a faster processor or newer silicon, but can they offer the fluidity of a system that is fully integrated into all parts of your digital life? That’s what the Pixel 10 delivers.

As I noted, the Pixel 10 has already seen multiple updates, smoothing out early thermal quirks and optimizing battery efficiency. These monthly security patches and Pixel Drops are a testament to the fact that your phone is a constantly evolving product.

In a recent development, with more updates due very soon, the prospect of an even more optimized experience, and many of the best bits of Google all rolled into one handset, it’s a damn good buy, especially as other OEMs are still struggling to get their own Android 17 updates out in a timely fashion. We’re several months on from the full launch, and barely anyone outside of Samsung has offered a wide rollout. Of course, all Pixel 10 devices get day-one updates, with six years of support still left on the clock.

Industry observers note that there is one sore point on the base Pixel 10 that I think might make it hard to recommend over the Pixel 10 Pro. The main camera is the same as the Pixel 9a and the 10a on the base 10. It makes it harder to suggest if you care about camera quality.

It has been revealed that it’s still super reliable and does take great photos, but it might not be the best in class like previous generations may have been. In fact, I’d go so far as to say that while it’s great you get a telephoto zoom lens, the lower-quality main sensor diminishes it somewhat.

Most people will be better off with the Pro because it has a lot more to work with, but the cameras are still very good on the Pixel 10 and are backed by Google’s excellent updates.

Industry observers note that even video quality stacks up, though I will say Google’s reliance on Video Boost as a workaround for lower-quality footage is a bit of a cop-out. However, it’s a good workaround, and the resulting footage is still excellent, even if I’m hoping for better on-device processing in future Pixel generations.

Ultimately, the camera is a prime example of the Pixel value proposition. You don’t need the absolute latest, greatest, multi-lens Pro Max Ultra setup to take amazing photos. You need a Pixel. The camera on the 10 series is still right up there with the best from Samsung, OnePlus, and others. It’s doing just as much with technically much less.

It has been revealed that the biggest reason that many people who are looking for a newly introduced phone might want to consider at least the Pixel 10 lineup is that, with discounts, you’re getting a great deal — especially since Google bumped the entry price on the Pixel 11. Sure, bigger, better, faster, and shinier phones exist. They don’t give you the same experience, though. You’re paying for something that others can’t replicate, even at higher price tags.

With more updates due very soon, the prospect of an even more optimized experience, and many of the best bits of Google all rolled into one handset, it’s a damn good buy.

Is the Pixel 10 the best option for a phone right now? Suppose you want arguably the best software and are willing to forgo a few of the bells and whistles. In that case, it is an excellent alternative for anyone looking to save a little money without sacrificing too much. It’s a better buy than the Pixel 10a for most people, in my opinion, and you’ll be hard-pressed to find a more compelling mix of software intelligence and hardware value.

Holo3.1: Fast & Local Computer Use Agents

📅 02 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that last March, we released Holo3, our state-of-the-art computer-use model.
  • Users want to run the same computer-use capabilities across desktop and mobile environments, with seamless integration with different agent frameworks.
  • This is why we are releasing the Holo3.1 family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that last March, we released Holo3, our state-of-the-art computer-use model. Adoption was immediate. Developers, enterprises, and partners started deploying Holo3 across a wide range of workflows, from browser automation and business software to internal tools and desktop applications. As adoption grew, we realized performance alone was no longer enough.

Users want to run the same computer-use capabilities across desktop and mobile environments, with seamless integration with different agent frameworks. They want deployment flexibility, from cloud inference to fully local execution on end-user devices.

This is why we are releasing the Holo3.1 family. Holo3.1 improves robustness across the three dimensions that matter most in production: environments (web, desktop, mobile), agent frameworks, and deployment targets. For the first time, we release quantized checkpoints optimized for local inference, including FP8, Q4 GGUF, and NVFP4.

Holo3.1 is a major step toward our vision of universal computer-use agents: systems that can operate across environments, integrate into any agent stack, and run wherever the workflow lives.

Based on the Qwen family, Holo3.1 was designed to improve robustness across the environments where computer-use agents are actually deployed, while retaining state-of-the-art performance.

As teams moved Holo3 from evaluation to production, we repeatedly observed the same challenge: strong performance in one setting does not necessarily transfer to another. Mobile devices, alternative agent harnesses, and different execution frameworks all introduce their own sources of distribution shift.

Holo3.1 expands Holo3's capabilities beyond browser and desktop control, delivering major gains on mobile environments. On AndroidWorld, our 35B-A3B model improves from 67% to 79.3%, while the smaller 4B and 9B variants improve from 58% to 72%.

To better support teams deploying Holo inside third-party agent stacks, Holo3.1 introduces native support for function-calling protocols in addition to the structured JSON outputs already available in Holo3.

Across OSWorld and our internal benchmark suite covering e-commerce, business software, and collaboration workflows, function-calling and native execution now achieve near-parity performance. Holo3.1 also delivers more than a 25% improvement over Holo3 when evaluated inside our Holotab product harness.

To further enable local and on-device inference, we are also releasing new model sizes including small models (0.8B, 4B, and 9B) for cost-effective and private deployment, in addition to the larger 35B-A3B model for state-of-the-art performance.

Performance versus cost for the Holo3.1 and Qwen 3.5 families. Overall performance averages the four H Corporate benchmarks first (so each family is equally weighted), then takes the mean across OSWorld, AndroidWorld, H Corporate, ScreenSpot-Pro, and OSWorld-G.

Sources indicate that this is our first release to ship quantized weights. We’re starting with 35B-A3B checkpoints, available in FP8, Q4 GGUF, and NVFP4.

For NVFP4, we used NVIDIA's Model Optimizer in a W4A16 configuration. These checkpoints enable fast local inference for Computer Use Agents with little to no degradation in model performance. FP8 and NVFP4 achieve the same OSWorld scores, only about two points below the full-precision BF16 checkpoint.

The speedups are substantial: on DGX Spark, NVFP4 W4A16 delivers 1.41× the total token throughput of FP8 and 1.74× that of BF16.

We also release Q4 GGUF checkpoints aimed at local deployment of Computer Use Agents on consumer hardware.

The agent itself runs locally on a Windows or Mac machine, while the model can either run on that same machine—we include reference numbers for Apple Silicon—or on a DGX Spark on the same network. In both cases, execution stays fully private and local, with nothing leaving the user's network.

On Spark, agent harness optimizations we developed with NVIDIA combined with the NVFP4 quantization above deliver a compound ~2× end-to-end speedup over the FP8 baseline, cutting average step time from 6.8s to 3.3s.

Agent request rate across platforms and precisions. On DGX Spark, vLLM with NVFP4 achieves the highest request rate in both Default and Fast modes, followed by Q4 GGUF and FP8. These improvements and more will land in an upcoming desktop agent harness.

The Holo3.1 family is available in four sizes:.

We are also releasing optimized FP8, NVFP4, and Q4 GGUF checkpoints for local and edge deployment.

We look forward to seeing what developers build with Holo3.1.

Hardware & Chips 📈 Bullish 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

AMD and Winbond vulnerabilities let attackers brute-force BitLocker PINs on millions of PCs

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that former owners of laptops gained yet another concern today.
  • Industry observers note that the paper covers many vulnerabilities, but we'll focus on the massive three.
  • An attacker makes brute-forcing easier by resetting, or pretending to increase, the counter that records the number of failed unlock attempts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that former owners of laptops gained yet another concern today. Firmware-backed drive encryption setups like Windows' BitLocker are meant to protect against someone stealing your laptop or desktop computer. Prospective thieves would have a hard time guessing your PIN, as they'll eventually have to wait 10 minutes for each attempt. That is, unless your machine uses a modern AMD CPU or relies on Winbond's SPI flash — in which case your data may be open for inspection in a few days, or even hours, as researchers from Technische Universität Berlin found out.

Industry observers note that the paper covers many vulnerabilities, but we'll focus on the massive three. All focus on having a way to brute-force an encrypted drive's password in a matter of days/hours rather than years. Physical access is required for the attacks, but hardware theft is precisely the scenario that disk encryption is meant to protect against.

An attacker makes brute-forcing easier by resetting, or pretending to increase, the counter that records the number of failed unlock attempts. On Intel- and AMD-based PCs using the fTPM for security — nearly all modern x86 consumer machines — this counter is stored encrypted in an SPI flash chip on the motherboard.

Standard procedure is to allow for 32 attempts in succession, then force the machine to wait 10 minutes for each additional one, resulting in many years for unlocking a short PIN — 19 years for a six-digit numerical PIN, under normal conditions. We should note the attacks likely extend to other fTPM-based disk encryption mechanisms, not just BitLocker. While encryption keys can be alphanumeric, Microsoft Windows does default to using a numeric PIN for sign-in, and most users don't use long ones.

First up: machines based on Winbond's RPMC-enabled SPI flash (variant with rollback protection), used by many OEMs across both Intel and AMD platforms. Although it's hard to pin down the number of affected machines, the paper claims Winbond has roughly a 25% market share for SPI flash — so, potentially millions of machines. With a simple voltage glitch, the researchers made the chip reveal the HMAC key, the datum that signs commands when the TPM and the SPI chip talk to each other.

With the HMAC in hand, the thief places a low-cost interposer board in front of the SPI chip to impersonate it. On a failed unlock, the computer will request a counter increase and get a confirmation, when in reality nothing happened — allowing for repeat attempts as fast as Windows lets them, at five per reboot. There is no fix for this vulnerability other than replacing the SPI chip with one that doesn't contain the bug.

The team glitched two specific Winbond chip models, but they theorize the glitch extends further into the maker's lineup, as the flaw allegedly lies with the RPMC engine design. Flash chips from other firms in the test were not affected to the same extent.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Sources indicate that as for AMD machines, the situation is both worse and better, with two related vulnerabilities. The team verified at least one of the two attacks across AMD machines from Zen 2 up to an AI 5 330 laptop. They theorize that considering the mechanisms, all contemporary AMD setups may be vulnerable, at least for standard consumer hardware using fTPM. That's multiple millions of machines potentially at risk, on the low side.

The first is simple enough. On the tested machines whose SPI flash didn't use RPMC — rollback protection — you can just make a copy of the SPI flash's contents when the counter is low, and just flash it again once you've used up your free tries. Bad enough, yes, but the second vulnerability should elicit facepalms from security architects.

According to recent reports, according to the paper, AMD's firmware controller for non-volatile storage — the bit that talks to the SPI flash — does not verify that the failed-attempt counter increase actually took place. It'll just issue the order to +1 it and be done, opening the avenue for an attacker to simply intercept that order (again, with a cheap board) and ignore it without even needing HMAC keys, so the counter never changes.

The latter vulnerability should be fixable via a firmware enhancement, almost certainly via AMD's AGESA software. The problem is one of practicality: in the past, updating AGESA on client hardware meant that every OEM had to create fresh BIOSes for affected machines, many of which are assuredly out of their support window.

Anyone who's lived through the Spectre and Meltdown days knows how hard it is in practice, as OEMs are exceedingly slow to publish updates, and have a distaste for providing fixes for hardware that's more than a few years old.

The researchers contacted every firm involved in their tests, informing them of their findings, but sadly "none of them has committed to fixing the root-cause vulnerabilities" — at least, as of this writing, only Microsoft confirmed a policy change recommending users enter six-digit PINs instead of the current four during setup.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Reachy Mini conversation app can now use tools hosted in public Hugging Face Spaces, called over MCP.
  • Below, we look at what a tool is, how profiles control what the robot can use, and the current limits of the remote path.
  • When you talk to the robot, what you get back isn't only a voice, it's a system that reacts to the conversation: the robot can move and respond non-verbally, when it's applicable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Reachy Mini conversation app can now use tools hosted in public Hugging Face Spaces, called over MCP. You can give your robot a new ability, like checking the weather or searching the web, by adding a Space from the Hub instead of editing the app. The tool keeps running in the Space itself, so no code is downloaded onto your machine. And you can publish your own tools for other people to use.

Adding a tool takes one command:.

Below, we look at what a tool is, how profiles control what the robot can use, and the current limits of the remote path.

When you talk to the robot, what you get back isn't only a voice, it's a system that reacts to the conversation: the robot can move and respond non-verbally, when it's applicable. The part we want to focus on here is the tools that make that possible. A tool is something the model can do during a conversation: play an emotion, move the head, look through the camera. Each tool has a name and a short description. The model reads those, decides when one is useful, calls it, and uses what comes back.

Today every tool is local and ships inside the app, and most of them are about the robot's body:.

A tool in the code isn't usable until it's enabled in a profile, a folder with two files that matter here: instructions.txt (the prompt) and tools.txt (the tools that are turned on).

The default profile enables the full set:.

If a name isn't in tools.txt, the model can't call it.

You can also write your own tool: add a Python file to the profile (or external_tools/), give it a name and description, and list that name in tools.txt.

Today there are built-in tools and custom local tools, and tools.txt decides which are active. This works well for the robot's body and keeps the trusted core small.

Industry observers note that the constraint here is that every tool has to be local Python. For move_head or play_emotion that's right: they talk to the hardware and belong in the app but a lot of useful things have nothing to do with the body, like web search, weather, or lookups. For those, keeping everything local is mostly friction:.

Remote tools add a third kind, alongside the built-in and custom local tools you already have, for capabilities that are easier to publish, share, and update on their own:.

We started with two canary tools, small test tools to exercise the new flow:.

They're enough to exercise the whole feature: install from the Hub, discover the remote tools, enable them per profile, and let the realtime backend call them exactly like built-in tools.

To use both at once, add each Space and their tools stack in the same profile:.

Now the robot can search the web and check the weather in the same conversation, which is exactly what the canary_web_search_weather profile below does.

In a recent development, add validates the Space on the Hub, probes the MCP endpoint, discovers its tools, and by default appends the tool IDs to the active profile's tools.txt. The active profile is default unless you've set REACHY_MINI_CUSTOM_PROFILE. Use --install-only to skip that step.

tools.txt is the gatekeeper: a remote tool is only active if its ID appears in the profile's tools.txt, alongside whatever built-in tools you want.

Installed sources are persisted in:.

Each installed Space gets a local alias derived from its slug, with hyphens, dots, and slashes collapsing to underscores:.

Remote tools are then namespaced with a double underscore:.

This keeps remote tool names from colliding with built-in ones and lets multiple Spaces coexist in the same profile.

Recent findings suggest that the implementation also strips redundant Space-name prefixes when possible, so a verbose remote tool name becomes a cleaner local ID. If stripping would cause a collision between two tools from the same Space, the code falls back to the fully namespaced name.

There is also a duplicate safety check at registry level: Tool.name values must be unique across the entire merged tool set. The app fails fast if two sources claim the same name.

For this work we created two focused canary profiles to isolate the MCP experiment from the full embodied tool set.

The first keeps a few expressive tools (emotions, head movement) and adds web search on top:.

The second is the same, plus the weather tool alongside search:.

The small physical tool set means Reachy Mini can still react expressively while answering current questions from the web.

In a recent development, the remote-tool plumbing gets the tools into the model. The prompts decide how the model uses them.

That was especially visible in the search-plus-weather canary. A combined question like:.

can be handled in at least three ways: weather first then search, search first then weather, or both in the same turn. If the prompt is vague, the model serialises the calls and creates unnecessary latency. So the canary prompts became part of the feature, not just incidental configuration.

Two things are worth calling out. First, the Space has to actually behave like an MCP server; if tool discovery fails, the install fails. Second, prompt instructions can encourage parallel calls but cannot guarantee them. If deterministic orchestration matters for a use case, that logic should move from the prompt into code.

If you want others to use your tool, publish it as a public Gradio Space that exposes the standard MCP endpoint, and keep the tools stateless so they work well over the network. Whether a Space installs depends on this runtime behavior, not on tags.

Tags aren't required for installation, but they help people find compatible Spaces:.

The app now has three kinds of tools sharing one registry: built-in, local custom, and remote MCP tools, and profiles still decide which of them a given assistant can reach. A small, trusted core stays at the center while the optional capabilities around it can be added, tested, and swapped without touching the app itself.

Sources indicate that what we're most curious about now is what people build. If you publish a tool Space, tag it reachy-mini-tool and mcp so others can find it. We'd love to see what Reachy Mini ends up able to do!

Acknowledgements: Many thanks to Fabien Danieau for proofreading this post and helping test the workflow, to Andres Marafioti for helping test it, and to Remi Fabre and the Pollen Robotics team for the ideas and feedback that shaped the remote tools workflow.

Great work on making Reachy even easier to customize!How can I add these MCP tools on a wireless Reachy Mini with a preinstalled conversation app?

It has been revealed that the tools.txt approach makes the MCP integration especially clear. I like how remote tools are kept separate from the built-in robot tools while still being enabled per profile. The distinction between installing a Space and actually activating its tool IDs in tools.txt also seems crucial, particularly when multiple remote tools are being used together.I’m also using an MCP server on my site, https://tinid.ph/, to work with AI agents, and it has been really useful for me. In particular, it has helped a lot with identifying and fixing technical issues on the site. The idea of keeping tools accessible to AI agents through MCP, rather than building every capability directly into the application, makes a lot of sense.

If you're looking at wiring up your home or figuring out your entire networking situation, nothing ever beats being plugged into an Ethernet port. The TP-Link LS1005G Lightwave 5-port unmanaged Ethernet switch is back down to its lowest-ever price at just $7.99 on Amazon as a part of their Black Friday sale. At over 53% off, an unmanaged switch buys you freedom and, crucially, more Ethernet ports to play around with. This device is ideal for those looking to connect essential devices via Ethernet, like networked cameras, an office full of electronics, or a multi-system homelab setup.

According to recent reports, when the switch is this cheap, it's difficult to overstate how useful it could be if you're a resident tinkerer like any of us on the Tom's Hardware staff team. Each port can deliver full gigabit speeds across a 10Gbps backplane on the switch. That means if you're running a rapid setup, you'll still get gigabit-level speeds across all devices that are connected to this unit.

It's also useful for those who have mesh networks, with only one single Ethernet port coming out of a satellite node. This unmanaged switch will give you access to more ports and more wired devices without the pitfalls of hooking things up over Wi-Fi, which can be prone to interference or latency. In this scenario, though, you're ideally looking at the satellite node running a wired backhaul across your network to maintain stability and avoid pitfalls like packet loss.

The TP-Link Litewave 5-Port Gigabit Ethernet Switch LS1005G provides four additional Ethernet ports, delivering reliable, high-speed wired internet for your gaming PC, NAS, console, TV, and other connected devices.

Given the price, it's crucial to note what you don't get with an inexpensive, unmanaged switch such as this. You won't receive any Power over Ethernet on the LS1005G switch, so if your networked cameras rely on it, you should look elsewhere. Additionally, as it's unmanaged, you cannot... well... manage it. Strictly speaking, 1Gbps should be more than enough bandwidth for most at-home use cases, such as NAS systems or sending files across your network. But if you're regularly sending larger files and have the infrastructure to support it, then looking at a unit with faster ports might be worthwhile for you, but if you don't think you'll hit the gigabit ceiling often, it's a perfect set-and-forget device.

Industry observers note that in particular, for the gamers among you, gigabit ports will be more than stable enough to support online gaming, even in titles that demand no packet loss, like online Rollback netcode in competitive fighting games like Street Fighter 6 and Fatal Fury: City of the Wolves. Remember, sustaining the harmony of a wired network does have its benefits! At under $8 on Amazon, TP-Link's unmanaged switch fits a huge variety of use cases and is also just handy to keep around, in case you'll need one later down the line.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) app is usually drawn as a language model plus a vector database.
  • This article reveals how to estimate that limit before you deploy, with a short script you can run, and then covers what else in the pipeline can slow responses down.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) app is usually drawn as a language model plus a vector database. When it goes live, the part that fails first is rarely the retrieval. It is GPU memory on the generation model, because a model that loads fine for one request can run out of memory when several users send long questions at once.

This article reveals how to estimate that limit before you deploy, with a short script you can run, and then covers what else in the pipeline can slow responses down.

Sources indicate that serving a model takes more than its weights. The GPU also holds:.

the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with the length of every active request.

activations and batching overhead.

memory used by the inference runtime itself.

SitePoint's guide to running a local LLM on 10GB of VRAM makes the same point for a single desktop GPU: the usable budget is the total VRAM minus overhead, and the KV cache grows with the context window, so the real model budget is smaller than the number on the box.

Sources indicate that for a RAG service, the KV cache matters even more. Retrieved passages are pasted into the prompt, so every request carries a long context, and every concurrent request holds its own cache.

It has been revealed that the cache size per token depends on the model's architecture: two tensors (keys and values) for every layer, for every KV head. This script turns those numbers into a rough limit on concurrent requests:.

def kv_bytes_per_token(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes=2):.

# Keys and values, for every layer, for one token.

return 2 *layers *kv_heads *head_dim *dtype_bytes.

def max_concurrent(vram_gb, weights_gb, ctx_tokens, per_token, reserve_gb=2.0):.

budget = (vram_gb - weights_gb - reserve_gb) * GIB.

return int(budget // (ctx_tokens * per_token)).

per_token = kv_bytes_per_token(32, 8, 128).

print(per_token // 1024, "KiB per token").

for ctx in (4096, 8192, 16384):.

n = max_concurrent(24, 16, ctx, per_token).

print(ctx, "tokens ->", n, "concurrent requests").

For a 24 GB GPU holding about 16 GB of fp16 weights with 2 GB kept in reserve, it prints:.

4096 tokens -> 12 concurrent requests.

8192 tokens -> 6 concurrent requests.

16384 tokens -> 3 concurrent requests.

Industry observers note that the numbers are estimates. Real runtimes add their own overhead, and the architecture values come from the model's configuration file, so read them from the model you actually use. The pattern is what matters: doubling the context length halves the number of requests that fit. A RAG prompt that stuffs in ten retrieved chunks costs real capacity.

Recent findings suggest that serving runtimes do not simply crash when the cache is full. The vLLM documentation on optimization and tuning explains that when KV cache space is insufficient for all batched requests, the engine preempts some of them and recomputes them later, which can hurt end-to-end latency. Its suggested remedies include giving the cache more memory, reducing the number of concurrent sequences or batched tokens, or sharding the model across GPUs.

Sources indicate that so the symptom of undersizing is often not an error. It is slow, uneven responses under load. Test with realistic prompt lengths and several simultaneous customers, not a single request.

Embedding and ingestion have a different profile from generation. Embedding is often lighter than serving a large language model, and some teams run it on CPU. Document parsing, chunking and tokenization also run on CPU, so a fast GPU cannot make up for a slow CPU upstream. SitePoint's tutorial on a local RAG system for private documents walks through chunking, embeddings, vector storage and reranking, and is a good map of which stages run where.

RAM: vector indexes, document loaders and caches all live in system memory, so large collections need more of it.

According to recent reports, storage: model files, indexes, logs and backups add up. Fast storage shortens model loading and re-indexing.

Network: if the vector database, application server and model server sit in different places, latency adds to every request.

Two layouts are common. A single instance runs everything and is simplest for prototypes and internal tools. Separated services put ingestion and retrieval on smaller machines and keep the GPU for generation, which scales better as traffic grows.

In a recent development, memory estimates only hold if the GPU memory is really yours. On a shared or time-sliced GPU, other workloads can take memory and compute away from your service, which makes capacity hard to initiative. Hosting providers describe this in different terms, such as passthrough, vGPU, MIG and time-slicing. For a view of how one GPU hosting provider explains those allocation methods, GPU Mart's GPU virtualization guide compares them. It is a hosting tech giant's page, so confirm any provider's claims about isolation and performance with your own load test.

Whatever provider you choose, ask these questions:.

Is the physical GPU assigned to you exclusively, or partitioned or time-sliced?

Do you have root access to install your own drivers, CUDA libraries and containers?

Which minimum commitments, regions and support terms apply?

It has been revealed that A small stack can run as a handful of containers: an API service for request handling and prompt assembly, an ingestion worker, a vector database and a model server. Keeping them separate lets you monitor each one's memory and CPU use and move the heavy one to bigger hardware without rewriting the rest.

For a service that stays up all month, a fixed monthly term is easier to forecast than hourly capacity. Hourly capacity suits testing quantization settings or processing a one-off document batch.

Is GPU memory always the bottleneck for RAG?

Industry observers note that not always. Generation usually hits memory first, but slow parsing, a small CPU or a distant vector database can dominate response time.

Does quantization solve the memory problem?

It shrinks the weights, but the KV cache still grows with context length and concurrency. Test with your real prompt sizes.

Should embeddings run on the GPU?

In a recent development, it depends on volume. Small workloads can run on CPU, while a large ingestion job may benefit from a GPU for a limited time.

Size a RAG service for the worst realistic moment, not the single-request demo. Estimate the KV cache from the model's architecture, remember that long retrieved contexts reduce how many requests fit, watch for preemption under load, keep CPU, RAM, storage and network in the plan, and find out whether the GPU is exclusive or shared. The script above is small, but it turns a vague worry about memory into numbers you can check.

#162663. Direct Preference Optimization Beyond Chatbots

📅 03 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2917 w)

Direct Preference Optimization Beyond Chatbots

📅 03 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In April, we released DharmaOCR, our specialized structured OCR model (available on Hugging Face) along with a paper detailing the methodology behind it and a benchmark demonstrating its superior quality and cost efficiency.
  • Recent findings suggest that across the tested open-source families, vanilla degeneration rates ranged from below 1% to above 33%.
  • A second training stage - applied after supervised fine-tuning (SFT), on the same documents, using the same model - reduced text degeneration in every family tested.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In April, we released DharmaOCR, our specialized structured OCR model (available on Hugging Face) along with a paper detailing the methodology behind it and a benchmark demonstrating its superior quality and cost efficiency. The paper benchmarked leading vision-language model families - both open-source and commercial - on a structured document extraction task: OCR on Brazilian Portuguese text. Among the reported metrics was text degeneration rate: the frequency with which a model produces a repetition loop instead of a transcription.

Recent findings suggest that across the tested open-source families, vanilla degeneration rates ranged from below 1% to above 33%. Supervised fine-tuning reduced those rates for most models - but rarely to production-acceptable levels. The pattern points to a structural limitation: SFT optimizes for correct outputs, but does not explicitly penalize degeneration. There appears to be a ceiling on how much task-focused fine-tuning alone can reduce this failure mode (Text Degeneration Article).

A second training stage - applied after supervised fine-tuning (SFT), on the same documents, using the same model - reduced text degeneration in every family tested. No exceptions. Average reduction: 59.4%. Best case: 87.6%.

Sources indicate that figure 1: DPO reduced degeneration relative to SFT in every family tested - average reduction of 59.4%, peak of 87.6% (Nanonets-OCR2–3B: 1.61% to 0.20%). The direction is invariant; only the magnitude varies.

That second stage was Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Almost all published DPO applications target chat alignment - models trained on human judgments about helpfulness or harmlessness (example: Rafailov et al., 2023). OCR carries none of that subjectivity: the task is objective, and there is no conversational context. There is, however, a clear preference signal. A correct transcription is chosen; a degeneration loop is rejected. DharmaOCR used that binary to construct a DPO training set, testing the technique not for alignment, but as a direct mitigation tool for a specific failure mode.

In a recent development, the training signal came from the model itself - specifically from the outputs it produced when it failed. How a failure mode becomes a training signal is a structural question about the failure, not the model.

It has been revealed that why SFT has a ceiling on degeneration is still an open question - but the leading conjecture points to loss granularity. SFT trains token by token: each prediction is evaluated in isolation, and a repetition loop is never penalized as a completion-level failure. DPO inverts that logic. The training signal is the full output - chosen or rejected - which means a degenerated completion can be explicitly labeled as the wrong outcome, not just a sequence of locally probable tokens.

Recent findings suggest that when a training objective maximizes the likelihood of observed sequences, it concentrates probability mass in the regions of distribution space those sequences occupy. A model that enters one of those high-probability attractor regions during inference assigns elevated probability to the same token at the next step - which increases the probability further, which sustains the loop until the sequence hits the maximum token limit. Text degeneration is the output of this geometry: a self-reinforcing repetition loop that an autoregressive model cannot exit without external intervention (Holtzman et al., 2020). It is not purely a decoding artifact. The attractor involves the training objective, the learned distribution, and how probability mass concentrates during inference - a systems-level failure rather than a failure localized to any single component.

The geometry of this failure is visible at the token level.

Figure 2: When a token dominates its own conditional distribution, every sampling step deepens the attractor. The decoder samples from this geometry; it does not determine it.

In a recent development, inference-layer interventions - repetition penalties, temperature adjustments, early-abort logic - operate on the sampling step. They contain the symptom without touching the distribution that produces it. The attractor persists.

Supervised fine-tuning moves the distribution closer to the task domain. For a structured generation pipeline, this means training on domain-specific documents, in the target language, with the required output format. The model gains fluency with longer sequences, constrained syntax, domain vocabulary. What SFT does not do is attack degeneration directly. Its objective - maximizing the likelihood of observed sequences - has no term that penalizes repetition loops. The failure mode is simply outside the scope of what the training signal optimizes for.

One model family in the DharmaOCR benchmark highlighted an unexpected pattern: vanilla degeneration rate of 0.60%, rising to 3.23% after SFT, before a subsequent DPO stage brought it to 1.41%. It is a single data point - an exception, not a rule - and it would be overstating the evidence to treat it as proof of a mechanism. What it does illustrate is that SFT does not reliably reduce degeneration. Capability and degeneration resistance can move independently.

According to recent reports, the distinction matters structurally. SFT and DPO are not interchangeable training stages performing the same operation at different intensities. SFT closes the distance between the model's prior distribution and the task domain. What it does not do is target degeneration as an objective - its effect on the failure mode is incidental, and the benchmark results show it is not consistent. The attractor that produces degeneration is not a problem with the model's proximity to the task - it is a problem with the shape of the distribution space the model now occupies.

Addressing that geometry requires a training signal built specifically to point the model away from its own failure modes. For a structured, non-conversational task with no human preference labels and no conventional "helpful versus harmful" distinction, constructing that signal is a design decision.

The DharmaOCR pipeline's contribution to DPO methodology is specific: it used the SFT model's own degenerate outputs as the rejected examples - not as noise to remove, but as the negative training signal the optimization needed.

DPO requires preference pairs: a chosen output and a rejected output for the same input, with a quality difference clear enough for the optimization to learn from. In chat alignment, human annotators produce those judgments - rating responses as more or less helpful, accurate, or safe. Structured generation tasks have no equivalent annotation source. An OCR pipeline either produces a correct transcription or it does not. Quality differences exist, but they are not produced by human preference rankings - they are produced by the task's own criteria for correctness.

The DharmaOCR pipeline identified a preference signal that structured generation tasks already produce: the range of outputs the SFT model generates in inference. A model capable of performing a structured task is also capable of failing at it in characteristic ways. Those failures - outputs that enter the degeneration attractor - are not noise to filter. They are the most informative negative signal available.

The paper implemented this on 23,726 training documents, generating multiple candidate responses per document with the SFT model and scoring each with an automated LLM judge. The pipeline is shown below.

Figure 3: The critical design decision is not in the pipeline's structure - it is in what the pipeline preserved: outputs displaying text degeneration were deliberately labeled as rejected examples, not filtered out as low-quality noise.

Industry observers note that the conventional response when degenerate outputs appear in training data is to remove them. They are low-quality signal; filtering produces a cleaner dataset. The DharmaOCR approach inverted this logic. Degenerate outputs were deliberately retained as the rejected examples in each (chosen, rejected) pair, because they represent exactly the failure mode the DPO stage was designed to suppress. Removing them would have discarded the clearest target available.

Recent findings suggest that the paper describes this as "preference-guided implicit unlikelihood" - the model is trained not only toward better outputs but away from a specific class of failure. Where SFT maximizes the likelihood of high-quality outputs, the DPO stage simultaneously penalizes outputs displaying the degeneration attractor geometry. The direction of the optimization is explicit in a way SFT alone cannot achieve.

Degenerate outputs are particularly well-suited as rejection examples because they represent a consistent failure mode rather than varied low-quality outputs. A transcription that misses words is low quality, but its failure is case-specific. Repetition loops, by contrast, appeared persistently across documents and model families even after SFT - a pattern consistent with a failure mode that likelihood-based optimization does not reliably correct. DPO applies its loss differently: at the completion level, with explicit rejection signals. The post-hoc analysis cannot establish causality, but the evidence suggests that what SFT's objective leaves unresolved, DPO's may address.

It has been revealed that this approach requires no specialized annotation infrastructure - only a model capable of producing both acceptable and identifiable-failure outputs, and a scoring model to label preference pairs. A rule-based mechanism could detect repetition loops mechanically - but it could not identify which outputs represented high-quality transcriptions worth preserving as chosen examples.

According to recent reports, the scoring model does both: it flags degeneration as the rejected output and validates clean extractions as the chosen one, keeping the model's extraction capability intact while the DPO signal penalizes the failure mode. Whether the resulting training signal successfully moves the distribution in the intended direction - and whether it does so consistently across architectures - is the evidence question.

The DPO stage reduced text degeneration in every model family tested - with reductions ranging from 37% to 88% and an average of 59.4% relative to SFT alone. The result held across architectures, parameter scales, and starting degeneration profiles that differed by more than one order of magnitude. One case in the dataset saw degeneration increase after the SFT stage before DPO corrected it. That case does not complicate the consistency. It confirms the mechanism more directly than any of the others.

Recent findings suggest that figure 1 shows the three-stage degeneration rate for each of the five model families tested: Vanilla, SFT, and SFT+DPO. In four of the five families, degeneration falls at each stage. The fifth family's bars move differently - and that difference is the most analytically important data point in the study.

The Qwen2.5-VL-3B result, read carefully, is not a complication. It is a confirmation. The model's vanilla degeneration rate was 0.60% - not because it was stable, but because it was too generic to produce long structured outputs at all. The model was not entering the degeneration attractor because it was not attempting the task seriously enough to find it.

In a recent development, SFT changed that. After domain adaptation, Qwen2.5-VL-3B became capable of the task - producing longer, more structured outputs with the domain vocabulary and format the pipeline required. That capability brought it into proximity with the degeneration attractor for the first time. Its degeneration rate rose to 3.23%.

This is the mechanism made empirically visible: SFT moved the model toward the task and toward the task's failure geometry simultaneously. These are not necessarily the same operation. A training stage that increases task capability can increase failure-mode exposure as a side effect - particularly when the failure mode lives at the edge of the capability frontier. Treated as the same operation, the Qwen2.5-VL-3B result looks like an error. Treated as distinct operations - which is what the SFT + DPO pipeline formally does - the result is consistent with the hypothesis that SFT and DPO address different failure dimensions.

Industry observers note that the DPO stage then brought the degeneration rate to 1.41%. It did not restore the vanilla baseline because it was not designed to: the model after SFT was more capable than it had been, and a return to 0.60% would have required undoing that capability. What the DPO stage did was address the failure geometry the SFT stage had introduced.

It has been revealed that the remaining four model families add quantitative weight to the same conclusion. Figure 1 shows the SFT-to-SFT+DPO comparison for all five.

Figure 1: DPO reduced degeneration relative to SFT in every family tested - average reduction of 59.4%, peak of 87.6% (Nanonets-OCR2–3B: 1.61% to 0.20%). The direction is invariant; only the magnitude varies.

Sources indicate that no model family indicated degeneration increasing after DPO. No family was immune to its effect. The consistency extends to gemma-3–4b-it, which entered the benchmark with the highest vanilla degeneration rate by an order of magnitude - 33.96%, compared to the next highest at 2.62% - and still reached a 75% reduction after the DPO stage. The reduction range - 37.3% to 87.6% - reflects differences in starting configuration and architecture, not inconsistency in the intervention's direction.

This is not a proof of universal applicability. DPO may not transfer to every domain, failure mode, or model family. What the DharmaOCR benchmark provides is evidence across five OCR architectures that the core hypothesis holds: optimizing over complete preference pairs - rather than maximizing token-level likelihood - addresses a failure mode that SFT structurally cannot target. The result was consistent in direction across every model family tested. That consistency, within the scope of this benchmark, is what the evidence supports.

It has been revealed that the DharmaOCR approach was possible because this pipeline satisfied a set of structural conditions that allowed a DPO training stage to function as designed - conditions whose presence or absence determines whether the same methodology applies elsewhere (Dharma OCR Paper on ArXiv). It was not possible because OCR is a unique domain.

The first condition is that the failure mode be identifiable as a distinct class of output, not just a point on a quality continuum. Text degeneration qualifies because a repetition loop is categorically different from a transcription that misses words or misreads a character. The output is not merely suboptimal - it is broken in a specific, behaviorally recognizable way. That categorical distinctness is what allowed the pipeline to construct preference pairs where the rejected examples represented a coherent failure geometry, not noise. A task whose failure modes blend into its range of acceptable variation lacks this property.

According to recent reports, the second condition is that a scoring mechanism can reliably distinguish acceptable outputs from failure-mode outputs without requiring human annotation. In the DharmaOCR pipeline, an automated LLM judge scored candidate responses against four task-specific criteria. The scoring did not need to be perfect - it needed to be consistent enough to produce preference pairs with a meaningful quality gap between chosen and rejected. Pairs with ambiguous quality differences contribute noise to DPO training, not signal. The judge's consistency was a design requirement, not an incidental feature.

Industry observers note that the third condition is sufficient volume - enough inference outputs to generate a preference dataset with meaningful variance in quality. This is not an extraordinary requirement by fine-tuning standards, but it is a real one.

In a recent development, when all three conditions are present, the methodological move is structurally available. The design decision at the center of the DharmaOCR pipeline - treating the model's own failure outputs as the rejected examples rather than filtering them - applies wherever a model's failures are categorically identifiable, scoreable, and sufficiently numerous.

Sources indicate that the practical implication for ML engineers building structured generation pipelines is direct. SFT is necessary - it closes the distance between a generalist model and a task-capable one. It is not sufficient for structured output reliability, because task capability and degeneration resistance are different properties of the distribution. A DPO stage after SFT is a one-time training investment. In the DharmaOCR results, the degeneration reduction did not come at the cost of extraction quality - the paper's benchmark results show both moving together (Specialization Beats Scale article).

Industry observers note that what makes a failure mode usable as training signal is not the domain - it is whether the failures are consistent enough, identifiable enough, and numerous enough to constitute a legible signal. In the DharmaOCR pipeline, they were. Whether the same holds in another context is a structural question about the task's failure mode, not a question about the model family or the domain.

Recent findings suggest that the DharmaOCR result does not depend on the domain being special. It depends on the failures being useful.

Text degeneration qualifies as useful because it is categorically distinct from acceptable outputs, consistently produced across inference runs, and reliably scoreable without human annotation. Those three properties - not the OCR context, not the model family, not the language - determined whether the preference dataset was tractable. A failure mode that satisfies them is not noise to remove. It is the most direct evidence available of where the distribution should not go.

Industry observers note that the DPO stage used that evidence. Degeneration fell in every model family tested - in models that entered the benchmark with vanilla rates below 1% and in models that entered with rates above 33%. The direction held. The pipeline did not discard its failures. It trained on them.

Sources indicate that interesting explanation of how Direct Preference Optimization can improve model alignment beyond traditional chatbot applications. I think techniques like this are crucial for making AI systems more reliable and better at understanding user intent. This is particularly relevant when building a customer service chatbot, where accurate, relevant, and helpful responses can make a major difference in the user experience. Consistency and understanding context are just as important as generating natural-sounding answers. It adds another useful perspective to the discussion.

This Amazon Ember TV Black Friday deal takes up to 40% off the tech giant’s own TV brand, making it ideal for a secondary set.

Amazon Fire TVs (now known as Amazon Ember TVs) are typically quite affordable and, of course, Black Friday week is making those prices even better than usual. Case in point, the firm’s most affordable TV is usually $329, but that same model is down to an incredible $199, making it ridiculously easy to recommend no matter how picky you might be about your TVs. And yes, this is the 2026 model, so you’re not buying something ancient.

I have no idea why Amazon is so obsessed with fire-related names (Kindle, Fire TV, Ember, etc.), but it’s hard to ignore the company’s leanings toward value-heavy products that cost very little to acquire. The Amazon Ember TV lineup sports 4K resolution, support for HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG, Dolby Audio, an ambient artwork screensaver, and lots of free streaming content built-in. It’s even got Amazon Luna built in, which gives you games like Star Wars Galactic Racer for free.

All three models ship with the latest Fire TV experience and Alexa+, which is a significantly smarter, LLM-powered version of Alexa (Alexa GPT, basically). It has apps for all the major streaming networks and even YouTube, but these don’t have the Google Play Store or a Google TV app, so keep that in mind before buying.

Of course, a $199 TV will not have the same image quality as a $600-plus TV, but that’s probably not an issue if this is just a secondary TV for a spare bedroom (or a backup TV).

#162661. Why GTA VI’s version of Florida feels so real

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1205 w)

Why GTA VI’s version of Florida feels so real

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Virtual city expert Emma Fraser explains what makes Rockstar’s latest open world work.
  • It has been revealed that there are plenty of reasons why Grand Theft Auto VI is so popular: the 13 years of anticipation, the relatable lead characters and romantic storyline, the sheer level of depth.
  • “There’s something about this particular game that is really discombobulating and distracting in a sense,” she states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Virtual city expert Emma Fraser explains what makes Rockstar’s latest open world work.

It has been revealed that there are plenty of reasons why Grand Theft Auto VI is so popular: the 13 years of anticipation, the relatable lead characters and romantic storyline, the sheer level of depth. But another major factor is the sense of place. The GTA series is unmatched when it comes to re-creating the feeling of a bustling, real-world city, and GTA VI’s fictional rendition of Florida is the studio’s most lifelike setting yet. It has functioning buses and trains, plentiful buildings you can go into and explore, residents you can chat with, and huge areas where you can interact with wildlife far away from the bright lights of the Miami-like Vice City. For Emma Fraser, an assistant professor at UC Berkeley who studies urban ruins and virtual cities, the sense of realism has created a unique sensation while playing.

“There’s something about this particular game that is really discombobulating and distracting in a sense,” she states. “Because you have these moments where you think, ‘I’m in a place, I’m experiencing a location.’ You comprehend intellectually that it’s not real or that it’s at best a representation, but you still have this feeling in your brain and you’ll still dream about being in that place.”.

In a recent development, fraser teaches courses on topics including urban geography and virtual worlds and has written papers exploring topics like “mapping in the digital age” and “the virtual spectacle of the end of the city.” She states she started researching video game cities in part because, despite their influence and reach, they’re an underexplored space in academia. “I’m a geographer, and geographers are obsessed with cities,” she explains. “So much of geography is thinking about: How do we imagine cities? How do we navigate cities? How do we build cities? How do we map cities? And video games have all of that, but they’re not taken that seriously as an academic interest.”.

It has been revealed that like much of the world, she’s been looking forward to GTA VI for years, particularly because of Rockstar’s on-the-ground approach to research. Before development on the game began, developers from the studio traveled to Florida to get an accurate picture. As GTA VI producer Rob Nelson told me, the starting point for the game was the setting, rather than the story or characters. “We just went around to feel it out,” he said. “Go to the Everglades, go to the Keys, go to the city, as many places as we can, and start thinking about what aspects of the place we want to incorporate.”.

Recent findings suggest that while there are plenty of open-world games, many of the most successful — from Elden Ring to The Witcher — are sent in fantastical spaces. GTA stands apart in how its various settings look and feel true to the real world. And Fraser believes that this is one of the key reasons the series has such universal appeal. “You know immediately how to function in a city,” she explains. “You know there’s going to be law enforcement, there are going to be city blocks, there are going to be pedestrians, cars, and buses. It’s this really interesting environment that gives you a lot of possibilities to get a player more immersed in your world, because they already know a lot about a city as a general concept.”.

“You can’t hold a whole city in your mind at one time.”.

Fraser describes GTA VI’s world as having “implied expansiveness.” It’s not a one-to-one re-creation of the real location. There are plenty of things missing; you don’t see schools or daycares, and parking spaces are relatively sparse. But the game gets enough details right to be recognizable. Fraser explains that as long as certain parts of the city look correct — the lighting, the coastline, the decoration of street corners, the major arterial roads — that’s enough to convince people that they’re in something resembling Miami.

Sources indicate that “You can’t hold a whole city in your mind at one time,” she notes. “Instead it’s these highlights. What [Rockstar] do very successfully in the game is those snapshots. They’ve got far more content that is recognizable as Florida or Miami than they’ve been able to fit into previous games. So it’s a much more overwhelming sense of being in that place.” The “implied expansiveness” also comes in the form of dialogue, radio programs, and TV highlights that suggest a much bigger world by discussing places and moments that exist outside of the game you can actually explore.

It has been revealed that this level of verisimilitude — combined with the fact that players can explore the city from multiple perspectives, everything from walking to flying a plane — has led to an experience that Fraser likens to virtual tourism, which can result in all kinds of different playstyles. “Some tourists are going to blow a lot of money on taxis and get to wherever they’re going as fast as they can,” she explains, “and some people just like sitting on a bus or a train and getting to know a place.” Similarly, there are certain players who will just experience the story and play through the main missions, and others who will get lost in side activities like bird watching.

“Some people just like sitting on a bus or a train and getting to know a place”.

According to recent reports, what’s also notable about GTA VI is how its relationship-focused premise is motivating some players to experience the world in a much less violent way. And that includes how they move through the city. Some people are driving more carefully to avoid killing civilians, while others are exploring spaces while both characters hang out together. “In the first few games, you’re this empty vessel. You’re a criminal, you’re doing criminal things,” indicates Fraser. “Whereas with GTA VI your motivation and the way you think about your character is really important.”.

It has been revealed that now that the game is out and millions of players are venturing through Vice City, Fraser is hoping to use it to research the ways that real and virtual worlds intersect when it comes to how we navigate cities. GTA VI offers a lot of choice in this regard; you can still steal a Lambo and speed through the streets, but you can also hop on a train, put on some headphones, and listen to a podcast while getting where you need to be. “Because this world is so fully furnished, and you have so many options, you might start to import your own real-world practices into the game,” she says.

But at this point, what has struck her most is the attention to detail that separates the universe of GTA VI from its contemporaries. “You can’t just generate a generic city and stick icons in, which is what a lot of games do,” she explains. “You aren’t going to get a sense of a real place if you do it that way.”.

#162660. Latest Update: Designing the hf CLI as an agent-optimized way to work with the Hub

📅 04 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2206 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Designing the hf CLI as an agent-optimized way to work with the Hub

📅 04 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2206 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, hf is the official command-line entrypoint to the Hugging Face Hub.
  • Sources indicate that the hf CLI has been primarily built for our people over the years.
  • Sources indicate that we started tracking agent usage of the Hub in April 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, hf is the official command-line entrypoint to the Hugging Face Hub. Anything you can do on the Hub from the Python SDK, you can do from your terminal: download and upload models, datasets and Spaces; create and manage repos, branches, tags and pull requests; run Jobs on HF infrastructure; manage Buckets, Collections, webhooks and Inference Endpoints.

Sources indicate that the hf CLI has been primarily built for our people over the years. But it's now increasingly used by coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more. So we rebuilt it to make it work for both audiences at once. This blog post summarizes what we did, and how we benchmarked it. We found that on complex, multi-step tasks the no-CLI baseline (an agent hand-rolling curl or the Python SDK) uses up to 6× as many tokens as the hf CLI.

Sources indicate that we started tracking agent usage of the Hub in April 2026. The hf CLI (and the huggingface_hub Python SDK it's built on) detects when a coding agent is driving it by reading the environment variables agents set: CLAUDECODE/CLAUDE_CODE for Claude Code, CODEX_SANDBOX for Codex, plus Cursor, Gemini, Pi, and the universal AI_AGENT. That single signal does two jobs: it shapes the CLI's output (more on that below) and it tags each Hub request with an agent/ user-agent, so we can attribute traffic to the agent driving it. The two largest by distinct users are Claude Code and Codex, well ahead of everything else, and they're the two agents we benchmark later in this article.

It has been revealed that the bars count distinct customers per agent; request volume is the sub-label. Claude Code alone is ~40k users and nearly 49M requests, with Codex close behind. These are early numbers (we only began attributing agent traffic in April 2026), but the scale is already significant, and we expect it to keep growing as coding agents become a standard way to work with the Hub.

Industry observers note that humans and coding agents expect different outputs for the same hf commands. A human wants rich terminal output: ANSI color, padded tables truncated to fit the screen, a green ✅ on success, ✔ for booleans, progress bars, prose hints. An agent wants the inverse: no ANSI, nothing truncated, every value in full since an agent can handle far denser output than a human, kept compact and structured to stay light on tokens. It also can't answer a CLI prompt and will happily re-run a command after a timeout. The rest of this section is how hf gives each side what it needs. We introduced agent-mode output in hf v1.9.0 and have been migrating the rest of the CLI to it gradually in the following releases.

When hf auto-detects agent use (via the environment variables mentioned above), it renders the same command differently. It optimizes output format for humans or agents without passing a flag:.

It has been revealed that A human gets an aligned table, truncated to fit the terminal, plus a hint on how to see more, with color cues for status (a green ✓ on success, red on error). An agent gets the complete record as TSV: full repo ids, full ISO timestamps, every tag, no ANSI codes, nothing truncated, clean to parse and light on tokens.

In practice, we've implemented logging methods like .table(...), .result(...), .json(), etc., which take raw data as input and handle the formatting. In addition to human and agent modes, we've introduced --json and --quiet options to make it easier to pipe commands together. The default mode is automatically chosen based on context, but consumers can always force the format of their choice with --format human | agent | json | quiet.

In a recent development, CLI commands rarely run in isolation: one step usually implies the next (git add, then git commit). Many hf commands now end with a hint: the exact next command to run, pre-filled with the IDs you just used, so a user or agent can chain straight to the next step instead of working it out from scratch. Start a Job in the background and it points you to its logs; create a Space and it points you to its boot status:.

Industry observers note that for a human that's a convenience. For an agent it's a rail: the next action is named, parameterized with the right ids, and ready to run, so it takes fewer steps working out what to do. Errors behave the same way, naming the fix instead of just failing:.

Hints, warnings and errors all go to stderr while data goes to stdout, so none of this guidance pollutes the output the agent is parsing.

In a recent development, hf never sits on an interactive prompt waiting for a key an agent can't press. A destructive command still asks a human to confirm, but in agent mode it fails fast with the fix in the message (Use --yes to skip confirmation.), and -y/--yes skips it. And because agents retry on timeouts and lost context, operations are built to be safe to repeat: hf repos create --exist-ok is a no-op if the repo already exists, and re-running an upload re-commits cleanly. Separately, the commands that move real data take a --dry-run that indicates exactly what they'll transfer before they run, which proves handy for humans and agents alike, since neither has to commit to a long download or blind sync:.

hf is built to be probed: run hf to see the resource groups, run --help on the one you need, and every --help ends with real, copy-pasteable examples (which an agent matches against far faster than it parses a description):.

The command tree is consistent, resource + verb with the obvious aliases (hf models ls, hf repos create, hf jobs ps, hf collections delete; list/ls, remove/rm), so once an agent learns one command it can guess the rest. And the output composes: -q prints one id per line to pipe into the next command, --json gives you something to hand to jq.

To find out whether the hf CLI is really more efficient for agents, we measured it. We built a small evaluation harness and ran the same set of Hub tasks through each way of driving the Hub, many times over, grading every run against the live Hub. Here's the headline before the methodology: across both agents the hf CLI comes out ahead, most clearly on complex, multi-step tasks where it uses far fewer tokens.

Industry observers note that (self-report error = the agent reported success on the 17 solvable tasks but the Hub stated otherwise. The hf CLI rows are the CLI with its skill installed; what the skill adds on top of the bare CLI (chiefly fewer tool calls) is broken out in the skill section below. Representative transcripts are published in this bucket.).

Industry observers note that we defined 18 non-trivial Hub tasks. Not "download a file", but the kind of thing you'd actually ask for: aggregate a trending org's models, inspect a repo's files and their sizes, upload a folder with include/exclude rules, delete files, copy files across repos, open a PR that adds a license, create a repo with a branch and a tag, sync and prune a bucket, build a collection. Each task goes to a fresh coding agent with exactly one way to talk to the Hub:.

Recent findings suggest that we run the hf CLI in two configurations, with and without its skill (a generated command reference we come back to in its own section). But the headline comparison below is simply hf CLI vs curl / the SDK; the skill's incremental effect is small enough that we break it out on its own rather than crowd it into the main results.

The config is deliberately clean: a fresh instance per run, no custom MCP servers, no CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, nothing in context to nudge behavior. The task and the tool go into a single prompt, and the agent finishes with a TASK_COMPLETE or TASK_FAILED marker, but we don't trust that marker (an agent will report success on work that never landed), so we grade every run independently by re-querying the live Hub: did the branch really get created, is the file actually gone, does the bucket exist? Each task/tool combination is run 10 times, since coding agents are non-deterministic, about 520 runs per agent (18 tasks × 3 tools × 10 reps, minus a cap on one billable Jobs task) and ~1,000 graded runs in total. We ran the whole thing twice, on the two most popular coding agents (Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6 and OpenAI Codex with GPT-5.5).

Industry observers note that the two charts below unpack the table above. First, task success on Sonnet, the agent where curl and the SDK struggle most:.

Without the CLI, curl and the SDK trail by ten points, because on Sonnet they simply can't finish parts of the job (the writes, mostly), while the hf CLI clears them.

According to recent reports, the second image reveals token impact on GPT-5.5, broken down per task. Each bar is the curl/SDK tokens divided by the CLI's on the same task, so 2.4× means the non-hf version burned 2.4 times as many tokens to do the same thing:.

On a one-shot read (count dataset rows, batch metadata) curl and the SDK are fine, and sometimes lighter. But as tasks get more complex and involve several dependent steps, the agent has to hand-roll the entire chain of REST calls (or dig through the SDK) and the cost blows up: 2.4× to 6× the CLI's on creating a repo with a branch and tag, deleting files, copying across repos, or syncing a bucket. The hf CLI lets the agent express the task as a few higher-level commands, rather than crafting a complex workflow.

Industry observers note that hf ships a skill: a compact reference of the whole command surface that an agent loads as context. It's auto-generated from the live hf command tree, one line per command (its signature, a one-line description, and the flags that matter), grouped by resource, with a short glossary of common options. It deliberately skips the self-explanatory flags so it stays terse and light on context, and it's regenerated every release. Run hf skills preview to print it, or install it with:.

What does it buy you? Mostly, the agent stops guessing. The clearest single view is how many commands each run takes, with the skill and without:.

On both agents that's about ten commands per task down to about seven, roughly 30% fewer tool calls. That's because the agent isn't probing --help to find the right command and argument. The skill won't cut your token bill, because it prepends a fixed slice of info to the context, so tokens remain about the same or slightly tick up for the same task. The Skill won't make the CLI more reliable either, but it will help the agent spend time running your task rather than finding out how the tool works. This could be particularly helpful when using hf with local models.

We ran each task in a fresh session, so the skill pays its context cost on every task. In a real multi-task session that cost amortizes (the agent learns the command surface once), so the token picture likely improves there; we didn't measure that case.

In a recent development, we benchmarked all this because we think it matters. Agents are becoming real owners of the Hub: they train models, build and clean datasets, and ship demos as Spaces, almost always on behalf of a person. TSMC gives a sneap peak at AI Design Kit: Agentic AI with foundry expertise

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1182 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware
